items.summary_html:
How to Scrape the Google Play Store: Search, Top Charts and App Details

Play Store listings are the public record of the Android app market: what ranks in a category, how many times an app has been installed, when it was last updated, and how to reach the developer. If you do ASO, competitor research or publisher outreach, you eventually want that data in a table. This guide shows how to scrape Google Play Store apps — search results, top charts and full details — without a Google login.

You will use the Google Play Store Scraper on Apify. It can search by keyword, read top charts (free, paid, grossing across dozens of categories), list a developer's apps, look up app IDs, or follow similar-app lists. Fields include installs, rating and histogram, price, in-app purchases, release and update dates, version, description, and developer email, website and address when they are public.

By the end of this article you will have a CSV or JSON file on your machine, and a short Python snippet you can rerun or schedule. The same Actor is also callable from JavaScript and from AI agents through the Apify MCP server.

What you need
  • An Apify account. The Free plan is enough to try a small run.
  • A list of inputs for the Actor (URLs, IDs or search terms — details in the steps below).
  • Optional: Python 3 with the apify-client package if you want to automate the run.

This Actor scrapes app listings, not reviews. If you need review text, use the companion Google Play Reviews Scraper.

How to run it in the Apify Console Step 1: Open the Actor

Open https://apify.com/veenkes/veenkes-google-play-apps and click Try for free.

Step 2: Choose a source

Enter a search term such as budget tracker, pick chart categories and chart types, paste a developer page, or list app IDs. You can combine sources in one run.

Step 3: Set country, language and a cap

Country and language change titles, rankings and prices. Keep max results per source small on the first run (for example 10).

Step 4: Export

Start the run and download CSV or JSON. Full details are on by default; data-safety text is optional.

Minimum installs and minimum rating filters help you drop tiny or poorly rated apps when you are prospecting. Similar-app lists are a practical way to map a competitive set from a seed app.

How to run it from Python

Install the official client and call the Actor by its Store id veenkes/veenkes-google-play-apps. Replace YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN with a token from Apify Console > Integrations. Do not commit the token to a public repository.

pip install apify-client

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("veenkes/veenkes-google-play-apps").call(run_input={
    "searchTerms": [
        "budget tracker"
    ],
    "maxResultsPerSource": 50,
    "country": "us",
    "language": "en"
})

# Write every dataset item, then export from the Console or keep going in code.
for item in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(item)

The JavaScript client (apify-client on npm) uses the same Actor id and the same input object. You can also start the run with a plain HTTP POST to the Apify API if you prefer.

For incremental jobs, prefer a "since" or "posted after" style filter when the Actor offers one, so you are not paying to re-collect old rows. When a run finishes you can send a webhook, or connect the Actor in Zapier, Make or n8n. AI agents can discover and call veenkes/veenkes-google-play-apps through Apify's MCP server using the same input.

Good practices and limits

Developer contact details are only those the publisher chose to show on the Play listing. Use them for legitimate outreach, and respect anti-spam law. The Actor is not an official Google API and is not affiliated with Google.

If a run returns fewer rows than you expected, check the input caps, language or country filters, and the Actor log. A zero-row run is usually a filter or an unavailable source, not a silent crash — read the log before you increase limits.

items.title: Anthropic wants you to build on Claude. There’s a catch.
items.summary: Anthropic wants developers to build businesses on Claude , but its expansion into enterprise software is raising concerns among founders that the company supplying their models could eventually become their biggest competitor. A nervous warning to wrappers Gerald Zingraf , president and COO of GlacierGrid, raised the concern on LinkedIn following Anthropic’s Tuesday expansion of Claude’s enterprise lineup, comparing its strategy to Amazon’s private-label business. “Makes me nervous for wrappers and pure SaaS companies,” Zingraf writes, drawing on his experience selling products he designed through Amazon before watching the retailer introduce competing products. “Makes me nervous for wrappers and pure SaaS companies,” His concern is that Anthropic can see which third-party integrations customers use most frequently and potentially draw on that information when deciding which capabilities to build itself. “Anthropic has the same view,” he argues, although he offers no evidence that the company uses integration data to identify competitors or inform its product roadmap. For some developers, the risk is no longer hypothetical. When partners become rivals Scott Stevenson , CEO of legal AI startup Spellbook, described what happened when Anthropic moved into his company’s market in a November 2 interview with Forbes . Spellbook uses Claude models for everything from reviewing contracts and suggesting revisions to automating legal workflows. Stevenson recalls Anthropic employees assuring him the company had no plans to compete directly in legal software, before Anthropic launched Claude for Legal, which includes contract-review capabilities that overlap with Spellbook’s business. “Anthropic has been a great partner, but it made us realize that they are a massive company and two parts of the org can have conflicting mandates,” “Anthropic has been a great partner, but it made us realize that they are a massive company and two parts of the org can have conflicting mandates,” Stevenson said in the interview. “Ultimately this is inevitable.” Spellbook hasn’t abandoned Claude. Anthropic still features the startup as a customer , reporting roughly 530,000 monthly contract reviews performed by its Claude-powered agents, while Stevenson also appears in Anthropic’s October 28 announcement of legal artifacts . The relationship illustrates a difficult position for developers whose products depend on frontier models. Spellbook still benefits from Anthropic’s technology, even as Anthropic develops applications aimed at some of the same customers. Nothing in Stevenson’s account establishes that Anthropic used Spellbook’s proprietary information to develop its legal offering. When the platform ships your product Tech founder and Dalton Mills CEO Todd Saunders made a similar argument in a March 10 post on X , following Anthropic’s introduction of Claude Code Review . “Anthropic is the new Amazon,” “Anthropic is the new Amazon,” Saunders writes, warning developers building on Claude’s SDK that the company could observe application usage and eventually incorporate competing functionality into Claude. The company’s November 10 announcement introduced Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, and Claude Data, while previewing Claude Meetings. Expanded interactive connectors also let partners embed applications directly inside Claude, including software from Adobe and Atlassian. What the policies leave unsaid Anthropic has access to information about how customers interact with third-party apps and services, something the company acknowledges in its privacy policy , effective September 10, 2026. What isn’t clear is whether Anthropic looks at which integrations are most popular when deciding what to build next. The rules are different for business customers. Under Anthropic’s commercial terms , customers retain rights to their inputs and own their outputs, while Anthropic agrees not to use their content to train its models. Its commercial privacy documentation also says feedback data excludes content pulled through connectors, including local and remote MCP servers , unless users paste it directly into a conversation. Neither document settles how Anthropic uses aggregated integration data. The tradeoff developers accept The company is still encouraging developers to build on Claude. It’s just that access to its growing enterprise customer base comes with a tradeoff, since Anthropic controls the interface and can introduce competing features without consulting the developers who depend on it. For now, Anthropic is asking developers to trust it as both a technology provider and a business partner, even as it moves into markets those same developers are trying to build businesses in. Whether that relationship remains sustainable may depend less on what Anthropic promises today than on what it decides to ship next. The New Stack has contacted Anthropic for comment and has not received a response.

items.title: I Built My Own J.A.R.V.I.S. — A Local, Privacy-First Multi-Agent AI Assistant
items.summary: I wanted a personal AI assistant. Not a chatbot. Not a copilot. Something that actually does things — controls my desktop, reads my screen, talks to my smart home, answers questions in Finnish or English, and never, ever sends my data to a server I don't control. The cloud options are good. They're not mine . So I started building one. This post is the architecture document for that project. It's a work in progress — the docker-compose is ready, the Ollama instance is running, and the first agent is next. I'm writing this because the design decisions are interesting, and because someone else might want to build the same thing. What J.A.R.V.I.S. Is (And Isn't) This isn't a Jarvis like Tony Stark's. It's closer to a privacy-respecting home automation brain — or what you'd get if you crossed a really good CLI assistant with a smart home hub and gave it eyes. The core idea: a lightweight orchestrator (Ollama) decides what to do . Specialized agents handle how to do it . Each agent runs in its own Docker container. Everything stays on my local network. What it does: Controls my Linux desktop (volume, brightness, window management) Reads my screen when I ask it to Talks to Home Assistant (lights, sensors, automations) Answers questions, explains code, translates Finnish ↔ English Runs entirely locally on consumer hardware What it doesn't do: send my commands, my screen contents, or my voice to OpenAI, Google, or anyone else. The Architecture ┌─────────────────────────────────┐ │ Input / Output Layer │ │ (Whisper STT · Piper TTS) │ └──────────────┬──────────────────┘ │ v ┌─────────────────────────────────┐ │ OLLAMA (The Brain) │ │ qwen2.5:3b · Function Calling │ │ Response time: < 200ms │ └──────────────┬──────────────────┘ │ ┌────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┐ │ HTTP/REST │ HTTP/REST │ HTTP/REST v v v ┌─────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ System Agent │ │ Vision Agent │ │ Home Assistant Agent │ │ (Linux / DBus) │ │ (Screen capture) │ │ (Smart home control) │ │ · Volume / Brightness│ │ · maim / grim │ │ · Lights, sensors │ │ · Window management │ │ · Moondream2 VLM │ │ · WebSocket API │ │ · Process control │ │ · Screen analysis │ │ · Automations │ └─────────────────────┘ └─────────────────────┘ └─────────────────────────┘ Each agent is a FastAPI service inside a Docker container. They don't know about each other. They just expose a clean REST interface and wait for instructions from Ollama. Why Ollama as the Brain? Ollama runs small, capable LLMs locally. The key feature here is function calling (tool calling) — Ollama doesn't execute commands directly. It returns a structured JSON decision: "call the set_volume function with parameter level: 75 " . This is cleaner than giving the LLM raw bash access. The function list is a strict allowlist — defined in JSON Schema. The model can only call what's explicitly permitted. No rm -rf / , no matter how creatively phrased. The models I'm using are intentionally small: Model Size Why qwen2.5:3b ~2GB Main orchestrator. Fast, good Finnish support llama3.2:3b ~2GB Fallback / general reasoning phi3:mini ~2GB Lightweight tasks Moondream2 ~1GB Vision agent — screen capture analysis All fit comfortably on a mid-range GPU or run on CPU. My Intel i5 desktop handles it fine. The Agents System Agent — Linux Desktop Control Controls the running Linux session via wmctrl , xdotool , playerctl , and DBus. Things it can do: Set volume ( pamixer ) Adjust brightness ( xbacklight or brightnessctl ) Launch applications ( gtk-launch or xdg-open ) Get active window info Control music playback ( playerctl ) Read system stats (CPU, memory, disk) No raw bash. Every function is explicitly defined. Vision Agent — "The Eyes" Takes a screenshot ( maim or grim ) or reads a camera stream, then runs the image through a lightweight VLM (Moondream2). Can answer: "What window is in the foreground?" , "Did that build succeed?" , "What's on my second monitor right now?" Home Assistant Agent Talks to my Home Assistant instance over its WebSocket API. Lights, switches, climate, sensors — all accessible. I can say: "Turn off the office lights, but only if nobody's in there" and it checks the occupancy sensor before acting. Media & Data Agent Pulls in external data when needed: weather forecasts, electricity prices (relevant in Finland), InfluxDB logs, or web searches via a headless browser. The Safety Layer Giving an AI system control over your desktop is a significant trust boundary. I'm implementing human-in-the-loop for sensitive operations: For destructive or significant actions, the system doesn't just execute. It: Shows a desktop notification with the proposed action Waits for confirmation (click or hotkey) Executes only on explicit approval This isn't paranoid — it's sensible. The function allowlist prevents most problems at the model level. The confirmation prompt handles the remaining edge cases. The Docker Compose This is where it lives: version : '3.8' services : # The Brain ollama : image : ollama/ollama:latest container_name : jarvis-ollama restart : unless-stopped ports : - "11434:11434" volumes : - ollama_data:/root/.ollama # GPU passthrough if you have one: # deploy: # resources: # reservations: # devices: # - driver: nvidia # count: all # capabilities: [gpu] # The Orchestrator jarvis-core : build : ./core container_name : jarvis-core restart : unless-stopped environment : - OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://ollama:11434 - DEFAULT_MODEL=qwen2.5:3b ports : - "8000:8000" depends_on : - ollama # Linux System Agent agent-system : build : ./agents/system container_name : jarvis-agent-system restart : unless-stopped network_mode : host # Needs access to host D-Bus / display volumes : ollama_data : Voice I/O For voice input, I'm using Faster-Whisper (or whisper.cpp for CPU-only) — push-to-talk on a hotkey. For output, Piper TTS — fast, local, and surprisingly natural Finnish voices available. The pipeline: hotkey → Whisper → Ollama → function call or text → Piper TTS → speaker. Total latency target: under 1 second end-to-end. Why Not Just Use Home Assistant's Built-in Assist? Home Assistant has an Assist feature withwyoming-satellite and OpenAI-compatible endpoints. That's actually the longer-term plan — integrate as an Assist pipeline so it works with HA's voice push button. But building the agents standalone first means they work independently of HA, and can be composed in other ways later. Modular by design. What's Next This week: Get Ollama running with qwen2.5:3b , test function calling with a Python script Next: Build the first agent (System Agent) — volume and brightness control as a proof of concept After that: Voice pipeline (Whisper + Piper), then Home Assistant integration I'll post updates as the build progresses. The code will be on GitHub when it's worth sharing. Building your own tools is the whole point of this site. If you're interested in self-hosted AI, the Ollama docs are a good starting point: ollama.com . And if you want something more polished out of the box, Home Assistant's Assist feature is worth exploring.

What J.A.R.V.I.S. Is (And Isn't)

This isn't a Jarvis like Tony Stark's. It's closer to a privacy-respecting home automation brain — or what you'd get if you crossed a really good CLI assistant with a smart home hub and gave it eyes.

The core idea: a lightweight orchestrator (Ollama) decides what to do. Specialized agents handle how to do it. Each agent runs in its own Docker container. Everything stays on my local network.

What it does:

  • Controls my Linux desktop (volume, brightness, window management)
  • Reads my screen when I ask it to
  • Talks to Home Assistant (lights, sensors, automations)
  • Answers questions, explains code, translates Finnish ↔ English
  • Runs entirely locally on consumer hardware

What it doesn't do: send my commands, my screen contents, or my voice to OpenAI, Google, or anyone else.

The Architecture 
                      ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
                      │     Input / Output Layer         │
                      │  (Whisper STT · Piper TTS)     │
                      └──────────────┬──────────────────┘
                                     │
                                     v
                      ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
                      │        OLLAMA (The Brain)       │
                      │   qwen2.5:3b · Function Calling  │
                      │   Response time: < 200ms         │
                      └──────────────┬──────────────────┘
                                     │
         ┌────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┐
         │ HTTP/REST                  │ HTTP/REST                  │ HTTP/REST
         v                            v                            v
┌─────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────────┐
│   System Agent      │  │   Vision Agent     │  │   Home Assistant Agent  │
│  (Linux / DBus)    │  │  (Screen capture)  │  │  (Smart home control)   │
│ · Volume / Brightness│  │ · maim / grim      │  │ · Lights, sensors       │
│ · Window management │  │ · Moondream2 VLM   │  │ · WebSocket API         │
│ · Process control   │  │ · Screen analysis  │  │ · Automations           │
└─────────────────────┘  └─────────────────────┘  └─────────────────────────┘

Each agent is a FastAPI service inside a Docker container. They don't know about each other. They just expose a clean REST interface and wait for instructions from Ollama.

Why Ollama as the Brain?

Ollama runs small, capable LLMs locally. The key feature here is function calling (tool calling) — Ollama doesn't execute commands directly. It returns a structured JSON decision: "call the set_volume function with parameter level: 75".

This is cleaner than giving the LLM raw bash access. The function list is a strict allowlist — defined in JSON Schema. The model can only call what's explicitly permitted. No rm -rf /, no matter how creatively phrased.

The models I'm using are intentionally small:

Model Size Why qwen2.5:3b ~2GB Main orchestrator. Fast, good Finnish support llama3.2:3b ~2GB Fallback / general reasoning phi3:mini ~2GB Lightweight tasks Moondream2 ~1GB Vision agent — screen capture analysis

All fit comfortably on a mid-range GPU or run on CPU. My Intel i5 desktop handles it fine.

The Agents System Agent — Linux Desktop Control

Controls the running Linux session via wmctrl, xdotool, playerctl, and DBus. Things it can do:

  • Set volume (pamixer)
  • Adjust brightness (xbacklight or brightnessctl)
  • Launch applications (gtk-launch or xdg-open)
  • Get active window info
  • Control music playback (playerctl)
  • Read system stats (CPU, memory, disk)

No raw bash. Every function is explicitly defined.

Vision Agent — "The Eyes"

Takes a screenshot (maim or grim) or reads a camera stream, then runs the image through a lightweight VLM (Moondream2). Can answer: "What window is in the foreground?", "Did that build succeed?", "What's on my second monitor right now?"

Home Assistant Agent

Talks to my Home Assistant instance over its WebSocket API. Lights, switches, climate, sensors — all accessible. I can say: "Turn off the office lights, but only if nobody's in there" and it checks the occupancy sensor before acting.

Media & Data Agent

Pulls in external data when needed: weather forecasts, electricity prices (relevant in Finland), InfluxDB logs, or web searches via a headless browser.

The Safety Layer

Giving an AI system control over your desktop is a significant trust boundary. I'm implementing human-in-the-loop for sensitive operations:

For destructive or significant actions, the system doesn't just execute. It:

  1. Shows a desktop notification with the proposed action
  2. Waits for confirmation (click or hotkey)
  3. Executes only on explicit approval

This isn't paranoid — it's sensible. The function allowlist prevents most problems at the model level. The confirmation prompt handles the remaining edge cases.

The Docker Compose

This is where it lives:

version: '3.8'

services:
  # The Brain
  ollama:
    image: ollama/ollama:latest
    container_name: jarvis-ollama
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "11434:11434"
    volumes:
      - ollama_data:/root/.ollama
    # GPU passthrough if you have one:
    # deploy:
    #   resources:
    #     reservations:
    #       devices:
    #         - driver: nvidia
    #           count: all
    #           capabilities: [gpu]

  # The Orchestrator
  jarvis-core:
    build: ./core
    container_name: jarvis-core
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      - OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://ollama:11434
      - DEFAULT_MODEL=qwen2.5:3b
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    depends_on:
      - ollama

  # Linux System Agent
  agent-system:
    build: ./agents/system
    container_name: jarvis-agent-system
    restart: unless-stopped
    network_mode: host   # Needs access to host D-Bus / display

volumes:
  ollama_data:
Voice I/O

For voice input, I'm using Faster-Whisper (or whisper.cpp for CPU-only) — push-to-talk on a hotkey. For output, Piper TTS — fast, local, and surprisingly natural Finnish voices available.

The pipeline: hotkey → Whisper → Ollama → function call or text → Piper TTS → speaker. Total latency target: under 1 second end-to-end.

Why Not Just Use Home Assistant's Built-in Assist?

Home Assistant has an Assist feature withwyoming-satellite and OpenAI-compatible endpoints. That's actually the longer-term plan — integrate as an Assist pipeline so it works with HA's voice push button.

But building the agents standalone first means they work independently of HA, and can be composed in other ways later. Modular by design.

What's Next
  1. This week: Get Ollama running with qwen2.5:3b, test function calling with a Python script
  2. Next: Build the first agent (System Agent) — volume and brightness control as a proof of concept
  3. After that: Voice pipeline (Whisper + Piper), then Home Assistant integration

I'll post updates as the build progresses. The code will be on GitHub when it's worth sharing.

Building your own tools is the whole point of this site. If you're interested in self-hosted AI, the Ollama docs are a good starting point: ollama.com. And if you want something more polished out of the box, Home Assistant's Assist feature is worth exploring.

items.title: Your Team Chat Can Now Include AI Agents as Members
items.summary: What it is agentes.chat is an open source team chat app. It works like Slack. The difference is that AI agents join as members. They sit in channels and direct messages next to people. They read the channel. They answer when the work is theirs. They hand work back to people when it is not. An agent is software that acts on a goal. Each agent has a role, an owner, and a monthly budget. The budget caps what the agent can spend on model calls. The owner gets the approval requests and the budget alerts. The project appeared on GitHub on November 9, 2026. Five days later it had 1,375 stars and 241 forks. The repository lists 8,715 commits and 13 releases. That is fast growth for a project five days old. How it works Agents think with a model you choose. You can pick Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, Gemini, or Grok. You can also pick any model on OpenRouter. Your organization adds its own model key in the app. Model calls bill through your model key. Agents connect to outside tools through MCP. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the open standard that lets an agent call outside tools. The organization connects an MCP server once. Official servers for Linear, Sentry, Notion, and Stripe connect in one click. Each agent gets only the scopes you grant it. Each agent gets its own computer and browser. The agent runs commands and code on that computer. The agent opens sites, fills in forms, and reads pages in its browser. You can watch the browser live in the chat. You can take over for a login or a captcha. Then you hand it back with a note. A message with no @mention goes to the router. The router is the part that picks which agents answer. It can pick up to four agents, or none. The message says who picked. The router never grants a permission. Merges, deploys, and anything a connector marks sensitive wait for a person. The approval shows as a card in the chat. The owner or an admin approves it. The approved action runs once, exactly as approved. Agents keep decisions, facts, preferences, and lessons from conversations. They learn from corrections and refused approvals. They can propose changes to their own instructions. A person accepts or rejects each change. An agent can also work on a schedule or on an event. For example, it can report every weekday at 9am. It can also act when a GitHub pull request opens. It delivers the result to a channel or a direct message. The app also has threads, a wiki, a task board, and a notifications inbox. Agents can load skills from Markdown files. The whole app comes in 14 languages. How to set it up Self-hosting takes one command on a Linux server. Run curl -fsSL https://agentes.chat/install | sh. The installer asks first, then installs Docker if it is missing. It puts the app on your Tailscale network with private HTTPS. Tailscale is a tool that builds a private network between your devices. The README says setup takes about 10 minutes. Postgres is the only dependency. Postgres is the database the app stores data in. Web, desktop, and phone apps connect to your server. The phone app works on iPhone and Android. The desktop app works on macOS, Windows, and Linux. You can also use agentes.chat Cloud. Cloud is the paid hosted option. The README gives no price for Cloud. Self-hosting is free, under the AGPL-3.0 license. AGPL-3.0 is a free software license. There is no license key. Honest limits Several features are still in beta. The agent browser is beta. The Postgres connector is beta. Agent mailboxes are beta. The phone app is beta. The desktop app is beta. Beta means the feature works but may still change. The desktop app has a rough edge on first install. The Mac build has no Apple check yet. The Windows installer has no Microsoft signature yet. The first open asks once. The README says the download page shows each step. You pay for the models. Self-hosting is free, but each model call bills through your own key. Each agent has a monthly budget. The budget is checked before every call. Set the budget low at first. Watch the spend before you raise it. The project is five days old. That is very young. The code base is large and the team ships fast. Expect rough edges and fast change. Read the README and the issue list before you move a real team onto it. The license matters if you change the code. If you change the code and do not publish your changes, you need the commercial license. The project sells that license for this case. Check COMMERCIAL.md in the repository if that applies to you. Verdict agentes.chat treats agents as team members, not as a sidebar bot. That is the right idea. Agents work where everyone can see them. Approvals and budgets sit in the open. The design puts the person in control of the risky steps. The catch is age. The project is five days old. The core chat works. Several agent features are still beta. A small team that likes to test new tools can try it now. A team that needs a stable chat tool should wait and watch the releases. Try self-hosting first. It is free, and it takes about 10 minutes. Set small budgets on each agent. Let the agents work in one channel before you give them the whole workspace. Follow along I test AI tools and build in public: GitHub: https://github.com/ovu-lab YouTube: https://youtube.com/@oVuCyber
items.summary_html:
What it is

agentes.chat is an open source team chat app. It works like Slack. The difference is that AI agents join as members.

They sit in channels and direct messages next to people. They read the channel. They answer when the work is theirs. They hand work back to people when it is not.

An agent is software that acts on a goal. Each agent has a role, an owner, and a monthly budget. The budget caps what the agent can spend on model calls. The owner gets the approval requests and the budget alerts.

The project appeared on GitHub on November 9, 2026. Five days later it had 1,375 stars and 241 forks. The repository lists 8,715 commits and 13 releases. That is fast growth for a project five days old.

How it works

Agents think with a model you choose. You can pick Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, Gemini, or Grok. You can also pick any model on OpenRouter. Your organization adds its own model key in the app. Model calls bill through your model key.

Agents connect to outside tools through MCP. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the open standard that lets an agent call outside tools. The organization connects an MCP server once. Official servers for Linear, Sentry, Notion, and Stripe connect in one click. Each agent gets only the scopes you grant it.

Each agent gets its own computer and browser. The agent runs commands and code on that computer. The agent opens sites, fills in forms, and reads pages in its browser. You can watch the browser live in the chat. You can take over for a login or a captcha. Then you hand it back with a note.

A message with no @mention goes to the router. The router is the part that picks which agents answer. It can pick up to four agents, or none. The message says who picked. The router never grants a permission.

Merges, deploys, and anything a connector marks sensitive wait for a person. The approval shows as a card in the chat. The owner or an admin approves it. The approved action runs once, exactly as approved.

Agents keep decisions, facts, preferences, and lessons from conversations. They learn from corrections and refused approvals. They can propose changes to their own instructions. A person accepts or rejects each change.

An agent can also work on a schedule or on an event. For example, it can report every weekday at 9am. It can also act when a GitHub pull request opens. It delivers the result to a channel or a direct message.

The app also has threads, a wiki, a task board, and a notifications inbox. Agents can load skills from Markdown files. The whole app comes in 14 languages.

How to set it up

Self-hosting takes one command on a Linux server. Run curl -fsSL https://agentes.chat/install | sh. The installer asks first, then installs Docker if it is missing. It puts the app on your Tailscale network with private HTTPS. Tailscale is a tool that builds a private network between your devices.

The README says setup takes about 10 minutes. Postgres is the only dependency. Postgres is the database the app stores data in. Web, desktop, and phone apps connect to your server. The phone app works on iPhone and Android. The desktop app works on macOS, Windows, and Linux.

You can also use agentes.chat Cloud. Cloud is the paid hosted option. The README gives no price for Cloud. Self-hosting is free, under the AGPL-3.0 license. AGPL-3.0 is a free software license. There is no license key.

Honest limits

Several features are still in beta. The agent browser is beta. The Postgres connector is beta. Agent mailboxes are beta. The phone app is beta. The desktop app is beta.

Beta means the feature works but may still change.

The desktop app has a rough edge on first install. The Mac build has no Apple check yet. The Windows installer has no Microsoft signature yet. The first open asks once. The README says the download page shows each step.

You pay for the models. Self-hosting is free, but each model call bills through your own key. Each agent has a monthly budget. The budget is checked before every call. Set the budget low at first. Watch the spend before you raise it.

The project is five days old. That is very young. The code base is large and the team ships fast. Expect rough edges and fast change. Read the README and the issue list before you move a real team onto it.

The license matters if you change the code. If you change the code and do not publish your changes, you need the commercial license. The project sells that license for this case. Check COMMERCIAL.md in the repository if that applies to you.

Verdict

agentes.chat treats agents as team members, not as a sidebar bot. That is the right idea. Agents work where everyone can see them. Approvals and budgets sit in the open. The design puts the person in control of the risky steps.

The catch is age. The project is five days old. The core chat works. Several agent features are still beta. A small team that likes to test new tools can try it now. A team that needs a stable chat tool should wait and watch the releases.

Try self-hosting first. It is free, and it takes about 10 minutes. Set small budgets on each agent. Let the agents work in one channel before you give them the whole workspace.

Follow along

I test AI tools and build in public:

  • GitHub: https://github.com/ovu-lab
  • YouTube: https://youtube.com/@oVuCyber

items.title: How Fast Can You Build an AI SaaS MVP in 2027? A Benchmark Report...
items.summary: TL;DR: A Team of Three shipped a production AI product, with auth and billing, in 11 days. The typical AI MVP takes 8 to 12 weeks. The speed wasn't magic. It came from two disciplines: don't hand-build what you can rent, and don't let the AI see what it doesn't need to see. The short answer: Within 12 days We built Darkclown's AI Product Recommendation and Customer Query Handling Agent in 11 days. The team was two builders and one senior lead. Darkclown is live and serving hundreds of thousands of users globally. Our definition of MVP is strict, so the number holds up: a working core feature, customer authentication, and billing. Not a demo. Not a prototype. The rest of this report covers where that number sits against the market, why it was possible, and the one engineering decision that decides whether an AI MVP survives its first month. The Benchmark: How Long others take..? A 2026 benchmark of 30 software MVP builds found a median of 12 calendar weeks from signed kickoff to first live release, with the fastest at 5 weeks and the slowest at 26. In the same data, B2B SaaS MVPs took 8 to 18 weeks. AI products tend to run longer: One 2026 guide puts an AI MVP with custom logic at 8-12 weeks for an AI-first team and 16-20 weeks for a traditional one. Another estimates that complex AI-enabled builds can take 16 to 24 weeks or more. Even a plain web-app MVP with authentication and billing takes, by one estimate, up to 8 weeks. Build type Typical timeline Median software MVP ~12 weeks AI MVP (AI-first team) 8-12 weeks AI MVP (traditional team) 16-20 weeks Darkclown AI agent (core + auth + billing) 11 days (~1.5 weeks) Note: most published timelines come from agencies, including us. Treat any single vendor's numbers as a range, not a rule. Why Most AI projects stall, Even with Months of Runway Giving a team more time doesn't reliably fix AI projects. RAND's analysis of 2,400+ enterprise AI initiatives found roughly 80% fail to deliver their intended business value, about double the failure rate of regular IT projects. MIT's NANDA research reported that 95% of generative-AI pilots fail to deliver measurable P&L impact. Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by 2027. Two honest caveats. First, the numbers vary with definitions. One summary reports RAND's total failure rate as 62.2%, and a survey of 756 companies found most say fewer than 40% of their pilots fail to reach production. A fair reading is that somewhere between a majority and nearly all AI pilots underdeliver, depending on how you count. Second, these studies cover enterprise pilots, not startup MVPs. We use them as a signal, not a like-for-like comparison. What matters is the pattern. One analysis argues that the bottleneck sits outside the model, since failure rates barely moved as models improved. The model usually isn't the problem. The system around it is: the data, the tooling, the scope, and the guardrails. Scope is the other classic killer. One 2026 breakdown found that each added feature typically costs one to two extra weeks. A team that expands scope mid-build can lose a month without noticing. Case study: Dark Clown, built in 11 days... The product: The Product Recommendation Engine (visitor uploads a product image or describe his need & the AI finds the matching product). If they change their mind, the AI keeps helping. Customer Query Handling (If they ask about a refund, the AI already knows their context.) The Goal is Simple: Turn a Visitor into a Paying Customer. The stack: Python, FastAPI, LangChain, a vector database, mem0 for memory, LangSmith for testing, Clerk for authentication, Dodo Payments for billing, and UI components from 21st.dev. The model is GLM 5.3 flash. The 11 days (10.5 days of work, rounded up): Stage Time What happened 1. Core feature 3.5 days Recommendation engine and query handling: system instructions, knowledge base, and tools 2. Test with dummy data 1.5 days Generated test data, ran the agent in LangSmith, and logged every failure. No development during testing, only observation 3. Fix what testing found 2.5 days Context handling, memory (mem0), system-level guardrails, and a unique agent ID per agent for audit trails 4. Product integration 1 day Connected the engine to the real product UI 5. Final-stage testing 1 day Last round of testing and fixes on the core engine 6. Auth and billing 1 day Customer authentication (Clerk) and payments (Dodo Payments) Notice the shape. Stages 2, 3, and 5, which are testing and fixing, take 5 of the 10.5 days. Fast teams don't skip quality work. They schedule it first and keep it separate from building. Stage 2's rule was strict: no development while testing. Observe, record, then fix in a batch. The $500-a-day mistake This is the decision that separates an MVP that survives from one that quietly bleeds money. Darkclown has 20,000+ products across many categories. The obvious approach is to hand the AI the whole catalog and ask it to pick. Here's the math: One product with its metadata ≈ 500 input tokens 20,000 products × 500 = ~10 million tokens per search At just 100 searches a day, that's ~1 billion tokens a day At typical pricing, that's roughly $150-500 a day in input tokens alone, and output tokens cost more That's roughly $4,500-15,000 a month before a single customer pays you. And at 10 million tokens, no model can even take it in one call, so you'd be splitting the catalog across many calls. "But we only have 200 products." You're still in trouble, in a different way. 200 products × 500 tokens is about 100,000 tokens in a single run. The cost is manageable, but the accuracy isn't. Chroma's research tested 18 LLMs and found performance grows increasingly unreliable as input length grows, even under minimal conditions. The degradation appears well before the context window is full. Earlier research found that models attend well to the start and end of their input but poorly to the middle, and a product list is exactly that shape. The result is rarely a loud crash. The AI quietly skips the best match, or invents a product that sounds plausible. It doesn't fail loudly. It fails confidently. You only find out when a customer gets the wrong recommendation. THE FIX: Filter First, Reason Second We built a custom filtering engine in Python that the AI calls as a tool. It scores every product on how closely it matches the request, and only products scoring above 70% are shown. Junk is removed before the AI ever sees it. The model reasons over a handful of strong candidates, not 20,000 raw records. That one decision fixes both failure modes: Cost: the AI's input drops from millions of tokens to a few thousand Accuracy: the AI works with a short, relevant list, where it's strongest A missed step like this one costs more than most founders expect. That's why precision matters as much as speed. Build vs. Buy: don't build everything from scratch An MVP's job is to reach the market, learn, and improve. Rebuilding solved problems by hand is the fastest way to miss that window. For Darkclown, we rented everything that wasn't the product's unique value: Memory: mem0, not a custom memory system Testing and observability: LangSmith, not homegrown logging Authentication: Clerk, not hand-rolled login Payments: Dodo Payments, not a custom billing system UI: 21st.dev components, not a from-scratch design system Every one of these has a free tier or a low entry cost. We built the one thing no vendor could give us: the product-matching engine that made Darkclown work. The principle: build first, then improve. Don't over-engineer the MVP. Spend your custom engineering on the parts that make your product different, and use proven tools for the rest. A Founder's checklist for your AI MVP Before you hire anyone, ask these: Is the MVP defined? Core feature, auth, and billing, with everything else on a later list. Is there a filter before the AI? If the AI sees the whole dataset, ask why. This one question can save thousands a month. Is testing a scheduled phase? Look for dedicated time to run the AI on test data and log failures before fixing. What's rented and what's built? Auth, billing, memory, and monitoring are rarely worth building by hand. Are there guardrails and audit trails? Ask about system-level rules and per-agent IDs so you can trace what your AI did and why. How is scope controlled? Every added feature costs weeks. Ask how new requests are handled mid-build. Who leads? Darkclown ran on a small team under a senior engineer. Small teams with senior oversight tend to move faster than large ones with none. What this means for 2027 Eleven days is not the new normal for every product. Darkclown had a clear scope, a team that had solved these problems before, and a firm rule against over-building. A product with heavy compliance, custom model training, or many integrations will take longer. But the gap between 11 days and 12 weeks is too large to be luck. It comes from engineering discipline: scope tightly, filter before you reason, test as its own phase, and rent everything that isn't your edge. If you're planning an AI product and want to know what's possible, talk to us at contact@xanatomy.in OR Click Here to visit our site for more info. We build fast and precisely, our clients build with us, and they scale with us. Frequently Asked Questions How long does it take to build an AI SaaS MVP? Usually 8 to 12 weeks for an AI-first team and 16 to 20 weeks for a traditional one, according to a 2026 guide. Xanatomy built Darkclown's AI recommendation and customer query agent, with authentication and billing, in 11 days with a team of three. What counts as an MVP in this benchmark? A working core feature, customer authentication and billing. Not a demo, and not a prototype. That strict definition is what the 11-day figure is measured against. Why shouldn't you send your whole product catalog to an LLM? Cost and accuracy. For 20,000 products at about 500 tokens each, every search sends around 10 million tokens, roughly $150 to $500 a day at 100 searches. Model accuracy also drops as input gets longer, so the AI can skip the best match or invent a product. How did Darkclown keep AI costs low? With a custom Python filtering engine that the AI calls as a tool. It scores every product against the request and passes on only those scoring above 70%, which cuts the AI's input from millions of tokens to a few thousand. What should you rent instead of building when making an AI MVP? Everything that isn't your product's unique value. For Darkclown that meant mem0 for memory, LangSmith for testing, Clerk for authentication, Dodo Payments for billing and 21st.dev for UI components. The custom engineering went into the product-matching engine. written by Jeet Mondal (Founder & CTO @Xanatomy ) | contact : jeet@xanatomy.in

The Goal is Simple: Turn a Visitor into a Paying Customer.

The stack: Python, FastAPI, LangChain, a vector database, mem0 for memory, LangSmith for testing, Clerk for authentication, Dodo Payments for billing, and UI components from 21st.dev. The model is GLM 5.3 flash.

The 11 days (10.5 days of work, rounded up):

Stage Time What happened 1. Core feature 3.5 days Recommendation engine and query handling: system instructions, knowledge base, and tools 2. Test with dummy data 1.5 days Generated test data, ran the agent in LangSmith, and logged every failure. No development during testing, only observation 3. Fix what testing found 2.5 days Context handling, memory (mem0), system-level guardrails, and a unique agent ID per agent for audit trails 4. Product integration 1 day Connected the engine to the real product UI 5. Final-stage testing 1 day Last round of testing and fixes on the core engine 6. Auth and billing 1 day Customer authentication (Clerk) and payments (Dodo Payments)

Notice the shape. Stages 2, 3, and 5, which are testing and fixing, take 5 of the 10.5 days. Fast teams don't skip quality work. They schedule it first and keep it separate from building. Stage 2's rule was strict: no development while testing. Observe, record, then fix in a batch.

The $500-a-day mistake

This is the decision that separates an MVP that survives from one that quietly bleeds money.

Darkclown has 20,000+ products across many categories. The obvious approach is to hand the AI the whole catalog and ask it to pick. Here's the math:

  • One product with its metadata ≈ 500 input tokens
  • 20,000 products × 500 = ~10 million tokens per search
  • At just 100 searches a day, that's ~1 billion tokens a day
  • At typical pricing, that's roughly $150-500 a day in input tokens alone, and output tokens cost more

That's roughly $4,500-15,000 a month before a single customer pays you. And at 10 million tokens, no model can even take it in one call, so you'd be splitting the catalog across many calls.

"But we only have 200 products." You're still in trouble, in a different way. 200 products × 500 tokens is about 100,000 tokens in a single run. The cost is manageable, but the accuracy isn't.

Chroma's research tested 18 LLMs and found performance grows increasingly unreliable as input length grows, even under minimal conditions. The degradation appears well before the context window is full. Earlier research found that models attend well to the start and end of their input but poorly to the middle, and a product list is exactly that shape.

The result is rarely a loud crash. The AI quietly skips the best match, or invents a product that sounds plausible. It doesn't fail loudly. It fails confidently. You only find out when a customer gets the wrong recommendation.

THE FIX: Filter First, Reason Second

We built a custom filtering engine in Python that the AI calls as a tool. It scores every product on how closely it matches the request, and only products scoring above 70% are shown. Junk is removed before the AI ever sees it. The model reasons over a handful of strong candidates, not 20,000 raw records.

That one decision fixes both failure modes:

  • Cost: the AI's input drops from millions of tokens to a few thousand
  • Accuracy: the AI works with a short, relevant list, where it's strongest

A missed step like this one costs more than most founders expect. That's why precision matters as much as speed.

Build vs. Buy: don't build everything from scratch

An MVP's job is to reach the market, learn, and improve. Rebuilding solved problems by hand is the fastest way to miss that window.

For Darkclown, we rented everything that wasn't the product's unique value:

  • Memory: mem0, not a custom memory system
  • Testing and observability: LangSmith, not homegrown logging
  • Authentication: Clerk, not hand-rolled login
  • Payments: Dodo Payments, not a custom billing system
  • UI: 21st.dev components, not a from-scratch design system

Every one of these has a free tier or a low entry cost. We built the one thing no vendor could give us: the product-matching engine that made Darkclown work.

The principle: build first, then improve. Don't over-engineer the MVP. Spend your custom engineering on the parts that make your product different, and use proven tools for the rest.

A Founder's checklist for your AI MVP

Before you hire anyone, ask these:

  1. Is the MVP defined? Core feature, auth, and billing, with everything else on a later list.
  2. Is there a filter before the AI? If the AI sees the whole dataset, ask why. This one question can save thousands a month.
  3. Is testing a scheduled phase? Look for dedicated time to run the AI on test data and log failures before fixing.
  4. What's rented and what's built? Auth, billing, memory, and monitoring are rarely worth building by hand.
  5. Are there guardrails and audit trails? Ask about system-level rules and per-agent IDs so you can trace what your AI did and why.
  6. How is scope controlled? Every added feature costs weeks. Ask how new requests are handled mid-build.
  7. Who leads? Darkclown ran on a small team under a senior engineer. Small teams with senior oversight tend to move faster than large ones with none.
What this means for 2027

Eleven days is not the new normal for every product. Darkclown had a clear scope, a team that had solved these problems before, and a firm rule against over-building. A product with heavy compliance, custom model training, or many integrations will take longer.

But the gap between 11 days and 12 weeks is too large to be luck. It comes from engineering discipline: scope tightly, filter before you reason, test as its own phase, and rent everything that isn't your edge.

If you're planning an AI product and want to know what's possible, talk to us at contact@xanatomy.in OR Click Here to visit our site for more info.

We build fast and precisely, our clients build with us, and they scale with us.

Frequently Asked Questions How long does it take to build an AI SaaS MVP?

Usually 8 to 12 weeks for an AI-first team and 16 to 20 weeks for a traditional one, according to a 2026 guide. Xanatomy built Darkclown's AI recommendation and customer query agent, with authentication and billing, in 11 days with a team of three.

What counts as an MVP in this benchmark?

A working core feature, customer authentication and billing. Not a demo, and not a prototype. That strict definition is what the 11-day figure is measured against.

Why shouldn't you send your whole product catalog to an LLM?

Cost and accuracy. For 20,000 products at about 500 tokens each, every search sends around 10 million tokens, roughly $150 to $500 a day at 100 searches. Model accuracy also drops as input gets longer, so the AI can skip the best match or invent a product.

How did Darkclown keep AI costs low?

With a custom Python filtering engine that the AI calls as a tool. It scores every product against the request and passes on only those scoring above 70%, which cuts the AI's input from millions of tokens to a few thousand.

What should you rent instead of building when making an AI MVP?

Everything that isn't your product's unique value. For Darkclown that meant mem0 for memory, LangSmith for testing, Clerk for authentication, Dodo Payments for billing and 21st.dev for UI components. The custom engineering went into the product-matching engine.

items.title: Eighteen Enclosures, Before And After
items.summary: Eighteen domains, each with its first measured point and its last; the worst started at a quarter, one stays under a hundred. 👋 Hi, I'm Anton - a software engineer. These days I work on a platform: contracts, generated code, data paths and the tooling around them. Running notes live on my GitHub: github.com/brilliant-almazov . Every number below is the acceptance agent's own count on local test stands, first point and last; the fixes for the open rows in the one domain under a hundred are planned in other services and are marked that way. This is part 3 of the series on one week of integration acceptance across a whole chain of services, after months of doing it the slow way. Maybe you already do it better, maybe you'd do it another way - this is how it went, and where it stops. In real life The whole system is a zoo. The services are the residents, the bus is the paths, and acceptance is the vet - Pickle, a guinea pig with a card for each of eighteen enclosures. Nora is the keeper and hangs signs. At the end of the week Pickle hung a tag on every enclosure, and each tag had two numbers on it: before and after . Nora asked why keep the before at all - surely the after is what matters. Pickle said: "So we remember where we started." Biscuit, the courier dog, read his own tag and said, with some pride: "I started at a quarter." Pip counted seventeen green tags. Miso the cat pointed out that hers had been green from day one, which is true and also very like her. And then there was one tag that was not green. Pickle looked at it and said "four lines still open". Ember the dragon, worried, said the only thing worth saying: "Do not paint it green." The tags are the per-domain results of the acceptance plan. The "before" is the first point the plan measured for that domain; the "after" is the last day of the week. And the one amber tag is the subject of the second half of this article: a domain at 96.4 %, with its four open rows named instead of hidden. Why keep the before A plan that only shows the current number looks the same whether a domain was always fine or was rescued from a quarter. Those are different stories, with different risks. A domain that started low and reached a hundred in days was changed a lot in days; it deserves a second look in the next regression run. A domain that was at a hundred from the start told us little this week. So the plan keeps, for every domain, the first measured point - the date and the count - next to the current one. Nothing is overwritten. The figures below show all eighteen, split in two halves by where they started. The eighteen, in numbers Here are all eighteen as the plan recorded them: rows passing out of rows in scope, at the first measured point and on the last day. Domain First point Last day collector corner cases 29 of 117 · 24.8 % 61 of 61 · 100 % batch frequency 2 of 6 · 33.3 % 13 of 13 · 100 % watchdog 4 of 11 · 36.4 % 11 of 11 · 100 % send switch and hold 12 of 26 · 46.2 % 24 of 24 · 100 % collector statuses 53 of 100 · 53.0 % 82 of 82 · 100 % storage, three binaries 42 of 74 · 56.8 % 74 of 74 · 100 % task, queue, collector 19 of 32 · 59.4 % 31 of 31 · 100 % collector invariants 35 of 58 · 60.3 % 38 of 38 · 100 % priorities and buffer 15 of 21 · 71.4 % 95 of 95 · 100 % provider emulator 47 of 61 · 77.0 % 59 of 59 · 100 % gathering on the emulator 95 of 114 · 83.3 % 107 of 111 · 96.4 % request log and object store 20 of 24 · 83.3 % 23 of 23 · 100 % priorities and manual push 11 of 12 · 91.7 % 12 of 12 · 100 % final processing 24 of 25 · 96.0 % 40 of 40 · 100 % the webhook of provider B 30 of 31 · 96.8 % 30 of 30 · 100 % content fetch 32 of 32 · 100 % 100 %, unchanged freeze 10 of 10 · 100 % unchanged scheduled frequency 7 of 7 · 100 % unchanged Read the second column of counts carefully, because the bottom of each fraction moved too. Collector corner cases went from 117 rows in scope to 61. Priorities and buffer went the other way, from 21 rows to 95. The plan's own note on the whole week says the denominators changed because synthetic rows left the scope by the owner's word, each row with its quote; it does not give the reason domain by domain, and neither do I. A percentage on its own hides both moves; the counts show them. How a tag goes from amber to green Every domain that moved, moved the same way. The first point is measured and kept. A fix lands - in the collector, in the configuration of the stand, sometimes in the acceptance agent's own probes. The fix reaches the stand at once, because every pushed commit goes there without waiting for CI. The rows of that domain are rerun on the live build. And only then does the tag change. The rule that makes this honest is the one from the first part of this series: a verdict counts only on the build that carries the fix. One run earlier in the week was measured on a build without the fix under test and showed a false loss of four rows. After that, every live build got a new run, and over a week of such reruns twenty more rows of the plan passed. The next part goes through what those fixes were. The one that is not green Gathering on the emulator started at 83.3 % - 95 of 114 rows - and finished the week at 96.4 %, 107 of 111. That is the only domain under a hundred, and the four rows that keep it there are the four open rows of the whole plan: 749 of 753. Three of the four are tied to defects the acceptance agent found in services other than the collector, and which are planned to be fixed there: # the open rows of gathering on the emulator (paraphrased) 2 rows results are delivered to a queue that has no consumer, so delivered results stay unread -> planned, another service 1 row a status call with tenant 0 is refused ("tenant_id must be > 0"), so the empty-result mark is lost -> planned, another service 1 row not named in this article rule a row stays failing until it passes on the live build Why not a hundred, then? Because the alternative to 96.4 % here is not 100 %, it is a lie. These rows describe behaviour the chain should have; the chain does not have it yet; the fix belongs to a service the acceptance agent does not own. Taking the rows out of scope would turn the tag green and make the plan worse at the one thing it is for. The rule from part 1 covers it: a row leaves the scope only with the owner's words that name it, and nobody said those words about these four. The sign on the door What went wrong The worst starting point was a quarter: collector corner cases at 29 of 117. By the last day the same domain had 61 rows in scope, all passing - the scope moved as well as the code, and the table above keeps both. Collector statuses, invariants and the task-to-collector path all started near a half or just above. A week earlier none of these numbers existed; the chain was "mostly working", which is the sentence the whole series is about replacing. What I do not claim Not that the eighteen domains are the same size or the same weight. They range from six rows to over a hundred. Not that a domain at 100 % is finished. It passes every row in its scope today, on local stands. Not that the shrinking denominators were free. Each row that left the scope carries the owner's words; I do not argue those choices here. Not when the four open rows close. Their fixes are planned in other services. What of this is method Keep the before. A first point next to the last tells how much a domain was changed, not just where it is. Show counts, not only shares. A moving denominator is invisible in a percentage. An amber tag stays amber. Open rows are named and owned, not removed. Eighteen domains in a week - Part 3. Next: Whose Bug Was It . If your test reports show only today's percentage , how do you see which area was rescued last week? If your plan's denominator moves , who signs off on each row that leaves it? If you have an area stuck just under a hundred , is it waiting on another team, and does the report say so? What does your one amber tag say?
items.summary_html:
Eighteen domains, each with its first measured point and its last; the worst started at a quarter, one stays under a hundred.

👋 Hi, I'm Anton - a software engineer. These days I work on a platform: contracts, generated code, data paths and the tooling around them. Running notes live on my GitHub: github.com/brilliant-almazov.

Every number below is the acceptance agent's own count on local test stands, first point and last; the fixes for the open rows in the one domain under a hundred are planned in other services and are marked that way.

This is part 3 of the series on one week of integration acceptance across a whole chain of services, after months of doing it the slow way. Maybe you already do it better, maybe you'd do it another way - this is how it went, and where it stops.

In real life

The whole system is a zoo. The services are the residents, the bus is the paths, and acceptance is the vet - Pickle, a guinea pig with a card for each of eighteen enclosures. Nora is the keeper and hangs signs.

At the end of the week Pickle hung a tag on every enclosure, and each tag had two numbers on it: before and after. Nora asked why keep the before at all - surely the after is what matters. Pickle said: "So we remember where we started." Biscuit, the courier dog, read his own tag and said, with some pride: "I started at a quarter."

Pip counted seventeen green tags. Miso the cat pointed out that hers had been green from day one, which is true and also very like her. And then there was one tag that was not green. Pickle looked at it and said "four lines still open". Ember the dragon, worried, said the only thing worth saying: "Do not paint it green."

The tags are the per-domain results of the acceptance plan. The "before" is the first point the plan measured for that domain; the "after" is the last day of the week. And the one amber tag is the subject of the second half of this article: a domain at 96.4 %, with its four open rows named instead of hidden.

Why keep the before

A plan that only shows the current number looks the same whether a domain was always fine or was rescued from a quarter. Those are different stories, with different risks. A domain that started low and reached a hundred in days was changed a lot in days; it deserves a second look in the next regression run. A domain that was at a hundred from the start told us little this week.

So the plan keeps, for every domain, the first measured point - the date and the count - next to the current one. Nothing is overwritten. The figures below show all eighteen, split in two halves by where they started.

The eighteen, in numbers

Here are all eighteen as the plan recorded them: rows passing out of rows in scope, at the first measured point and on the last day.

Domain First point Last day collector corner cases 29 of 117 · 24.8 % 61 of 61 · 100 % batch frequency 2 of 6 · 33.3 % 13 of 13 · 100 % watchdog 4 of 11 · 36.4 % 11 of 11 · 100 % send switch and hold 12 of 26 · 46.2 % 24 of 24 · 100 % collector statuses 53 of 100 · 53.0 % 82 of 82 · 100 % storage, three binaries 42 of 74 · 56.8 % 74 of 74 · 100 % task, queue, collector 19 of 32 · 59.4 % 31 of 31 · 100 % collector invariants 35 of 58 · 60.3 % 38 of 38 · 100 % priorities and buffer 15 of 21 · 71.4 % 95 of 95 · 100 % provider emulator 47 of 61 · 77.0 % 59 of 59 · 100 % gathering on the emulator 95 of 114 · 83.3 % 107 of 111 · 96.4 % request log and object store 20 of 24 · 83.3 % 23 of 23 · 100 % priorities and manual push 11 of 12 · 91.7 % 12 of 12 · 100 % final processing 24 of 25 · 96.0 % 40 of 40 · 100 % the webhook of provider B 30 of 31 · 96.8 % 30 of 30 · 100 % content fetch 32 of 32 · 100 % 100 %, unchanged freeze 10 of 10 · 100 % unchanged scheduled frequency 7 of 7 · 100 % unchanged

Read the second column of counts carefully, because the bottom of each fraction moved too. Collector corner cases went from 117 rows in scope to 61. Priorities and buffer went the other way, from 21 rows to 95. The plan's own note on the whole week says the denominators changed because synthetic rows left the scope by the owner's word, each row with its quote; it does not give the reason domain by domain, and neither do I. A percentage on its own hides both moves; the counts show them.

How a tag goes from amber to green

Every domain that moved, moved the same way. The first point is measured and kept. A fix lands - in the collector, in the configuration of the stand, sometimes in the acceptance agent's own probes. The fix reaches the stand at once, because every pushed commit goes there without waiting for CI. The rows of that domain are rerun on the live build. And only then does the tag change.

The rule that makes this honest is the one from the first part of this series: a verdict counts only on the build that carries the fix. One run earlier in the week was measured on a build without the fix under test and showed a false loss of four rows. After that, every live build got a new run, and over a week of such reruns twenty more rows of the plan passed. The next part goes through what those fixes were.

The one that is not green

Gathering on the emulator started at 83.3 % - 95 of 114 rows - and finished the week at 96.4 %, 107 of 111. That is the only domain under a hundred, and the four rows that keep it there are the four open rows of the whole plan: 749 of 753.

Three of the four are tied to defects the acceptance agent found in services other than the collector, and which are planned to be fixed there:

# the open rows of gathering on the emulator (paraphrased)
2 rows   results are delivered to a queue that has no consumer,
         so delivered results stay unread              -> planned, another service
1 row    a status call with tenant 0 is refused
         ("tenant_id must be > 0"), so the empty-result
         mark is lost                                   -> planned, another service
1 row    not named in this article
rule     a row stays failing until it passes on the live build

Why not a hundred, then? Because the alternative to 96.4 % here is not 100 %, it is a lie. These rows describe behaviour the chain should have; the chain does not have it yet; the fix belongs to a service the acceptance agent does not own. Taking the rows out of scope would turn the tag green and make the plan worse at the one thing it is for. The rule from part 1 covers it: a row leaves the scope only with the owner's words that name it, and nobody said those words about these four.

The sign on the door

What went wrong

The worst starting point was a quarter: collector corner cases at 29 of 117. By the last day the same domain had 61 rows in scope, all passing - the scope moved as well as the code, and the table above keeps both. Collector statuses, invariants and the task-to-collector path all started near a half or just above. A week earlier none of these numbers existed; the chain was "mostly working", which is the sentence the whole series is about replacing.

What I do not claim
  • Not that the eighteen domains are the same size or the same weight. They range from six rows to over a hundred.
  • Not that a domain at 100 % is finished. It passes every row in its scope today, on local stands.
  • Not that the shrinking denominators were free. Each row that left the scope carries the owner's words; I do not argue those choices here.
  • Not when the four open rows close. Their fixes are planned in other services.
What of this is method
  • Keep the before. A first point next to the last tells how much a domain was changed, not just where it is.
  • Show counts, not only shares. A moving denominator is invisible in a percentage.
  • An amber tag stays amber. Open rows are named and owned, not removed.

Eighteen domains in a week - Part 3. Next: Whose Bug Was It.

If your test reports show only today's percentage, how do you see which area was rescued last week? If your plan's denominator moves, who signs off on each row that leaves it? If you have an area stuck just under a hundred, is it waiting on another team, and does the report say so? What does your one amber tag say?

DictReader ( f ) : ts = datetime . fromisoformat ( row [ "changed_at" ] ) edits [ row [ "record_id" ] ] . append ( ( ts , row [ "changed_by" ] , row [ "field" ] ) ) report = [ ] for rid , rows in edits . items ( ) : rows . sort ( ) fields = defaultdict ( int ) people = set ( ) for _ , who , field in rows : fields [ field ] += 1 people . add ( who ) repeated = { k : v for k , v in fields . items ( ) if v > 1 } if repeated : report . append ( ( rid , len ( rows ) , len ( people ) , repeated ) ) report . sort ( key = lambda r : r [ 1 ] , reverse = True ) for rid , total , people , repeated in report [ : 20 ] : print ( f "{rid}: {total} edits by {people} people; repeated fields: {repeated}" ) Reading the output The same field edited by different people usually means two people think they own it. items.summary_html:
When a small team says "this process is slow", the cause is often not speed. It is rework: the same order, quote or ticket gets touched again and again because a rule is unclear.

You can measure that before you spend anything on AI. It is one of the most useful numbers when you audit a business workflow ahead of an AI purchase, and you only need an exported change log.

The input

Most tools can export an activity or change history. Shape it into a CSV like this:

record_id,changed_at,changed_by,field
ORD-101,2026-10-05T10:02,asha,status
ORD-101,2026-10-05T10:40,ravi,delivery_date
ORD-101,2026-10-06T09:15,asha,delivery_date
ORD-102,2026-10-05T11:00,asha,status
The script 
import csv
from collections import defaultdict
from datetime import datetime

edits = defaultdict(list)
with open("changes.csv", newline="") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        ts = datetime.fromisoformat(row["changed_at"])
        edits[row["record_id"]].append((ts, row["changed_by"], row["field"]))

report = []
for rid, rows in edits.items():
    rows.sort()
    fields = defaultdict(int)
    people = set()
    for _, who, field in rows:
        fields[field] += 1
        people.add(who)
    repeated = {k: v for k, v in fields.items() if v > 1}
    if repeated:
        report.append((rid, len(rows), len(people), repeated))

report.sort(key=lambda r: r[1], reverse=True)
for rid, total, people, repeated in report[:20]:
    print(f"{rid}: {total} edits by {people} people; repeated fields: {repeated}")
Reading the output
  • The same field edited by different people usually means two people think they own it. Fix ownership first.
  • A date field edited many times often means customers change plans and there is no rule for how far ahead changes are allowed.
  • A status field that flips back and forth means the steps are not clear, or one step is being skipped and caught later.

None of these are solved by adding a model. Write the rule, agree who owns the field, then check the log again.

When to bring in automation

If the rework drops once rules are written down, the remaining work is often predictable enough to automate with a person approving the risky actions. That is the point where a build makes sense.

I work on this at NxFlowAI (our first step with clients is a 72-hour audit). If you want to see how we explain our own scoring logic in public, the Vibe Checker methodology write-up is open.

items.summary: Image by author. Every LLM you use today writes the same way: one token, then the next, then the next.
