items.summary_html:
Image by author.

Every LLM you use today writes the same way: one token, then the next, then the next. A 1,000-token answer means about 1,000 steps in a line, and step 501 cannot start until step 500 is done. Your GPU can do a lot of work in parallel, but text generation keeps it waiting in a queue. That’s a big reason long answers feel slow.

Stanford’s new Next-Concept Modeling (NCM) tries a different route. It sketches the whole answer roughly first, then adds detail level by level, like a blurry WhatsApp photo that gets sharper as it loads. On OpenWebText it writes 1,024 tokens in 32 passes instead of 1,024.

The paper headline is “31x faster”. That number is real, but most people read it wrong, and I’ll come to that.

The first half of this post explains the idea in plain words. The second half is what I actually ran on an RTX 4060 laptop GPU with Stanford’s released checkpoints: a BBC article summarized level by level, ten more articles checked against BBC’s own summaries, two inputs that broke it, a Sudoku score, and a diffusion model for comparison.

I also made a video on this, you can watch it right here:

https://medium.com/media/914efbefcc86d06ea48f4c4f116a087a/hrefTwo ways models write today

Autoregressive LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, Llama) predict one token at a time. Each new token depends on everything before it, so the steps can’t run side by side. More output means more steps, always.

Diffusion language models came in to remove that queue. Think of a fill-in-the-blanks exam paper. The model starts with the whole answer as blanks, and in every round it fills many blanks at once and fixes the ones it got wrong earlier. No waiting in line, so it can be fast: Google DeepMind’s experimental Gemini Diffusion samples at about 1,479 tokens per second.

The cost is that diffusion needs many rounds, and every round looks at the whole answer again. Cut the rounds to save time and quality drops. I show that with a real diffusion model later in this post.

NCM is a third way.

Source: Next-Concept Modeling paper (arXiv 2610.14162), Figure 2How NCM works

NCM is really two models working together.

1. The compressor. It takes a piece of text and squeezes it into a list of numbers called codes. A code is just a position in a list, like ordering by item number in a restaurant with 4,096 dishes on the menu. If token IDs feel familiar, codes are the same kind of thing: not human-readable on their own.

The key part is that the codes come in levels. The first level has only a few codes and carries the rough gist. Every level after that has more codes and stores only what the earlier levels missed. By the last level there’s enough detail to get the exact words back. This compressor is very good at its job: it rebuilds the original text exactly 98.8 to 100% of the time, depending on the task.

That’s what the “concept” in the name means. It isn’t a human idea or a sentence. It’s the information sitting in the top, coarse levels. The name sounds a little grander than the thing, and that’s fine.

The compressor: each level adds only what the levels above it missed. Image by author.

2. The writer. This is the model that generates. Like an LLM that only outputs token IDs, it only outputs codes. It writes all codes of level 1 in one go, then all codes of level 2, and so on. Inside a level nothing waits in line. The only waiting is between levels, because each level corrects the one above it.

After the last level, the compressor’s decoder turns the codes into words. That’s the first moment any text exists.

The writer on a real BBC article (my run in Step 2): one level per pass, readable text only at the end. Image by author.

So the number of passes equals the number of levels, not the number of tokens. That’s the whole source of the speed.

Passes for a 1,024-token answer. LLM and NCM numbers are from the paper (OpenWebText); the diffusion rounds are from my MDLM run. Image by author.The details that bite
  • “31x faster” is compared to diffusion models, not to ChatGPT. On XSum summarization NCM matches the strongest diffusion model’s ROUGE-L (28.0 vs 26.6) while being 31x faster. It’s one experimental fast method beating another one. There is no comparison with any production LLM.
  • A same-size LLM still writes better text. On OpenWebText the normal autoregressive model scores a generation perplexity of 35.45 against NCM’s 83.12 (lower is better). Translation too: 25.2 BLEU vs 22.6.
  • The biggest NCM trained so far is 725M parameters. Nobody knows yet whether it holds up at the size of the models we use daily.
  • No streaming. Chat apps feel fast because tokens appear as they’re written. NCM’s early levels aren’t readable words (you’ll see that below), so the user sees nothing until the last level is done.
  • Fixed depth. Even a short reply goes through every level.
What “31x faster” is actually compared against. Image by author.

Where it does look promising: it needed about 4x fewer training tokens on OpenWebText (127B vs 500B+) to get its results, and it does very well on puzzles where every part of the answer depends on every other part. More on that in Step 5.

Source: Next-Concept Modeling paper (arXiv 2610.14162), Figure 1The build

Everything below runs on Stanford’s released code and checkpoints, on an NVIDIA RTX 4060 Laptop GPU. The decoding settings are the same ones the repo’s official eval uses.

Step 0: what “cutting rounds” does to a diffusion model

Before NCM, I ran MDLM (170M parameters, trained on OpenWebText), one of the diffusion models the paper compares against. Same prompt and seed, a 1,024-token canvas, once with 48 rounds and once with only 8:

for steps in [48, 8]:
    print(f"{steps} rounds, {res['secs']} s:  {text}\n")
48 rounds, 5.38 s:  Scientists have found that Paris is receiving support from around the world in this regard.  The numbers see many lines in the fight against pollution. To see these improvements other industrial solutions will be limited
8 rounds, 1.38 s:  Scientists have found that the grasp is of, is not innate. Humans function like adults, except of the many lines, the liver sense a leak and see essential closing to get released and be gone

Neither is great writing; it’s a small model. But 48 rounds gives sentences, 8 rounds gives word salad. That’s the trade-off NCM is trying to escape: fewer rounds without falling apart.

Step 1: load the summarizer

The XSum checkpoint is trained on BBC news: give it an article, it writes a one-line summary. Loading it means loading both halves:

tk = VQVAETokenizer.from_config(cfg.tokenizer)          # the compressor (text <-> codes)
net = NextConceptTransformer(vqvae_local=tk.vqvae, config=cfg.model).cuda()  # the writer
levels = list(tk.vqvae.vq.levels)
print("codes per level:", levels)
print("passes:", len(levels), "| summary length in codes:", levels[-1])
codes per level: [4, 6, 10, 14, 20, 26, 32, 40, 48]
passes: 9 | summary length in codes: 48
writer: 88M params

Nine levels, so nine passes for the whole summary. Level 1 has 4 codes, the last level has 48.

Step 2: watch one summary sharpen, level by level

Normally you only see the final line. Here I asked the decoder to turn every level into words. The input is a BBC article about a fasting-style diet that helped the pancreas heal itself (in mice):

codes = net.generate(None, x, temperature=1.0, top_k=1, top_p=0.0, cfg_scale=0.0, cfg_null_eos=EOS)
_, z_levels = tk.vqvae.vq.idx_to_zhats(codes, return_zlevels=True)
texts = [to_text(pick_tokens(tk.vqvae.decoder(z))[0].tolist()) for z in zs]
level 1 ( 4 codes)  decades - eurozone
level 2 ( 6 codes)  habits - cancer
level 3 (10 codes)  discovered containing - cause.
level 4 (14 codes)  have that iodinere - type.
level 5 (20 codes)  have diet iodine emits theas - cause type.
level 6 (26 codes)  Scientists discovered diet that causes pancreas possibly root causes 2.
level 7 (32 codes)  Scientists discovered vegan diet reduces causes the pancre - possibly root of type diabetes.
level 8 (40 codes)  Scientists discovered a vegan diet reduces causes in the pancre - possibly cause root causes type 2 diabetes.
level 9 (48 codes)  Scientists have discovered a vegan diet that causes in the pancreas - possibly cause the causes of type 2 diabetes.

passes: 9  time: 0.30 s  article tokens: 479

Three things stand out.

Level 1 has nothing to do with the article. “Decades, eurozone” is what four coarse codes look like when you force them into words. That’s exactly why streaming doesn’t work: the early levels are not a short, rough version of the answer you could show a user.

By level 6 the topic is there: scientists, diet, pancreas, type 2. The words are still broken, but the model clearly knows what the article is about.

The final line has the gist, and the details are off. The article describes a fasting-mimicking diet that resembles a vegan diet and helped regenerate pancreas cells. NCM says “a vegan diet that causes… type 2 diabetes”. Right neighbourhood, wrong claim.

The whole thing took 9 passes and well under half a second: 0.30 s in this notebook run, and between 0.18 and 0.39 s across my other runs on the same laptop. I didn’t run an LLM on the same article, so I’m not putting a speed ratio next to that number.

Step 3: ten more articles, against BBC’s own summaries

One article is an anecdote. So I took the first ten articles of the XSum test set and printed NCM’s line next to the summary BBC actually wrote. A few of them:

[1] NCM: A man has been arrested in connection with a number of firearms ammunition and ammunition were seized in Edinburgh.
    BBC: A man has appeared in court after firearms, ammunition and cash were seized by police in Edinburgh.
[6] NCM: British declining Houvenaghel has been sacked by the British Cycling for its "systematic failings" in the sport.
    BBC: A "medal at any cost" approach created a "culture of fear" at British Cycling, says former rider Wendy Houvenaghel.
[7] NCM: A coffee coffee coach at a restaurant in the US to sell a coffee shop he owns to sell or buy off a sum.
    BBC: Have you heard the one about the computer programmer who bought a failing comedy club in Texas and turned it into a million dollar a year business?
[9] NCM: Celtic manager Brendan Rodgers says he is excited to fans to his fans as he prepare to face Queens Park Rangers on Sunday.
    BBC: Manager Brendan Rodgers is sure Celtic can exploit the wide open spaces of Hampden when they meet Rangers in Sunday's League Cup semi-final.
time per summary: 0.32-0.36 s, 9 passes each

Counting all ten by hand: 8 of 10 got the topic right (the right people, place and event). 2 of 10 were garbled (article 5, about the Essilor and Luxottica merger, came out as invented brand names; article 7 became a coffee shop). Even the good ones bend facts: Houvenaghel wasn’t sacked, and Celtic were playing Rangers, not Queens Park Rangers.

For an 88M research model that’s decent. It’s nowhere near what an LLM gives you, and the paper doesn’t claim it is.

Step 4: give it something that isn’t BBC news

Two inputs from outside its training world: a short article about Voyager 1 and the NCM paper itself.

for name in ["voyager-1-one-light-day.pdf", "ncm-paper-2610.14162.pdf"]:
voyager-1-one-light-day.pdf  (574 tokens, reads 512)
  NCM: The latest launch of space Nasa agency - Nasa's astronaut spacecraft mission - has launched its launch launch from the Nasa space astronauts astronaut - and an unmanned space mission.
ncm-paper-2610.14162.pdf  (30810 tokens, reads 512)
  NCM: acy-acy--Quible and analyticalocrographed, test, unique scenery, digital technology and tablets.

Two lessons here. It’s a specialist: a space article becomes “launch launch… astronaut astronaut”, and a research paper becomes nonsense. And it only reads the first 512 tokens. The paper is 30,810 tokens long, so the model saw the title page and part of the abstract. Easy to miss if you only look at the output.

Step 5: where it actually shines, Sudoku

In Sudoku you can’t fill row 1 and move on. Every number depends on numbers elsewhere on the board, which is bad news for a model that writes left to right. NCM looks at the whole board at every level.

I ran the released 25M Sudoku checkpoint on all 2,000 hard test boards:

merged 1 shards -> 2000 sudoku-hard outputs
 solved %  solved  cell %  valid %
    86.15 1723/2000   98.35    86.15

1,723 of 2,000 hard boards solved, 86.15%, which matches the paper’s 86.1%. A same-size autoregressive model solves about 1% in the paper’s table, and the strongest non-autoregressive baseline in the table 81.3%.

Source: Next-Concept Modeling paper (arXiv 2610.14162), Table 3What to do with this today

1. Keep building on LLMs. NCM is a research model, not a product. The checkpoints are small, task-specific and clearly behind same-size LLMs on open text and translation.

2. Read speed claims with “faster than what?” The 31x is against diffusion models, on one task, on one H100. Speed headlines in this space almost always need that question.

3. Watch it for “whole answer at once” problems. Puzzles, constraint-style outputs and tasks where every part depends on every other part are where coarse-to-fine already wins.

4. Watch the training-cost angle. Getting results with about 4x fewer training tokens matters as good data gets more expensive.

The short version
  • NCM compresses text into levels of codes, writes each level in one parallel pass, and decodes words only at the end.
  • Passes = levels, so 1,024 tokens take 32 passes instead of 1,024.
  • “31x faster” is vs diffusion models, not vs ChatGPT or any production LLM.
  • On my laptop: 9 passes, under half a second per BBC summary; the gist was right in 8 of 10, details often wrong.
  • No streaming: early levels aren’t readable text.
  • It shines on Sudoku (86% of hard boards) and trails same-size LLMs on open text.

Diffusion language models showed that writing doesn’t have to happen in a queue. NCM borrows its level-by-level idea from VAR, which did coarse-to-fine for images, and brings it to text. It isn’t the model you ship next sprint, but it’s a clear sign that not every piece of writing has to happen one token at a time. Credit to the Hazy Research and Scaling Intelligence teams at Stanford, with Together AI, for releasing the code and checkpoints so anyone can check these numbers on their own GPU.

Video version: watch the NCM video on YouTube

The full code

Everything above comes from one notebook. Here is all of it, so you can run it on your own GPU. It needs a CUDA GPU; the XSum summarizer fits easily in 8 GB.

Setup, once. Clone the repo, install it, and download the released checkpoints and test data:

git clone https://github.com/HazyResearch/ncm.git repo
pip install -r repo/requirements.txt pypdf
cd repo
hf download hazyresearch/ncm-checkpoints --local-dir artifacts
hf download hazyresearch/ncm-datasets --repo-type dataset --local-dir data
python evaluate.py --config config/eval/sudoku-hard.yaml --checkpoint-dir artifacts/sudoku/hard --data-dir data/sudoku/hard --out eval/sudoku-hard-full

The last command runs the Sudoku checkpoint on all 2,000 hard boards and saves the generations; the notebook only re-scores them. Then point NCM_HOME at the folder that holds repo/, and put any PDFs you want summarized in demo/docs/ (I saved a BBC article as bbc-article.pdf).

Settings and paths

import os, sys, time, json, pickle, re, contextlib, io, warnings, subprocess
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
PROJ = os.environ["NCM_HOME"]   # folder with repo/ (git clone of HazyResearch/ncm), hf-cache/ and demo/docs/
os.environ["HF_HOME"] = os.path.join(PROJ, "hf-cache")
os.environ["TRANSFORMERS_VERBOSITY"] = "error"
REPO = os.path.join(PROJ, "repo")
sys.path.insert(0, REPO); os.chdir(REPO)

Load the XSum summarizer

import torch
print(torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))
from omegaconf import OmegaConf
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
from models.next_concept import NextConceptTransformer
from tokenization.vqvae_tokenizer import VQVAETokenizer
 
cfg = OmegaConf.load("config/eval/xsum.yaml")
cfg.tokenizer.vqvae.checkpoint_path = "artifacts/xsum/tokenizer.pt"
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()):
    tk = VQVAETokenizer.from_config(cfg.tokenizer)          # the compressor (text <-> codes)
    tk.vqvae = tk.vqvae.cuda().eval()
    net = NextConceptTransformer(vqvae_local=tk.vqvae, config=cfg.model).cuda()  # the writer
sd = torch.load("artifacts/xsum/generator.pt", map_location="cpu", weights_only=False)
net.load_state_dict(sd["model"], strict=True); net.eval()
 
levels = list(tk.vqvae.vq.levels)
print("codes per level:", levels)
print("passes:", len(levels), "| summary length in codes:", levels[-1])
print(f"writer: {sum(p.numel() for p in net.parameters())/1e6:.0f}M params")

Decoding helpers (same settings as the repo’s official eval)

# helpers: the same decoding settings as the repo's official eval (scripts/eval_shard.py)
G = cfg.generation
P = int(cfg.model.prefix_len)
EOS, PAD = tk.pre_tokenizer.eos_token_id, tk.pre_tokenizer.pad_token_id
src_tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2")   # only to tokenize the article
ALLOW = sd["inference"]["token_unigram"].double().cuda()
freq, mu = float(G.frequency_penalty), float(G.frequency_deficit)
ADJ = [float(v) for v in str(G.adjacency_penalty).split(",")]
 
def pick_tokens(logits):
    B, T, V = logits.shape
    lg = logits.double(); allow = (ALLOW[:V] * T)[None, :]
    al, aw, ad = ADJ[0], int(ADJ[1]), ADJ[2]
    cnt = torch.zeros(B, V, dtype=torch.float64, device=lg.device)
    out = torch.empty(B, T, dtype=torch.long, device=lg.device); hist = []
    for t in range(T):
        step = lg[:, t, :].clone()
        step -= freq * (cnt - allow).clamp_min(0.0)
        step += mu * ((T - t) / T) * (allow - cnt).clamp_min(0.0)
        for j, h in enumerate(reversed(hist[-aw:])):
            step.scatter_add_(1, h[:, None], torch.full((B, 1), -al * ad ** j, dtype=torch.float64, device=lg.device))
        p = step.argmax(-1); out[:, t] = p; hist.append(p)
        cnt.scatter_add_(1, p[:, None], torch.ones(B, 1, dtype=torch.float64, device=lg.device))
    return out
 
def to_text(ids):
    ids = list(ids)
    if EOS in ids: ids = ids[:ids.index(EOS)]
    return tk.pre_tokenizer.decode([t for t in ids if t not in (EOS, PAD)], skip_special_tokens=True).strip()

Summarize a PDF and decode every level

@torch.no_grad()
def summarize(article, every_level=False):
    ids = src_tok(article)["input_ids"]
    x = torch.tensor([(ids[:P] + [PAD] * P)[:P]], device="cuda")   # the model reads the first 512 tokens
    torch.cuda.synchronize(); t0 = time.perf_counter()
    codes = net.generate(None, x, temperature=1.0, top_k=1, top_p=0.0, cfg_scale=0.0, cfg_null_eos=EOS)
    torch.cuda.synchronize(); secs = time.perf_counter() - t0
    _, z_levels = tk.vqvae.vq.idx_to_zhats(codes, return_zlevels=True)
    zs = z_levels if every_level else z_levels[-1:]
    texts = [to_text(pick_tokens(tk.vqvae.decoder(z))[0].tolist()) for z in zs]
    return texts, secs, len(ids)
 
from pypdf import PdfReader
def read_pdf(path):
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", " ".join(p.extract_text() or "" for p in PdfReader(path).pages)).strip()
 
article = read_pdf(os.path.join(PROJ, "demo", "docs", "bbc-article.pdf"))
summarize(article)  # warm-up
texts, secs, n_tok = summarize(article, every_level=True)
for k, (n, t) in enumerate(zip(levels, texts), 1):
    print(f"level {k} ({n:2d} codes)  {t}")
print(f"\npasses: {len(levels)}  time: {secs:.2f} s  article tokens: {n_tok}")

Ten XSum test articles against BBC’s own summaries

passages = pickle.load(open("data/xsum/passages.pickle", "rb"))
refs = pickle.load(open("data/xsum/reference_summaries.pickle", "rb"))
 
def article_text(item):
    if isinstance(item, str): return item
    art = list(item[:P]); art = art[:art.index(PAD)] if PAD in art else art
    return src_tok.decode(art)
 
def ref_text(r):
    return r if isinstance(r, str) else to_text(r)
 
times = []
for i in range(10):
    (s,), secs, _ = summarize(article_text(passages[i])); times.append(secs)
    print(f"[{i}] NCM: {s}\n    BBC: {ref_text(refs[i])}\n")
print(f"time per summary: {min(times):.2f}-{max(times):.2f} s, {len(levels)} passes each")

Inputs that aren’t BBC news

for name in ["voyager-1-one-light-day.pdf", "ncm-paper-2610.14162.pdf"]:
    (s,), secs, n_tok = summarize(read_pdf(os.path.join(PROJ, "demo", "docs", name)))
    print(f"{name}  ({n_tok} tokens, reads {min(n_tok, P)})\n  NCM: {s}\n")

Score the Sudoku run

r = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "scripts/eval_merge.py", "--config", "config/eval/sudoku-hard.yaml",
                    "--glob", "eval/sudoku-hard-full/shard_*.pkl"], capture_output=True, text=True, encoding="utf-8", env={**os.environ, "PYTHONIOENCODING": "utf-8"})
print(r.stdout.strip()[-600:])

The diffusion comparison in Step 0 uses the sampler from the MDLM repo with the kuleshov-group/mdlm-owt weights, so it isn’t repeated here.

Sources

  • Paper: Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation (arXiv 2610.14162)
  • Blog: Hazy Research, 12 Oct 2026
  • Project page: Scaling Intelligence, Stanford
  • Code: HazyResearch/ncm (MIT)
  • Diffusion baseline: MDLM, kuleshov-group/mdlm-owt

items.title: I was flying when the FAA grounded all flights. Everything was chaos, and I got stuck on the tarmac for hours.
items.summary: I got stuck in Miami airport amid the FAA grounding chaos. Gentry Hale I was at 35,000 feet when my captain said an air traffic control issue grounded flights. Several passengers and I were worried it was related to cybersecurity or AI. We landed in Miami but couldn't deplane for hours, and I ended up paying $600 for a hotel room. I spend a huge portion of my life on airplanes as a frequent traveler and journalist, so I'm used to the usual delays , missed connections, and last-minute flight changes that come with commercial air travel. But I have never experienced anything like the crippling air traffic control outage on Friday, November 13, that displaced thousands of passengers and crews and canceled over 12,500 flights. I had been at cruising altitude, flying back from a vacation in the Caribbean island of Curaçao toward my home in Salt Lake City, when the Federal Aviation Administration halted departing flights across the entire US. Before Friday, the FAA had only ordered a nationwide ground stop twice in modern history: once in January 2023, following a failure of a key pilot-alert system , and after the September 11 terrorist attacks. Given the rare track record, I wasn't thrilled to find myself midair when I heard the news. What should have been a quick two-hour layover in Miami unraveled into a chaotic overnight delay, with hours spent on a gridlocked tarmac as passengers raced for vanishing hotel rooms and flight inventory. We learned about the nationwide shutdown at 35,000 feet Before boarding in Curaçao, my flight had already been delayed by about 30 minutes, and I jokingly texted a friend that it better not be delayed any further because I refused to spend the night in Miami. I should have knocked on wood, because about 40 minutes out from landing, the cabin speakers crackled to life. The captain said he was sure some of us had WiFi and had seen messages about a nationwide ground stop , then confirmed it was true. Trying to keep chill while we sat on the plane for hours and sparred over hotels and new flights. Gentry Hale Hushed conversations throughout the cabin ensued, and I looked to my neighbor to check the news since I didn't have WiFi myself. This was the first time in a long time I was nervous on a plane. I read that officials said a telecommunications issue was affecting Air Route Traffic Control Centers, the regional facilities responsible for directing and guiding aircraft at higher altitudes between airports. I also read that officials did not believe the disruption was the result of AI or a cyberattack — something that I'd been wondering about. For some reason, that scared me even more. What was it, then? My next thought: If air traffic control has a communications failure, how are we going to land? I was relieved when the captain informed us that planes already in the sky, including mine, were cleared to land at their destinations, and that the order had frozen departures. Although I didn't know it at the time, officials later said that pilots, air traffic controllers , and dispatchers have various backup methods and digital tools for communication, and pilots are trained to navigate and land without comms. Still, the timing of the halt was unnerving, coming after the widespread Microsoft cloud disruptions the day before and the National Weather Service data hiccups earlier Friday. Landing in Miami was only the beginning of the chaos When our wheels finally touched down at Miami International Airport, I checked my phone and saw that the captain had kept us informed to the best of his knowledge; no further news had been released, but at least we had been able to land. But now we were stuck on the plane. Because inbound flights were still arriving while outbound planes sat at their gates, the airport's ramp space was gridlocked. With nowhere to park and unload passengers, our plane sat idling on the tarmac for the next two hours. There were too many planes for the number of gates at Miami airport during Friday's FAA outage. Giorgio VIERA / AFP via Getty Images Around 7:30 p.m., about an hour after landing, passengers around me began murmuring that rebooking options were finally appearing in the American Airlines app. When I refreshed my screen, every option required flying out the following evening on grueling 12- to 14-hour itineraries with multiple layovers. Unwilling to spend a half-day hopping around the US from Florida to Utah, I accepted that I would spend the full weekend in Miami. But before I booked something for Sunday or Monday, I refreshed the list one more time. Buried at the very bottom was a single direct flight departing at 7:45 p.m. on Saturday night. I booked it immediately, snagging one of the final three open seats — and crossed my fingers that the snowball effect would slow by then and my flight would actually take off. Hotel rooms disappeared almost as quickly as flights were canceled Still trapped on the tarmac, another problem emerged: finding a place to sleep. Around me, passengers were frantically refreshing booking apps as airport hotels sold out in real time. I barely managed to book a room at the Hyde Hotel in Midtown Miami, about 15 minutes away. It wasn't cheap — $621 for the night, to be exact. The airline wasn't required to help me out in the uncontrollable flight disruption, and I'm not sure my travel insurance will reimburse me, so I've accepted I may eat that money. The passenger pick-up area was swarming with cars as people dispersed to their hotels. Gentry Hale When I finally deplaned around 8 p.m., cleared customs, and arrived at the lobby, the front desk agent told me the hotel had surged from about 40% full at 5 p.m. local time to sold out by 9 p.m. — filled to capacity by displaced flyers in under four hours. Even in a major hospitality hub like Miami, inventory evaporates quickly when thousands of stranded travelers are competing for the same beds. Despite the pain in my wallet, knowing I wasn't spending the night on an airport terminal floor felt like I had won the lottery. I was reminded that no matter how much I prepare, I'm at the whim of the air system Once I reached my hotel, I refreshed my news app to see that the FAA had lifted the nationwide ground stop, allowing departures to slowly resume, but the effects had already disrupted the whole country. Air travel is notorious for its snowball effect: a single thunderstorm in Dallas or Atlanta can trigger cascading delays thousands of miles away as planes and crews get displaced . A simultaneous shutdown of the entire US airspace system was a whole other beast. A friend scheduled to fly to Las Vegas had his trip canceled before he had even left for the airport. But another friend flying from Panama to Denver ended up stranded in Houston — her second overnight stall in 48 hours after weather disruptions the day before. I'm lucky I got a hotel; rooms were getting scarce by the time I booked. Joe Raedle/Getty Images For someone who flies regularly, the unexpected chaos was a reality check. I can build buffer time into my schedule, book early-morning departures and pack carry-on only, but none of that will protect me when a backbone of the national airspace system goes offline. Lying in my hotel room in Miami, I'll admit I felt a flicker of hesitation about stepping back onto a plane Saturday evening. The thought of pilots losing clear communication with the ground is terrifying. But that fear is merely one of the trade-offs we accept every time we board a flight to see the world — and I know the pilots are highly trained to deal with emergencies like lost comms. Read the original article on Business Insider

I spend a huge portion of my life on airplanes as a frequent traveler and journalist, so I'm used to the usual delays, missed connections, and last-minute flight changes that come with commercial air travel.

But I have never experienced anything like the crippling air traffic control outage on Friday, November 13, that displaced thousands of passengers and crews and canceled over 12,500 flights.

I had been at cruising altitude, flying back from a vacation in the Caribbean island of Curaçao toward my home in Salt Lake City, when the Federal Aviation Administration halted departing flights across the entire US.

Before Friday, the FAA had only ordered a nationwide ground stop twice in modern history: once in January 2023, following a failure of a key pilot-alert system, and after the September 11 terrorist attacks.

Given the rare track record, I wasn't thrilled to find myself midair when I heard the news.

What should have been a quick two-hour layover in Miami unraveled into a chaotic overnight delay, with hours spent on a gridlocked tarmac as passengers raced for vanishing hotel rooms and flight inventory.

We learned about the nationwide shutdown at 35,000 feet

Before boarding in Curaçao, my flight had already been delayed by about 30 minutes, and I jokingly texted a friend that it better not be delayed any further because I refused to spend the night in Miami.

I should have knocked on wood, because about 40 minutes out from landing, the cabin speakers crackled to life.

The captain said he was sure some of us had WiFi and had seen messages about a nationwide ground stop, then confirmed it was true.

Trying to keep chill while we sat on the plane for hours and sparred over hotels and new flights.

Gentry Hale

Hushed conversations throughout the cabin ensued, and I looked to my neighbor to check the news since I didn't have WiFi myself. This was the first time in a long time I was nervous on a plane.

I read that officials said a telecommunications issue was affecting Air Route Traffic Control Centers, the regional facilities responsible for directing and guiding aircraft at higher altitudes between airports.

I also read that officials did not believe the disruption was the result of AI or a cyberattack — something that I'd been wondering about. For some reason, that scared me even more. What was it, then?

My next thought: If air traffic control has a communications failure, how are we going to land?

I was relieved when the captain informed us that planes already in the sky, including mine, were cleared to land at their destinations, and that the order had frozen departures.

Although I didn't know it at the time, officials later said that pilots, air traffic controllers, and dispatchers have various backup methods and digital tools for communication, and pilots are trained to navigate and land without comms.

Still, the timing of the halt was unnerving, coming after the widespread Microsoft cloud disruptions the day before and the National Weather Service data hiccups earlier Friday.

Landing in Miami was only the beginning of the chaos

When our wheels finally touched down at Miami International Airport, I checked my phone and saw that the captain had kept us informed to the best of his knowledge; no further news had been released, but at least we had been able to land.

But now we were stuck on the plane. Because inbound flights were still arriving while outbound planes sat at their gates, the airport's ramp space was gridlocked.

With nowhere to park and unload passengers, our plane sat idling on the tarmac for the next two hours.

There were too many planes for the number of gates at Miami airport during Friday's FAA outage.

Giorgio VIERA / AFP via Getty Images

Around 7:30 p.m., about an hour after landing, passengers around me began murmuring that rebooking options were finally appearing in the American Airlines app.

When I refreshed my screen, every option required flying out the following evening on grueling 12- to 14-hour itineraries with multiple layovers.

Unwilling to spend a half-day hopping around the US from Florida to Utah, I accepted that I would spend the full weekend in Miami. But before I booked something for Sunday or Monday, I refreshed the list one more time.

Buried at the very bottom was a single direct flight departing at 7:45 p.m. on Saturday night. I booked it immediately, snagging one of the final three open seats — and crossed my fingers that the snowball effect would slow by then and my flight would actually take off.

Hotel rooms disappeared almost as quickly as flights were canceled

Still trapped on the tarmac, another problem emerged: finding a place to sleep.

Around me, passengers were frantically refreshing booking apps as airport hotels sold out in real time. I barely managed to book a room at the Hyde Hotel in Midtown Miami, about 15 minutes away.

It wasn't cheap — $621 for the night, to be exact.

The airline wasn't required to help me out in the uncontrollable flight disruption, and I'm not sure my travel insurance will reimburse me, so I've accepted I may eat that money.

The passenger pick-up area was swarming with cars as people dispersed to their hotels.

Gentry Hale

When I finally deplaned around 8 p.m., cleared customs, and arrived at the lobby, the front desk agent told me the hotel had surged from about 40% full at 5 p.m. local time to sold out by 9 p.m. — filled to capacity by displaced flyers in under four hours.

Even in a major hospitality hub like Miami, inventory evaporates quickly when thousands of stranded travelers are competing for the same beds. Despite the pain in my wallet, knowing I wasn't spending the night on an airport terminal floor felt like I had won the lottery.

I was reminded that no matter how much I prepare, I'm at the whim of the air system

Once I reached my hotel, I refreshed my news app to see that the FAA had lifted the nationwide ground stop, allowing departures to slowly resume, but the effects had already disrupted the whole country.

Air travel is notorious for its snowball effect: a single thunderstorm in Dallas or Atlanta can trigger cascading delays thousands of miles away as planes and crews get displaced. A simultaneous shutdown of the entire US airspace system was a whole other beast.

A friend scheduled to fly to Las Vegas had his trip canceled before he had even left for the airport. But another friend flying from Panama to Denver ended up stranded in Houston — her second overnight stall in 48 hours after weather disruptions the day before.

I'm lucky I got a hotel; rooms were getting scarce by the time I booked.

Joe Raedle/Getty Images

For someone who flies regularly, the unexpected chaos was a reality check. I can build buffer time into my schedule, book early-morning departures and pack carry-on only, but none of that will protect me when a backbone of the national airspace system goes offline.

Lying in my hotel room in Miami, I'll admit I felt a flicker of hesitation about stepping back onto a plane Saturday evening. The thought of pilots losing clear communication with the ground is terrifying.

But that fear is merely one of the trade-offs we accept every time we board a flight to see the world — and I know the pilots are highly trained to deal with emergencies like lost comms.

items.title: The Better AI Gets at Coding, the Less Code It Should Write
items.summary: A font store, a local Noto install, and why reuse is the real test of a coding agent. I’m building smallsymbols , a visual emoji atlas that compares four emoji renderers. In the authoring tools behind it, I work with Cursor. When I asked it to build a feature that generates derived images, it didn’t use the font store I had already written for the project. It used the Noto font installed locally on my machine. I noticed because I still had an older version installed, and some of the derived graphics looked visibly different: Noto draws a few emojis differently in the newer version than in the one on my system. This article was drafted with AI assistance from my notes and ideas. The projects, experiences and opinions are my own. The font store exists to prevent exactly that kind of mismatch. It manages emoji fonts in multiple versions and formats — Noto as SVG and PNG, for example — and makes sure everything uses one consistent font version. The feature still ran on my machine. It was also architecturally wrong. A design decision had been bypassed. And it wasn’t a one-off. The agent has gone around the font store more than once, with the same pattern: a path that worked locally and never went through the place that was supposed to own the fonts. The font store is a decision, not leftover architecture The font store is one place that knows which font versions and formats exist, and that every renderer and every derived graphic should use the same one. That sounds like bookkeeping. It is actually a product decision: if you’re comparing renderers, or generating graphics from the same emoji, they have to start from the same font version. Otherwise you aren’t looking at a renderer difference, or at a stable derived image. You’re looking at an accidental mix of versions. Renderers and derived graphics share one font version through the store. The agent’s shortcut used the older local Noto, so a few emojis looked different. This is not a workaround I introduced because opening a font file directly is too hard for humans. It bundles a responsibility so that different parts of the software don’t make contradictory assumptions. When Cursor ignored it and reached for whatever Noto happened to be on my system, it solved the immediate problem — generate the images — and quietly violated the decision that was supposed to apply to all of them. Generating code is not the same as building software. The first can succeed while the second comes out inconsistent. That is a quality failure, not a step toward more autonomy. The code can look fine. The feature can even produce output. It is still wrong in the same family of ways I wrote about in My Coding Agent Passed Every Test. The Code Was Wrong. , just under a different test. Last time, the tests were green and the logic was wrong. This time, the problem wasn’t a hard-coded example. It was a design decision the agent didn’t reuse. The claim that we won’t need abstractions There’s a popular argument that as models get better, we won’t need programming languages at all. AI will skip source code and emit machine code, even optimized binaries, directly from a description of the outcome. Elon Musk put a version of this at a public xAI all-hands in February 2026 . He said things may move, by the end of the year, “to where you don’t even bother doing coding,” because “the AI just creates the binary directly,” and that traditional coding is “an intermediate step that actually will not be needed.” I don’t think the interesting question is the timeline. Programming languages are abstractions. Compilers already produce binaries. The hard part of software is not the last translation step. It is keeping a decision in one place so the next change does not contradict the last one. Abstractions do that work for agents at least as much as they do for humans. My font store is already that problem, at the application layer. No need to wait for machine code. More code, less reuse What happened in my repo is a small case of a larger pattern: agents are very good at producing new code, and much less reliable at using what is already there. GitClear’s 2026 report The Maintainability Gap , based on 623 million analyzed changes from 2023 to 2026, found that cross-file function calls — a signal of reuse — are down 35 percent. Refactoring, measured as “moved” code, fell from 21 percent of changed lines in 2022 to 3.8 percent in 2026, while copy-and-paste rose from 9.4 percent to 15.7 percent. The report’s own framing is not that AI writes bad code, but that the default workflow is incentivized to deliver “atomic code — a happy-path, a passing test, a closed ticket” and to tax the reuse that makes a codebase cheaper to own later. GitClear sells code-quality tools, and this is a correlation with the AI era, not a controlled experiment. I still recognize the shape. New code that stands alone, instead of calling the function you already have, is exactly what the local Noto font was. What I do now Better AI should not mean the agent writes more. It should mean the agent is better at seeing what it does not need to write. Software engineering is the art of not having to solve the same problem again. An abstraction is how that decision stays in force. I don’t assume Cursor will find the font store on its own. I use targeted search and review prompts that look specifically for the wrong usage: did this go through the font store, or did it open a font some other way? The habit is close to the second-agent reviews I described in the earlier article, only the questions here are about architecture, not about whether the tests were hard-coded. When I plan a new feature, wiring up the font store is part of the plan, not an afterthought. And I search the repo for font files that have newly appeared. A new font file is a concrete smell that something bypassed the store. None of this is glamorous, and I do it because the failure does not always announce itself. I only caught this case because my local font was out of date, and a few emojis looked wrong. This is also why files like AGENTS.md have caught on: a “README for agents,” now an open standard used by tens of thousands of projects and stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation. The industry is betting that agents write better software when you tell them about the architecture that already exists, not when you delete the layers. Instructions alone are not a guarantee, though. I still search and review, because an agent that can write the code can also walk around the rule. The agent that writes less We still tend to picture a smarter coding agent as one that produces more code, faster. I think that’s the wrong picture. The agent that spends an hour reading the repository and then changes five lines to call a function that already exists is doing the better job, not the slower one. In AI Won’t Rewrite Photoshop , I argued that agents make shared software more valuable, not less. The same idea applies one level down, inside your own repo. And in Building Got Cheaper. Madness Became Affordable. I wrote that cheaper building raises your ambition. It also makes it cheap to rebuild a problem you already solved. That’s the kind of madness not to afford. The better AI gets at coding, the less new code it should need to write. The Better AI Gets at Coding, the Less Code It Should Write was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
A font store, a local Noto install, and why reuse is the real test of a coding agent.

I’m building smallsymbols, a visual emoji atlas that compares four emoji renderers. In the authoring tools behind it, I work with Cursor. When I asked it to build a feature that generates derived images, it didn’t use the font store I had already written for the project. It used the Noto font installed locally on my machine. I noticed because I still had an older version installed, and some of the derived graphics looked visibly different: Noto draws a few emojis differently in the newer version than in the one on my system.

This article was drafted with AI assistance from my notes and ideas. The projects, experiences and opinions are my own.

The font store exists to prevent exactly that kind of mismatch. It manages emoji fonts in multiple versions and formats — Noto as SVG and PNG, for example — and makes sure everything uses one consistent font version. The feature still ran on my machine. It was also architecturally wrong. A design decision had been bypassed. And it wasn’t a one-off. The agent has gone around the font store more than once, with the same pattern: a path that worked locally and never went through the place that was supposed to own the fonts.

The font store is a decision, not leftover architecture

The font store is one place that knows which font versions and formats exist, and that every renderer and every derived graphic should use the same one. That sounds like bookkeeping. It is actually a product decision: if you’re comparing renderers, or generating graphics from the same emoji, they have to start from the same font version. Otherwise you aren’t looking at a renderer difference, or at a stable derived image. You’re looking at an accidental mix of versions.

Renderers and derived graphics share one font version through the store. The agent’s shortcut used the older local Noto, so a few emojis looked different.

This is not a workaround I introduced because opening a font file directly is too hard for humans. It bundles a responsibility so that different parts of the software don’t make contradictory assumptions. When Cursor ignored it and reached for whatever Noto happened to be on my system, it solved the immediate problem — generate the images — and quietly violated the decision that was supposed to apply to all of them. Generating code is not the same as building software. The first can succeed while the second comes out inconsistent.

That is a quality failure, not a step toward more autonomy. The code can look fine. The feature can even produce output. It is still wrong in the same family of ways I wrote about in My Coding Agent Passed Every Test. The Code Was Wrong., just under a different test. Last time, the tests were green and the logic was wrong. This time, the problem wasn’t a hard-coded example. It was a design decision the agent didn’t reuse.

The claim that we won’t need abstractions

There’s a popular argument that as models get better, we won’t need programming languages at all. AI will skip source code and emit machine code, even optimized binaries, directly from a description of the outcome.

Elon Musk put a version of this at a public xAI all-hands in February 2026. He said things may move, by the end of the year, “to where you don’t even bother doing coding,” because “the AI just creates the binary directly,” and that traditional coding is “an intermediate step that actually will not be needed.”

I don’t think the interesting question is the timeline. Programming languages are abstractions. Compilers already produce binaries. The hard part of software is not the last translation step. It is keeping a decision in one place so the next change does not contradict the last one. Abstractions do that work for agents at least as much as they do for humans. My font store is already that problem, at the application layer. No need to wait for machine code.

More code, less reuse

What happened in my repo is a small case of a larger pattern: agents are very good at producing new code, and much less reliable at using what is already there.

GitClear’s 2026 report The Maintainability Gap, based on 623 million analyzed changes from 2023 to 2026, found that cross-file function calls — a signal of reuse — are down 35 percent. Refactoring, measured as “moved” code, fell from 21 percent of changed lines in 2022 to 3.8 percent in 2026, while copy-and-paste rose from 9.4 percent to 15.7 percent. The report’s own framing is not that AI writes bad code, but that the default workflow is incentivized to deliver “atomic code — a happy-path, a passing test, a closed ticket” and to tax the reuse that makes a codebase cheaper to own later.

GitClear sells code-quality tools, and this is a correlation with the AI era, not a controlled experiment. I still recognize the shape. New code that stands alone, instead of calling the function you already have, is exactly what the local Noto font was.

What I do now

Better AI should not mean the agent writes more. It should mean the agent is better at seeing what it does not need to write. Software engineering is the art of not having to solve the same problem again. An abstraction is how that decision stays in force.

I don’t assume Cursor will find the font store on its own. I use targeted search and review prompts that look specifically for the wrong usage: did this go through the font store, or did it open a font some other way? The habit is close to the second-agent reviews I described in the earlier article, only the questions here are about architecture, not about whether the tests were hard-coded.

When I plan a new feature, wiring up the font store is part of the plan, not an afterthought. And I search the repo for font files that have newly appeared. A new font file is a concrete smell that something bypassed the store. None of this is glamorous, and I do it because the failure does not always announce itself. I only caught this case because my local font was out of date, and a few emojis looked wrong.

This is also why files like AGENTS.md have caught on: a “README for agents,” now an open standard used by tens of thousands of projects and stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation. The industry is betting that agents write better software when you tell them about the architecture that already exists, not when you delete the layers. Instructions alone are not a guarantee, though. I still search and review, because an agent that can write the code can also walk around the rule.

The agent that writes less

We still tend to picture a smarter coding agent as one that produces more code, faster. I think that’s the wrong picture. The agent that spends an hour reading the repository and then changes five lines to call a function that already exists is doing the better job, not the slower one.

In AI Won’t Rewrite Photoshop, I argued that agents make shared software more valuable, not less. The same idea applies one level down, inside your own repo. And in Building Got Cheaper. Madness Became Affordable. I wrote that cheaper building raises your ambition. It also makes it cheap to rebuild a problem you already solved. That’s the kind of madness not to afford.

The better AI gets at coding, the less new code it should need to write.

The Better AI Gets at Coding, the Less Code It Should Write was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: What is MCP and How It Gives AI One Standard Way to Plug Into Your Tools
items.summary: The Model Context Protocol is often called “USB-C for AI.” Here is what it actually is, how the pieces fit together, what a tiny MCP server looks like in Python, and what to watch out for before you connect one. Think about the drawer of old phone chargers most of us have at home. One cable for this phone, a different one for that tablet, another for the headphones. Every device had its own plug. Then USB-C came along, and slowly one cable started working with almost everything. AI apps had a similar problem with tools. Every time you wanted a chatbot or agent to read your files, query a database, or check a ticket in some system, someone had to write a custom connector for that exact app and that exact tool. The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is an attempt to fix that with one shared plug. The problem MCP solves In the article on AI agents, we saw that a language model becomes much more useful when it can use tools. But the model doesn’t run tools by itself. The app around it does. And each app used to wire up each tool in its own way. Here’s the engineering problem in numbers. Say there are 5 AI apps and 10 tools people want to connect. If every app builds its own connector for every tool, that’s 5 × 10 = 50 separate integrations to write and maintain. With a shared standard, each app implements the protocol once and each tool implements it once. That’s 5 + 10 = 15 pieces of work, and any app can talk to any tool. When Anthropic open-sourced MCP in November 2024, this is exactly how they described it: AI models were “trapped behind information silos,” and every new data source needed “its own custom implementation” [1]. MCP replaces those one-off integrations with a single protocol. What MCP actually is MCP is an open standard for how AI applications talk to external tools and data. It’s not a model, and it’s not a product. It’s a set of rules, like HTTP is for websites. It also doesn’t decide how the AI uses what it gets. The official docs are clear that MCP only covers the exchange of context. How the app uses the model is up to the app [2]. The three main pieces MCP uses a client-server setup with three roles [2]: Host. The AI application the user actually works in, like Claude Desktop, VS Code, or ChatGPT. Client. A small connector inside the host. The host creates one client for each server it connects to. Server. A program that offers capabilities to the AI. For example, a GitHub server, a Postgres server, or a server for your company’s internal order system. Going back to the charger drawer: the host is your laptop, each client is a USB-C port, and each server is a device you plug in. A server can run locally on your machine, talking to the host through standard input and output (called stdio), or remotely over the internet using a transport called Streamable HTTP [2]. Either way, the messages themselves use JSON-RPC 2.0, a simple, well-known format for “call this method with these inputs, get this result back.” What a server can offer An MCP server can expose three main kinds of things, called primitives [2]: Tools. Actions the AI can take, like “search tickets,” “run this SQL query,” or “create a calendar event.” Resources. Data the AI can read for context, like a file’s contents or a database schema. Prompts. Reusable templates, like a ready-made “summarize this bug report” instruction. The flow is simple. The client asks the server what it offers (for tools, that’s a tools/list request). The server replies with each tool’s name, a description, and a schema for its inputs. The host passes that list to the model. When the model decides to use a tool, the host sends a tools/call request to the right server and hands the result back to the model [2]. Same pattern as tool calling in any agent. The model decides. The code does. MCP just standardizes the “code does” part. A tiny MCP server in Python This is where it gets practical. With the official Python SDK [3], a working server is a few lines. Here’s a toy server for a small online shop: from mcp.server import MCPServer mcp = MCPServer("Shop") ORDERS = {"4512": "Held at Lahore warehouse since Monday"} @mcp.tool() def order_status(order_id: str) -> str: """Look up the delivery status of an order by its ID.""" return ORDERS.get(order_id, "Order not found") That’s the whole thing. The function’s type hints become the input schema, and the docstring becomes the description the model reads. No hand-written JSON, no protocol code. You can test it in the MCP Inspector with uv run mcp dev server.py, which comes with the SDK’s cli extra [3]. Once it’s running, any MCP-compatible host can discover order_status and let the model call it. In a real project, you’d replace the dictionary with a call to your actual database or API. The point is that you write this connector once, and it works with every host that speaks MCP. Who uses it MCP spread fast. In December 2025, about a year after launch, Anthropic donated MCP to the Agentic AI Foundation, a new fund under the Linux Foundation co-founded by Anthropic, Block, and OpenAI, with support from Google, Microsoft, AWS, Cloudflare, and Bloomberg [4][5]. The Linux Foundation is the same neutral home behind projects like Kubernetes and Node.js. At that time, the MCP team reported over 10,000 active servers and client support in ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, VS Code, and more [4]. So it’s no longer one company’s experiment. It’s shared infrastructure. What to watch out for MCP makes connecting tools easy. That’s also the risk. Tool descriptions are instructions too. The model reads each tool’s description to decide how to use it. In April 2025, security researchers at Invariant Labs showed “tool poisoning” attacks, where a malicious server hides instructions inside a tool description. In their demo, an innocent-looking “add two numbers” tool told the agent to read private config files and quietly pass them along [6]. It’s a form of prompt injection, aimed at the tool list instead of the chat. Descriptions can change later. The same researchers showed a server can look harmless when you approve it and change its tool descriptions afterward, which they called a “rug pull” [6]. More tools, more power. A server that can send email or edit records gives the AI that power too. A mistake now becomes an action. A few habits help, in line with the official security guidance [7]: Security practices Only install servers from sources you trust, the same way you’d treat any package you run. Give each server the smallest permissions it needs. Read-only where possible. Keep a human approval step for risky actions like sending, deleting, or paying. Treat everything a tool returns as untrusted data, not as instructions. The short version MCP is an open standard that gives AI apps one common way to connect to tools and data. Instead of writing a custom connector for every app and every tool, you build an MCP server once, and any MCP-compatible host can use it. It has three roles (host, client, server) and three main things a server can offer (tools, resources, prompts). Under the hood, it’s JSON-RPC messages over stdio or HTTP. It’s genuinely useful for anyone building agents. Just remember that every server you plug in is new code your AI will trust, so choose and limit them carefully. So the next time someone says “we added MCP support,” a good follow-up question is: “Which servers, and what are they allowed to do?” References [1] Anthropic, “Introducing the Model Context Protocol,” Nov 25, 2024. https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-context-protocol [2] Model Context Protocol docs, “Architecture overview.” https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture [3] MCP Python SDK, official GitHub repository. https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk [4] MCP Blog, “MCP joins the Agentic AI Foundation,” Dec 9, 2025. https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2025–12–09-mcp-joins-agentic-ai-foundation/ [5] The Linux Foundation, “Linux Foundation Announces the Formation of the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF),” Dec 9, 2025. https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/linux-foundation-announces-the-formation-of-the-agentic-ai-foundation [6] Invariant Labs, “MCP Security Notification: Tool Poisoning Attacks,” Apr 2025. https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-security-notification-tool-poisoning-attacks [7] Model Context Protocol, “Security Best Practices.” https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/basic/security_best_practices I write one simple AI explainer every week. Follow if you want the next one. What is MCP and How It Gives AI One Standard Way to Plug Into Your Tools was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

One cable for this phone, a different one for that tablet, another for the headphones. Every device had its own plug. Then USB-C came along, and slowly one cable started working with almost everything.

AI apps had a similar problem with tools. Every time you wanted a chatbot or agent to read your files, query a database, or check a ticket in some system, someone had to write a custom connector for that exact app and that exact tool.

The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is an attempt to fix that with one shared plug.

The problem MCP solves

In the article on AI agents, we saw that a language model becomes much more useful when it can use tools. But the model doesn’t run tools by itself. The app around it does. And each app used to wire up each tool in its own way.

Here’s the engineering problem in numbers. Say there are 5 AI apps and 10 tools people want to connect. If every app builds its own connector for every tool, that’s 5 × 10 = 50 separate integrations to write and maintain.

With a shared standard, each app implements the protocol once and each tool implements it once. That’s 5 + 10 = 15 pieces of work, and any app can talk to any tool.

When Anthropic open-sourced MCP in November 2024, this is exactly how they described it: AI models were “trapped behind information silos,” and every new data source needed “its own custom implementation” [1]. MCP replaces those one-off integrations with a single protocol.

What MCP actually is

MCP is an open standard for how AI applications talk to external tools and data. It’s not a model, and it’s not a product. It’s a set of rules, like HTTP is for websites.

It also doesn’t decide how the AI uses what it gets. The official docs are clear that MCP only covers the exchange of context. How the app uses the model is up to the app [2].

The three main pieces

MCP uses a client-server setup with three roles [2]:

Host. The AI application the user actually works in, like Claude Desktop, VS Code, or ChatGPT.

Client. A small connector inside the host. The host creates one client for each server it connects to.

Server. A program that offers capabilities to the AI. For example, a GitHub server, a Postgres server, or a server for your company’s internal order system.

Going back to the charger drawer: the host is your laptop, each client is a USB-C port, and each server is a device you plug in.

A server can run locally on your machine, talking to the host through standard input and output (called stdio), or remotely over the internet using a transport called Streamable HTTP [2]. Either way, the messages themselves use JSON-RPC 2.0, a simple, well-known format for “call this method with these inputs, get this result back.”

What a server can offer

An MCP server can expose three main kinds of things, called primitives [2]:

Tools. Actions the AI can take, like “search tickets,” “run this SQL query,” or “create a calendar event.”

Resources. Data the AI can read for context, like a file’s contents or a database schema.

Prompts. Reusable templates, like a ready-made “summarize this bug report” instruction.

The flow is simple. The client asks the server what it offers (for tools, that’s a tools/list request). The server replies with each tool’s name, a description, and a schema for its inputs. The host passes that list to the model. When the model decides to use a tool, the host sends a tools/call request to the right server and hands the result back to the model [2].

Same pattern as tool calling in any agent. The model decides. The code does. MCP just standardizes the “code does” part.

A tiny MCP server in Python

This is where it gets practical. With the official Python SDK [3], a working server is a few lines. Here’s a toy server for a small online shop:

from mcp.server import MCPServer

mcp = MCPServer("Shop")

ORDERS = {"4512": "Held at Lahore warehouse since Monday"}

@mcp.tool()
def order_status(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Look up the delivery status of an order by its ID."""
    return ORDERS.get(order_id, "Order not found")

That’s the whole thing. The function’s type hints become the input schema, and the docstring becomes the description the model reads. No hand-written JSON, no protocol code.

You can test it in the MCP Inspector with uv run mcp dev server.py, which comes with the SDK’s cli extra [3]. Once it’s running, any MCP-compatible host can discover order_status and let the model call it.

In a real project, you’d replace the dictionary with a call to your actual database or API. The point is that you write this connector once, and it works with every host that speaks MCP.

Who uses it

MCP spread fast. In December 2025, about a year after launch, Anthropic donated MCP to the Agentic AI Foundation, a new fund under the Linux Foundation co-founded by Anthropic, Block, and OpenAI, with support from Google, Microsoft, AWS, Cloudflare, and Bloomberg [4][5]. The Linux Foundation is the same neutral home behind projects like Kubernetes and Node.js.

At that time, the MCP team reported over 10,000 active servers and client support in ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, VS Code, and more [4]. So it’s no longer one company’s experiment. It’s shared infrastructure.

What to watch out for

MCP makes connecting tools easy. That’s also the risk.

Tool descriptions are instructions too. The model reads each tool’s description to decide how to use it. In April 2025, security researchers at Invariant Labs showed “tool poisoning” attacks, where a malicious server hides instructions inside a tool description. In their demo, an innocent-looking “add two numbers” tool told the agent to read private config files and quietly pass them along [6]. It’s a form of prompt injection, aimed at the tool list instead of the chat.

Descriptions can change later. The same researchers showed a server can look harmless when you approve it and change its tool descriptions afterward, which they called a “rug pull” [6].

More tools, more power. A server that can send email or edit records gives the AI that power too. A mistake now becomes an action.

A few habits help, in line with the official security guidance [7]:

Security practices

Only install servers from sources you trust, the same way you’d treat any package you run.

Give each server the smallest permissions it needs. Read-only where possible.

Keep a human approval step for risky actions like sending, deleting, or paying.

Treat everything a tool returns as untrusted data, not as instructions.

The short version

MCP is an open standard that gives AI apps one common way to connect to tools and data. Instead of writing a custom connector for every app and every tool, you build an MCP server once, and any MCP-compatible host can use it.

It has three roles (host, client, server) and three main things a server can offer (tools, resources, prompts). Under the hood, it’s JSON-RPC messages over stdio or HTTP.

It’s genuinely useful for anyone building agents. Just remember that every server you plug in is new code your AI will trust, so choose and limit them carefully.

So the next time someone says “we added MCP support,” a good follow-up question is: “Which servers, and what are they allowed to do?”

References

[1] Anthropic, “Introducing the Model Context Protocol,” Nov 25, 2024. https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-context-protocol

[2] Model Context Protocol docs, “Architecture overview.” https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture

[3] MCP Python SDK, official GitHub repository. https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk

[4] MCP Blog, “MCP joins the Agentic AI Foundation,” Dec 9, 2025. https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2025–12–09-mcp-joins-agentic-ai-foundation/

[5] The Linux Foundation, “Linux Foundation Announces the Formation of the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF),” Dec 9, 2025. https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/linux-foundation-announces-the-formation-of-the-agentic-ai-foundation

[6] Invariant Labs, “MCP Security Notification: Tool Poisoning Attacks,” Apr 2025. https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-security-notification-tool-poisoning-attacks

[7] Model Context Protocol, “Security Best Practices.” https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/basic/security_best_practices

items.title: Everything That Led to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s Fall
items.summary: Jensen Huang is gone from Nvidia, the chipmaker he co-founded 33 years ago. The origins of that downfall go back to the 2010s—to when Alice Huang, one of the women with whom he allegedly had an affair, was setting herself up to become a major Nvidia customer. Their relationship went unnoticed for a long time, but then it became just one element in a growing array of scandals around Jensen that eventually led to his resignation on Wednesday. As the drama widened, it came to include two more alleged affairs, a confrontation at Jensen’s home and a fateful board meeting. Below, you’ll find a curated timeline of what happened.

items.title: I watched Jensen Huang speak 9 days before his resignation. Two things stand out now.
items.summary: Jensen Huang in San Francisco on Nov. 3 without his famous leather jacket. Alistair Barr/Business Insider A version of this story originally appeared in the AI Insider newsletter. Sign up for Business Insider's weekly AI Insider newsletter here . Nine days before Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO, I sat near the front row at a San Francisco conference and watched him discuss the future of AI. Two things struck me that day. Both seem more significant now. First, Huang wasn't wearing his famous black leather jacket . Instead, as you can see in the photo I took, he wore a dark fabric zip-up. At the time, I thought it was funny. His jacket had become such a recognizable part of his image that seeing him without it was a bit jarring. Now, with revelations about his extramarital affairs and allegations involving a possible Chinese spy , I wonder whether the wardrobe change meant something. The initial allegations were already public by November 3. Of course, that's hindsight talking. Maybe a jacket is just a jacket. The second thing was more consequential. Fireworks AI CEO Lin Qiao (left) interviewing Jensen Huang at the startup's conference in San Francisco on Nov. 3, 2026. Alistair Barr/Business Insider Near the end of the conversation, Fireworks AI CEO Lin Qiao asked Huang about his unusual management style. He had 60 executives reporting directly to him . Huang explained that he'd designed this structure more than 30 years ago, when personal computers and email were transforming business. Rather than a traditional hierarchy, he wanted information flowing freely among executives empowered to make decisions. Then came the obvious question: What should a company's leadership structure look like in the AI age? "I don't know the answer to that," Huang replied. At the time, I thought that was a bit odd. Nvidia is leading the AI revolution and Jensen leads Nvidia. Wouldn't he be thinking of how best to run this company in the future? Today, that exchange seems especially relevant. With Huang gone, Nvidia faces an extraordinary succession challenge . Sixty direct reports may have worked brilliantly under its founder. But it also means there isn't an obvious deputy to take the reins. If he'd had two or three direct reports, those people would have had more experience with more responsibility. But 60 direct reports, by definition, means that each one of those execs only had a small piece of Nvidia to oversee. Does this mean Nvidia is doomed? I'm not sure. The way Jensen described Nvidia's structure back on Nov. 3 provides some hope. Huang said he gave executives considerable freedom to make decisions and work together, rather than taking orders from the top. Instead of a rigid management hierarchy, Nvidia organized itself around projects, with teams forming and changing as needed. "Irrespective of whatever internal or external threats and opportunities, the company will naturally adapt itself, it should adapt itself to new opportunities," he said. "That was the organization I created." The talk ended on a poignant note. Again, with hindsight, I can't help thinking he knew something was coming. "I'm super proud of you," he told Fireworks' Qiao. "Don't forget us little people someday." Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here . Reach out to me via email at abarr@businessinsider.com Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
Jensen Huang in San Francisco on Nov. 3 without his famous leather jacket.

Alistair Barr/Business Insider

  • A version of this story originally appeared in the AI Insider newsletter.
  • Sign up for Business Insider's weekly AI Insider newsletter here.

Nine days before Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO, I sat near the front row at a San Francisco conference and watched him discuss the future of AI.

Two things struck me that day. Both seem more significant now.

First, Huang wasn't wearing his famous black leather jacket. Instead, as you can see in the photo I took, he wore a dark fabric zip-up. At the time, I thought it was funny. His jacket had become such a recognizable part of his image that seeing him without it was a bit jarring.

Now, with revelations about his extramarital affairs and allegations involving a possible Chinese spy, I wonder whether the wardrobe change meant something. The initial allegations were already public by November 3.

Of course, that's hindsight talking. Maybe a jacket is just a jacket.

The second thing was more consequential.

Fireworks AI CEO Lin Qiao (left) interviewing Jensen Huang at the startup's conference in San Francisco on Nov. 3, 2026.

Alistair Barr/Business Insider

Near the end of the conversation, Fireworks AI CEO Lin Qiao asked Huang about his unusual management style. He had 60 executives reporting directly to him.

Huang explained that he'd designed this structure more than 30 years ago, when personal computers and email were transforming business. Rather than a traditional hierarchy, he wanted information flowing freely among executives empowered to make decisions.

Then came the obvious question: What should a company's leadership structure look like in the AI age?

"I don't know the answer to that," Huang replied.

At the time, I thought that was a bit odd. Nvidia is leading the AI revolution and Jensen leads Nvidia. Wouldn't he be thinking of how best to run this company in the future?

Today, that exchange seems especially relevant.

With Huang gone, Nvidia faces an extraordinary succession challenge. Sixty direct reports may have worked brilliantly under its founder. But it also means there isn't an obvious deputy to take the reins.

If he'd had two or three direct reports, those people would have had more experience with more responsibility. But 60 direct reports, by definition, means that each one of those execs only had a small piece of Nvidia to oversee.

Does this mean Nvidia is doomed? I'm not sure. The way Jensen described Nvidia's structure back on Nov. 3 provides some hope.

Huang said he gave executives considerable freedom to make decisions and work together, rather than taking orders from the top. Instead of a rigid management hierarchy, Nvidia organized itself around projects, with teams forming and changing as needed.

"Irrespective of whatever internal or external threats and opportunities, the company will naturally adapt itself, it should adapt itself to new opportunities," he said. "That was the organization I created."

The talk ended on a poignant note. Again, with hindsight, I can't help thinking he knew something was coming.

"I'm super proud of you," he told Fireworks' Qiao. "Don't forget us little people someday."
