items.title: Claude Fable 5.2 vs. GPT-6 Astra: A lower list price didn’t mean a lower bill
items.summary: Anthropic is positioning its new model , Claude Fable 5.2 , for demanding coding and technical work. Anthropic launched Fable 5.2 on Nov. 9 and reported higher scores than OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on two coding benchmarks. Fable 5.2 also has lower standard API rates. Anthropic’s launch benchmarks put Fable 5.2 ahead of Astra, 49.1% to 42.8% on FrontierCode 2.0 and 69.9% to 65.5% on FrontierSWE v2. Fable’s 49.1% came at X high effort. At High, its default on the Claude API , it scored 45.3%. Benchmark leads don’t always carry over to real work. The cost side is less simple than the price list. Tokens are the chunks of text a model reads and writes, and AI companies bill by them. At standard API rates, Fable 5.2 costs $8 per million uncached input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra in September at standard API rates of $10 per million uncached input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. “The price per task is what matters,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman said at Astra’s launch. Both APIs charge for reasoning tokens as output and have separate rates for cached input . In my experience, Anthropic’s models have used more tokens than OpenAI’s. I put this positioning to the test and ran Fable 5.2 against Astra on tasks that simulate real developer work. The tests I ran both models on the same three tasks, once each, through each vendor’s API at default settings. Each test is worth 50 points, and I used a script to grade all the answers. Here are the tests: Bug fix : I planted 10 bugs in a 2,600-line billing codebase and wrote a support ticket describing 10 customer complaints. The ticket’s guesses about the causes are wrong, two of the codebase’s own tests are wrong, and one bug only shows up after another is fixed. Code review : I planted 45 defects in its VAT ID checks for 27 countries, its IBAN rules, its European Central Bank payment calendar, and its date formats for 50 locales in an EU invoicing package. The models had to prove each defect with an input the code gets wrong and identify the correct answer. Flagging false alarms cost the models points. Code writing : The model wrote the same helpers from scratch, including VAT ID validation for 27 countries, IBAN checks for 34 countries, the payment calendar, and long dates. Bug fix Fable 5.2 and Astra fixed all 10 bugs and passed all 50 hidden checks, both in 12 turns (the matching number of turns surprised me). The difference is in how much each model spent to get there. Fable 5.2 used more than 17,000 reasoning tokens, and Astra used 819 (wow). Astra passed the checks in about two minutes at an estimated cost of 98 cents. Fable 5.2 took more than five minutes and cost an estimated $2.51. The numbers: Fable 5.2 : 12 turns, 696,863 in, 36,135 out (17,387 reasoning), $2.51, 326 s. Astra : 12 turns, 231,854 in, 6,823 out (819 reasoning), $0.98, 122 s. Code review This is the only test where the scores differ. Fable 5.2 scored 49, and Astra scored 45. Fable 5.2 proved 44 of the 45 defects and raised no false alarms across 71 findings. Astra proved 41 and incorrectly classified one Spanish ID as valid. Astra missed defects in check-digit rules for Spain, Ireland, and Luxembourg. Both models missed the same Spanish defect: two swapped letters in a 23-letter lookup table. Fable 5.2’s thoroughness came at a price. It cost more than six times what Astra did and took more than four times as long. If your code handles invoices (or simple approvals), one validation rule the review misses can get real invoices rejected, so Fable 5.2’s four extra points may be worth the higher price. For a routine review, Astra found 91% of the defects for 16% of the cost. Each model ran once, so a four-point gap could shift on another run. The numbers: Fable 5.2 : 26 turns, 2,207,564 in, 103,240 out (77,641 reasoning), $6.05, 993 s. Astra : 12 turns, 192,018 in, 8,664 out (4,307 reasoning), $0.95, 227 s. Code writing Both models scored 50 of 50. Each one wrote working checks for 27 countries’ VAT IDs and 34 countries’ IBANs with no libraries to lean on. Neither model had trouble here. Both passed all the checks in one run. Astra took 23 turns, almost as many as Fable 5.2’s 24. Fable 5.2 still cost 2.3 times as much and took 1.7 times as long for the same score. In this run, the extra tokens didn’t raise the score. The numbers: Fable 5.2: 24 turns, 1,495,712 in, 87,542 out (47,458 reasoning), $4.83, 838 s. Astra: 23 turns, 460,271 in, 24,007 out (9,328 reasoning), $2.06, 483 s. Results Test Claude Fable 5.2 GPT-6 Astra Bug fix (of 50) 50 50 Code review (of 50) 49 45 Code writing (out of 50) 50 50 Total tokens in / out 4,400,139 / 226,917 884,143 / 39,494 Estimated cost $13.39 $3.99 Total time 2,157 s 832 s Fable 5.2 led on code review and tied Astra on the other two tasks. Across the two tied tasks, its estimated API cost was 2.4 times Astra’s ($7.34 vs. $3.04), and it took 1.9 times as long (1,164 vs. 605 seconds). What do I think? For tasks like these, I’d start with Astra. It matched Fable 5.2’s scores on bug fixing and code writing at about 41% of the estimated cost, and it finished all three tasks faster. I’d consider Fable 5.2 for a careful code review, where it found three more defects in this test. Both models missed defects. Fable 5.2’s standard token rates are lower, but it used about five times as many tokens as Astra across these three runs. Brockman’s point about price per task held up here.

Anthropic is positioning its new model, Claude Fable 5.2, for demanding coding and technical work. Anthropic launched Fable 5.2 on Nov. 9 and reported higher scores than OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on two coding benchmarks. Fable 5.2 also has lower standard API rates.

Anthropic’s launch benchmarks put Fable 5.2 ahead of Astra, 49.1% to 42.8% on FrontierCode 2.0 and 69.9% to 65.5% on FrontierSWE v2. Fable’s 49.1% came at X high effort. At High, its default on the Claude API, it scored 45.3%. Benchmark leads don’t always carry over to real work.

The cost side is less simple than the price list. Tokens are the chunks of text a model reads and writes, and AI companies bill by them. At standard API rates, Fable 5.2 costs $8 per million uncached input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra in September at standard API rates of $10 per million uncached input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. “The price per task is what matters,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman said at Astra’s launch. Both APIs charge for reasoning tokens as output and have separate rates for cached input.

In my experience, Anthropic’s models have used more tokens than OpenAI’s. I put this positioning to the test and ran Fable 5.2 against Astra on tasks that simulate real developer work.

The tests

I ran both models on the same three tasks, once each, through each vendor’s API at default settings. Each test is worth 50 points, and I used a script to grade all the answers. Here are the tests:

  • Bug fix: I planted 10 bugs in a 2,600-line billing codebase and wrote a support ticket describing 10 customer complaints. The ticket’s guesses about the causes are wrong, two of the codebase’s own tests are wrong, and one bug only shows up after another is fixed.
  • Code review: I planted 45 defects in its VAT ID checks for 27 countries, its IBAN rules, its European Central Bank payment calendar, and its date formats for 50 locales in an EU invoicing package. The models had to prove each defect with an input the code gets wrong and identify the correct answer. Flagging false alarms cost the models points.
  • Code writing: The model wrote the same helpers from scratch, including VAT ID validation for 27 countries, IBAN checks for 34 countries, the payment calendar, and long dates.
Bug fix

Fable 5.2 and Astra fixed all 10 bugs and passed all 50 hidden checks, both in 12 turns (the matching number of turns surprised me).

The difference is in how much each model spent to get there. Fable 5.2 used more than 17,000 reasoning tokens, and Astra used 819 (wow). Astra passed the checks in about two minutes at an estimated cost of 98 cents. Fable 5.2 took more than five minutes and cost an estimated $2.51.

The numbers:

  • Fable 5.2: 12 turns, 696,863 in, 36,135 out (17,387 reasoning), $2.51, 326 s.
  • Astra: 12 turns, 231,854 in, 6,823 out (819 reasoning), $0.98, 122 s.
Code review

This is the only test where the scores differ. Fable 5.2 scored 49, and Astra scored 45. Fable 5.2 proved 44 of the 45 defects and raised no false alarms across 71 findings. Astra proved 41 and incorrectly classified one Spanish ID as valid. Astra missed defects in check-digit rules for Spain, Ireland, and Luxembourg. Both models missed the same Spanish defect: two swapped letters in a 23-letter lookup table.

Fable 5.2’s thoroughness came at a price. It cost more than six times what Astra did and took more than four times as long. If your code handles invoices (or simple approvals), one validation rule the review misses can get real invoices rejected, so Fable 5.2’s four extra points may be worth the higher price. For a routine review, Astra found 91% of the defects for 16% of the cost. Each model ran once, so a four-point gap could shift on another run.

The numbers:

  • Fable 5.2: 26 turns, 2,207,564 in, 103,240 out (77,641 reasoning), $6.05, 993 s.
  • Astra: 12 turns, 192,018 in, 8,664 out (4,307 reasoning), $0.95, 227 s.
Code writing

Both models scored 50 of 50. Each one wrote working checks for 27 countries’ VAT IDs and 34 countries’ IBANs with no libraries to lean on. Neither model had trouble here. Both passed all the checks in one run.

Astra took 23 turns, almost as many as Fable 5.2’s 24. Fable 5.2 still cost 2.3 times as much and took 1.7 times as long for the same score. In this run, the extra tokens didn’t raise the score.

The numbers:

  • Fable 5.2: 24 turns, 1,495,712 in, 87,542 out (47,458 reasoning), $4.83, 838 s.
  • Astra: 23 turns, 460,271 in, 24,007 out (9,328 reasoning), $2.06, 483 s.
Results
TestClaude Fable 5.2GPT-6 AstraBug fix (of 50)5050Code review (of 50)4945Code writing (out of 50)5050Total tokens in / out4,400,139 / 226,917884,143 / 39,494Estimated cost$13.39$3.99Total time2,157 s832 s

Fable 5.2 led on code review and tied Astra on the other two tasks. Across the two tied tasks, its estimated API cost was 2.4 times Astra’s ($7.34 vs. $3.04), and it took 1.9 times as long (1,164 vs. 605 seconds).

What do I think?

For tasks like these, I’d start with Astra. It matched Fable 5.2’s scores on bug fixing and code writing at about 41% of the estimated cost, and it finished all three tasks faster. I’d consider Fable 5.2 for a careful code review, where it found three more defects in this test. Both models missed defects.

Fable 5.2’s standard token rates are lower, but it used about five times as many tokens as Astra across these three runs. Brockman’s point about price per task held up here.

items.title: The Pentagon is testing war robots that can hunt in packs without GPS and find battlefield targets on their own. Humans still call the shots.
items.summary: The uncrewed ground vehicles mapped out the area as they drove, not relying on GPS to navigate. DARPA The Pentagon research arm DARPA tested autonomous ground robots in GPS-denied environments. The robots mapped out the area and located enemy targets. Once the targets were identified, the human operator overseeing the process decided next steps. The Pentagon's research arm tested how ground drones could be sent out in groups to look for and hunt down targets while keeping a human operator in the loop to make decisions. The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency , or DARPA, program examined how uncrewed ground vehicles, or UGVs, could quickly drive, map out terrain, and gather information on their own in contested environments. Lessons will inform ongoing developments in uncrewed technologies across the US military, officials said. Last month, DARPA experimented with four autonomous UGVs at an exercise at Fort Knox, Kentucky, as part of its Robotic Autonomy in Complex Environments with Resiliency, or RACER, program. During the exercise, the ground robots conducted surveillance of the surrounding area, independently searching for enemy forces for an operator located away from the action. Jason Gregory, technical advisor at DARPA, told Business Insider that "we're moving sensors and effectors forward to the tactical edge while keeping the operator in safety out of harm's way," but humans still "maintained control and custody and situational awareness at all times." Once launched, the UGVs went off on their missions. Gregory said they could work together or independently depending on the scenario. Meanwhile, the human operator supervised the UGVs, assigned them tasks, checked their findings, and then decided how best to engage enemy targets. At the Fort Knox demonstration, the operator used satellite imagery to task the robots. One UGV stopped in place once it spotted a potential target — a closed box holding a drone inside — and then the human operator decided to launch a simulated rocket at the target. An important part of the recent RACER robotic testing program was ensuring that the UGVs could perform their tasks without GPS. Instead, the robots built the map as they moved. The US military has said it needs to be prepared to fight through contested or denied environments where GPS isn't readily available, and is looking into alternative precision navigation and timing solutions, as well as more traditional tactics. Once a potential enemy target has been identified, a human operator decides the next steps. DARPA The military is also considering other possible disruptions, such as terrain interference or loss of signal. "We developed this new software so that ground vehicles could use only their onboard sensors to make decisions to move as fast as possible," Gregory said. The software was tested on four-wheel, all-terrain UGVs as well as tracked UGVs to ensure it could be deployed on different hardware. While teams worked to build systems using commercial technologies, the RACER program also involved five years of research to better understand the scientific and technical challenges of autonomy, artificial intelligence algorithms, and ground mobility. DARPA's work also relied on observations from Russia's war in Ukraine on the distinct role of ground robots and how operators employ them in different situations. Autonomous UGVs face distinct challenges depending on the terrain, environment, and climate. In the desert, for example, robots might need to navigate sand, rocks, and other obstacles, while extreme heat might strain the batteries and communications systems. Swamplands, forests, muddy fields, and snow can also make operations more difficult, requiring robots to be able to adapt to very different conditions. RACER's demonstration offers lessons for the broader US military. While some are specific to autonomous ground robots , others — including operating without GPS, teaming humans with machines, and maintaining human oversight in robotic operations — could apply to uncrewed systems across the military. items.title: Post-training Stages and Preference Data — It is much easier to judge than to generate
items.summary: Goal: understand the stages of LLM post-training, then what preferences are, why post-training needs them, and how preference data is collected. Part 1: Post-training Stages 1. Pre-training builds knowledge, post-training builds behavior • Pre-training: the model reads a huge amount of text and learns to predict the next word, which gives it knowledge but no manners. • Post-training: it takes far less compute, yet largely decides how well a model follows instructions, how safe it is and how it reasons (Developers Digest, n.d.). • Recipe: the sequence of post-training steps a lab follows; a canonical recipe is the standard version of its time. The recipe changed more in the last year than in the three years before (Lambert & Timbers, 2026). Note. Era summary as in Lambert and Timbers (2026). 2. Stage 1: SFT, learning from example answers • Abbreviation: SFT is supervised fine-tuning, training a model on example prompts paired with ideal answers. • Main difference from pre-training: pre-training learns from raw text, so the model continues text; SFT learns from prompt-and-answer pairs, so it learns to answer. It teaches format and tone quickly, but the model can only imitate what it has been shown. • Analogy: an apprentice cook learning from a head chef’s recipe book. The apprentice picks up the house style fast, but only knows the dishes in the book, and a surprise ingredient leaves them guessing. 3. Stage 2: preference tuning, learning which answer people prefer • Abbreviations: – RL: reinforcement learning, learning from scores on the model’s own attempts. – RLHF: RL from human feedback, where the scores come from a judge trained on human preferences. – PPO: proximal policy optimization, an RL algorithm that keeps each update small. – DPO: direct preference optimization, which trains directly on pairs of answers marked better and worse, with no separate reward model and no RL loop (Rafailov et al., 2023). • Main difference from SFT: SFT copies one ideal answer; preference tuning learns from rankings of several answers, so it can tell which of two good answers is better. The rankings train a reward model (a separate judge model) and the main model adjusts to earn higher scores. The weakness is reward hacking: the model learns to please the judge instead of being right. DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop. • Analogy: the cook makes four versions of a dish and a tasting panel ranks them. A critic learns to score like the panel, and the cook adjusts toward what the critic likes. DPO skips the critic and learns from pairs. Rejection sampling keeps only the critic’s best of ten versions for practice. Reward hacking is fancy plating that wins over the critic without better food. • DPO vs RL: DPO trains offline on a fixed dataset, so it is simpler, more stable and fast to iterate on, but limited by the dataset’s coverage, a slightly lower performance ceiling. Online RL such as PPO generates fresh completions and can explore new regions, often reaching higher peak performance, at the cost of more compute and more moving parts (Ivison et al., 2024; Tajwar et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024). • DPO data: it needs feedback data, not necessarily human feedback. UltraFeedback was the first prominent open synthetic preference dataset and helped kickstart the DPO era (Cui et al., 2023), and Tülu 3 followed with larger synthetic-feedback recipes (Lambert et al., 2024). 4. Stage 3: RLVR, learning from answers that can be checked • Abbreviations: – RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards, where a program checks whether the answer is correct. – GRPO: group relative policy optimization, which scores a group of answers and reinforces the above-average ones. – AI2: the Allen Institute for AI, which introduced the RLVR term (Lambert et al., 2024). • Main difference from preference tuning: a learned judge can be fooled; a program that checks the math result, the code tests or a numeric range is cheap, objective and hard to game, but only works where an answer can be checked. This is also how models learn to think: careful attempts win more often, so they get reinforced. • Analogy: swap the tasting panel for a thermometer and a timer. A rushed, raw dish fails the reading and earns nothing; a cook who checks the oven and adjusts earns the reward. After thousands of dishes, checking as you go becomes the habit, and that habit is what learning to think looks like. 5. Stage 4: specialists first, then distillation • Abbreviations: – MOPD: multi-teacher on-policy distillation; several specialist teachers train one student on the student’s own answers. – KL: Kullback-Leibler divergence, a score for how different two models’ next-word probabilities are; reverse KL penalizes the student for saying things the teacher would never say (Gu et al., 2024). • Main difference from RLVR: one RLVR run on every domain got expensive and conflict-prone, because mixing math, code and agentic RL trades capabilities off against each other. Specialists are cheap and parallelizable, and on-policy distillation matured. So one specialist is trained per domain, then a general student writes its own answers and the relevant teacher marks it token by token (Lambert & Timbers, 2026; Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). Distillation means a student learns from a teacher’s outputs (Hinton et al., 2015), and on-policy means it learns from its own attempts, including its own mistakes (Agarwal et al., 2024). • Analogy: a kitchen with a pastry, a grill and a sauce chef, each trained separately. A trainee cooks whole dishes alone and the matching chef tastes every spoonful as it cooks, so the correction lands at the exact step. Training one trainee on all three at once is how habits clash, such as high heat that suits a grill but ruins a custard. Note. Summary of Stages 1 to 4 above; stage order as in Lambert and Timbers (2026). 6. Where human experts fit • SFT: expert-written answers. • Preference tuning: expert rankings. • RLVR: rubrics, for example in finance and law. A good rubric accepts more than one valid method, and in a MOPD pipeline the finance teacher is only as good as the tasks and rubrics behind it. Rubrics are already delivering gains beyond verifiable domains (Gunjal et al., 2025). • Hard-to-verify tasks: the DeepSeek-V4 report describes rubric-guided RL data scored by a generative reward model, which works with only a small set of diverse human annotations (DeepSeek-AI, 2026). Part 2: Preference Data 1. Preferences are what we reach for when there is no right answer • Why it works: it is far easier to judge than to generate, so people can tell which answer is better even when they could not write it themselves (Lambert, n.d.). Note. Examples and framing as in Lambert (n.d.). 2. Three branches converge into RLHF • Optimal control: a framework for optimization with dynamic programming and mathematical underpinnings, which led to reinforcement learning and then deep RL (Lambert et al., 2023). • Deep learning: neural networks and the scaling of data and problem complexity, which led to large language models (Lambert et al., 2023). • Economics and decision theory: individual preferences, decision theory and methods for comparing preferences (Lambert et al., 2023). Note. Figure from Lambert et al. (2023), shown with the original attribution. 3. Utility: from logic to number • Port-Royal Logic: it supports the idea that decision quality is an outcome weighted by its probability (Arnauld, 1662). 4. Reward: giving the model a direction • Value function: gives directions toward preferred behavior (Singh et al., 2009). • Decisions: are made to transition to higher-valued states (Singh et al., 2009). 5. Interface of preference data • Likert score: the rater gives a response a score on a fixed scale, as in early Claude’s preference interface (Bai et al., 2022). • A/B test: the rater chooses between two responses (Lambert, n.d.). • Pairwise with ties: the rater chooses between two responses or marks a tie, as in the Chatbot Arena public evaluation (Chiang et al., 2024). • A single bit: thumbs up or thumbs down on one response (Lambert, n.d.). • Pick from many: the rater picks the best from several responses, the default in image models (Lambert, n.d.). 6. Ratings and rankings • Ratings: a score on one completion in isolation (Lambert, n.d.). • Rankings: relative comparisons between responses, often on a Likert scale (Bai et al., 2022). 7. The unaudited gap • Chain: Spec → Data → Behaviour; the Spec is the documented intended behavior, for example the Model Spec (OpenAI, 2024). • Unaudited link: the step from Data to Behaviour is not checked, meaning nobody verifies whether the values written down by the annotators are actually reflected in the final model (Lambert, n.d.). Appendix • A1. Origin of weights – They are the billions of numbers inside a model, starting as small random values. Pre-training nudges them until they encode grammar, facts and reasoning patterns; post-training makes comparatively small adjustments. • A2. Token, vector, embedding table – A token is a chunk of text with a fixed ID, a label with no meaning of its own. A vector is a list of numbers that represents meaning. The embedding table turns each token ID into its starting vector. Only the embedding table and the layers that transform vectors are weights; tokens and vectors are the data flowing through them. • A3. RL vs SFT – Studying a book of grandmaster games (SFT) versus playing thousands of games and learning only whether you won (RL). SFT is capped near the quality of its examples; RL can go beyond them. • A4. Two reward models in Llama 2 – Helpfulness and safety can pull against each other, like a taste critic and a health inspector: the tastiest dish can break the health rules, and a kitchen that plays it too safe serves nothing. For risky prompts the safety score takes priority. • A5. R1-Zero vs R1, and cold start – R1-Zero was the experiment, pure RL with strong reasoning but messy output; R1 was the product. A cold start gives the model a small SFT warm-up so it already writes in a clean, consistent format, and RL then spends its effort on correctness instead of readability. • A6. Rubrics and rubric weights – A rubric is a judging checklist of yes-or-no items any judge can run on any answer, like “the middle is fully cooked” at a baking contest. Rubric weights, from 1 to 10, set how many points each item is worth. They are not model weights: the weighted score becomes the reward that adjusts the model’s weights. • A7. Teacher marking vs golden answer and reward model – No. The student writes its own answer and only the relevant teacher marks it at every token. A golden answer is one fixed text and a reward model gives one score at the end, while a teacher gives an opinion on every word. • A8. Conflicting skills in the student – Much less than in one mixed RL run, because each question gets feedback from one teacher only. The conflict does not vanish, since the student has finite capacity and the mix of questions still has to be tuned. • A9. KL divergence and reverse KL – Zero means two distributions are identical. Reverse KL punishes the student for putting probability on words the teacher thinks are unlikely, so it avoids mistakes the expert would never make and commits to good answers. • A10. Trace distillation SFT vs the final climb in MAI-Thinking-1 – A trace is written step-by-step reasoning, and a climb is Microsoft AI’s word for a long RL run that keeps improving a score. In trace distillation SFT, traces from three specialists (SWE and agentic; STEM; helpfulness and safety) are collected and one model is fine-tuned on them. The final climb is one more RL run on that consolidated model. Like three tutors writing binders of worked solutions that one student studies, then sits mock exams with a grader. Goal: understand the stages of LLM post-training, then what preferences are, why post-training needs them, and how preference data is collected.Part 1: Post-training Stages1. Pre-training builds knowledge, post-training builds behavior

• Pre-training: the model reads a huge amount of text and learns to predict the next word, which gives it knowledge but no manners.

• Post-training: it takes far less compute, yet largely decides how well a model follows instructions, how safe it is and how it reasons (Developers Digest, n.d.).

• Recipe: the sequence of post-training steps a lab follows; a canonical recipe is the standard version of its time. The recipe changed more in the last year than in the three years before (Lambert & Timbers, 2026).

Note. Era summary as in Lambert and Timbers (2026).

2. Stage 1: SFT, learning from example answers

• Abbreviation: SFT is supervised fine-tuning, training a model on example prompts paired with ideal answers.

• Main difference from pre-training: pre-training learns from raw text, so the model continues text; SFT learns from prompt-and-answer pairs, so it learns to answer. It teaches format and tone quickly, but the model can only imitate what it has been shown.

• Analogy: an apprentice cook learning from a head chef’s recipe book. The apprentice picks up the house style fast, but only knows the dishes in the book, and a surprise ingredient leaves them guessing.

3. Stage 2: preference tuning, learning which answer people prefer

• Abbreviations:

– RL: reinforcement learning, learning from scores on the model’s own attempts.

– RLHF: RL from human feedback, where the scores come from a judge trained on human preferences.

– PPO: proximal policy optimization, an RL algorithm that keeps each update small.

– DPO: direct preference optimization, which trains directly on pairs of answers marked better and worse, with no separate reward model and no RL loop (Rafailov et al., 2023).

• Main difference from SFT: SFT copies one ideal answer; preference tuning learns from rankings of several answers, so it can tell which of two good answers is better. The rankings train a reward model (a separate judge model) and the main model adjusts to earn higher scores. The weakness is reward hacking: the model learns to please the judge instead of being right. DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop.

• Analogy: the cook makes four versions of a dish and a tasting panel ranks them. A critic learns to score like the panel, and the cook adjusts toward what the critic likes. DPO skips the critic and learns from pairs. Rejection sampling keeps only the critic’s best of ten versions for practice. Reward hacking is fancy plating that wins over the critic without better food.

• DPO vs RL: DPO trains offline on a fixed dataset, so it is simpler, more stable and fast to iterate on, but limited by the dataset’s coverage, a slightly lower performance ceiling. Online RL such as PPO generates fresh completions and can explore new regions, often reaching higher peak performance, at the cost of more compute and more moving parts (Ivison et al., 2024; Tajwar et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024).

• DPO data: it needs feedback data, not necessarily human feedback. UltraFeedback was the first prominent open synthetic preference dataset and helped kickstart the DPO era (Cui et al., 2023), and Tülu 3 followed with larger synthetic-feedback recipes (Lambert et al., 2024).

4. Stage 3: RLVR, learning from answers that can be checked

• Abbreviations:

– RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards, where a program checks whether the answer is correct.

– GRPO: group relative policy optimization, which scores a group of answers and reinforces the above-average ones.

– AI2: the Allen Institute for AI, which introduced the RLVR term (Lambert et al., 2024).

• Main difference from preference tuning: a learned judge can be fooled; a program that checks the math result, the code tests or a numeric range is cheap, objective and hard to game, but only works where an answer can be checked. This is also how models learn to think: careful attempts win more often, so they get reinforced.

• Analogy: swap the tasting panel for a thermometer and a timer. A rushed, raw dish fails the reading and earns nothing; a cook who checks the oven and adjusts earns the reward. After thousands of dishes, checking as you go becomes the habit, and that habit is what learning to think looks like.

5. Stage 4: specialists first, then distillation

• Abbreviations:

– MOPD: multi-teacher on-policy distillation; several specialist teachers train one student on the student’s own answers.

– KL: Kullback-Leibler divergence, a score for how different two models’ next-word probabilities are; reverse KL penalizes the student for saying things the teacher would never say (Gu et al., 2024).

• Main difference from RLVR: one RLVR run on every domain got expensive and conflict-prone, because mixing math, code and agentic RL trades capabilities off against each other. Specialists are cheap and parallelizable, and on-policy distillation matured. So one specialist is trained per domain, then a general student writes its own answers and the relevant teacher marks it token by token (Lambert & Timbers, 2026; Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). Distillation means a student learns from a teacher’s outputs (Hinton et al., 2015), and on-policy means it learns from its own attempts, including its own mistakes (Agarwal et al., 2024).

• Analogy: a kitchen with a pastry, a grill and a sauce chef, each trained separately. A trainee cooks whole dishes alone and the matching chef tastes every spoonful as it cooks, so the correction lands at the exact step. Training one trainee on all three at once is how habits clash, such as high heat that suits a grill but ruins a custard.

Note. Summary of Stages 1 to 4 above; stage order as in Lambert and Timbers (2026).

6. Where human experts fit

• SFT: expert-written answers.

• Preference tuning: expert rankings.

• RLVR: rubrics, for example in finance and law. A good rubric accepts more than one valid method, and in a MOPD pipeline the finance teacher is only as good as the tasks and rubrics behind it. Rubrics are already delivering gains beyond verifiable domains (Gunjal et al., 2025).

• Hard-to-verify tasks: the DeepSeek-V4 report describes rubric-guided RL data scored by a generative reward model, which works with only a small set of diverse human annotations (DeepSeek-AI, 2026).

Part 2: Preference Data1. Preferences are what we reach for when there is no right answer

• Why it works: it is far easier to judge than to generate, so people can tell which answer is better even when they could not write it themselves (Lambert, n.d.).

Note. Examples and framing as in Lambert (n.d.).

2. Three branches converge into RLHF

• Optimal control: a framework for optimization with dynamic programming and mathematical underpinnings, which led to reinforcement learning and then deep RL (Lambert et al., 2023).

• Deep learning: neural networks and the scaling of data and problem complexity, which led to large language models (Lambert et al., 2023).

• Economics and decision theory: individual preferences, decision theory and methods for comparing preferences (Lambert et al., 2023).

Note. Figure from Lambert et al. (2023), shown with the original attribution.

3. Utility: from logic to number

• Port-Royal Logic: it supports the idea that decision quality is an outcome weighted by its probability (Arnauld, 1662).

4. Reward: giving the model a direction

• Value function: gives directions toward preferred behavior (Singh et al., 2009).

• Decisions: are made to transition to higher-valued states (Singh et al., 2009).

5. Interface of preference data

• Likert score: the rater gives a response a score on a fixed scale, as in early Claude’s preference interface (Bai et al., 2022).

• A/B test: the rater chooses between two responses (Lambert, n.d.).

• Pairwise with ties: the rater chooses between two responses or marks a tie, as in the Chatbot Arena public evaluation (Chiang et al., 2024).

• A single bit: thumbs up or thumbs down on one response (Lambert, n.d.).

• Pick from many: the rater picks the best from several responses, the default in image models (Lambert, n.d.).

6. Ratings and rankings

• Ratings: a score on one completion in isolation (Lambert, n.d.).

• Rankings: relative comparisons between responses, often on a Likert scale (Bai et al., 2022).

7. The unaudited gap

• Chain: Spec → Data → Behaviour; the Spec is the documented intended behavior, for example the Model Spec (OpenAI, 2024).

• Unaudited link: the step from Data to Behaviour is not checked, meaning nobody verifies whether the values written down by the annotators are actually reflected in the final model (Lambert, n.d.).

Appendix

• A1. Origin of weights

– They are the billions of numbers inside a model, starting as small random values. Pre-training nudges them until they encode grammar, facts and reasoning patterns; post-training makes comparatively small adjustments.

• A2. Token, vector, embedding table

– A token is a chunk of text with a fixed ID, a label with no meaning of its own. A vector is a list of numbers that represents meaning. The embedding table turns each token ID into its starting vector. Only the embedding table and the layers that transform vectors are weights; tokens and vectors are the data flowing through them.

• A3. RL vs SFT

– Studying a book of grandmaster games (SFT) versus playing thousands of games and learning only whether you won (RL). SFT is capped near the quality of its examples; RL can go beyond them.

• A4. Two reward models in Llama 2

– Helpfulness and safety can pull against each other, like a taste critic and a health inspector: the tastiest dish can break the health rules, and a kitchen that plays it too safe serves nothing. For risky prompts the safety score takes priority.

• A5. R1-Zero vs R1, and cold start

– R1-Zero was the experiment, pure RL with strong reasoning but messy output; R1 was the product. A cold start gives the model a small SFT warm-up so it already writes in a clean, consistent format, and RL then spends its effort on correctness instead of readability.

• A6. Rubrics and rubric weights

– A rubric is a judging checklist of yes-or-no items any judge can run on any answer, like “the middle is fully cooked” at a baking contest. Rubric weights, from 1 to 10, set how many points each item is worth. They are not model weights: the weighted score becomes the reward that adjusts the model’s weights.

• A7. Teacher marking vs golden answer and reward model

– No. The student writes its own answer and only the relevant teacher marks it at every token. A golden answer is one fixed text and a reward model gives one score at the end, while a teacher gives an opinion on every word.

• A8. Conflicting skills in the student

– Much less than in one mixed RL run, because each question gets feedback from one teacher only. The conflict does not vanish, since the student has finite capacity and the mix of questions still has to be tuned.

• A9. KL divergence and reverse KL

– Zero means two distributions are identical. Reverse KL punishes the student for putting probability on words the teacher thinks are unlikely, so it avoids mistakes the expert would never make and commits to good answers.

• A10. Trace distillation SFT vs the final climb in MAI-Thinking-1

– A trace is written step-by-step reasoning, and a climb is Microsoft AI’s word for a long RL run that keeps improving a score. In trace distillation SFT, traces from three specialists (SWE and agentic; STEM; helpfulness and safety) are collected and one model is fine-tuned on them. The final climb is one more RL run on that consolidated model. Like three tutors writing binders of worked solutions that one student studies, then sits mock exams with a grader. That is why it is closer to R1 than to V4 (Microsoft AI, 2026).

items.title: Even San Francisco Is Turning Against AI
items.summary: For years, San Francisco has been a haven for AI optimists, leaving many of them baffled when they travel beyond the Bay Area and encounter people outside their industry who despise the tech. Increasingly, though, not even the City by the Bay is managing to keep AI hatred at, well, bay — at least if its dating scene is any indication. According to on the ground reporting by The Verge , AI has become a dealbreaker among the lovelorn on dating apps, despite the city being the intellectual heart of the AI boom. “Hinge has a prompt where you can say, ‘We’ll get along if.” Sometimes people will be like, ‘F*ck AI,'” a 25-year-old analyst told the outlet. It only took her a few minutes of swiping to pull up a profile that said: “You should *not* go out with me if… you use AI.” Even local voters are swiping left on the tech. Several Bay Area cities, including San Francisco, Oakland, and Richmond, have passed short-term moratoriums on data center construction over the past few months. Other intrusions of tech into daily life have caused friction among locals, including the proliferation of AI food slop posters and self-driving robotaxis . Some consider AI a central concern in their search for a partner for altogether different reasons. Another lonely heart The Verge talked to works at an AI safety nonprofit and can’t help but factor in how AI might soon destroy the world when he considers his future love life and considerations like having kids. “A lot of people are planning for what they want their life to look like five, 10, 15 years down the line,” he told the outlet. “For me, it’s hard to have that planning conversation because I don’t really expect a long-term future.” So would he date someone who works in AI? He’s not quite sure. “They don’t think very hard about the societal impacts of their actions because they’re mostly in it for the paycheck or because it’s interesting,” he added. Of course, this is San Francisco we’re talking about. So naturally people consider AI important to dating because they use the tech to optimize their love escapades. One 21-year-old software engineer explained to the Verge how he used AI to automate his dating life since he’s too busy running a startup. He lets an AI agent control his Hinge account where it mimics how he texts and acts while automatically messaging women, gauges if a woman makes a good match, and automatically marks down a date on his calendar “If you are a founder, you have to put a value on your time, so you can’t be doing low-leverage activities. Protect your dopamine, folks,” he told the site, claiming that he goes on two dates a week. His AI dating scheme, he boasted, has lowered his “CPN” — or, with all apologies in advance, “cost per nut.” Only in San Francisco. You take the AI luddites with the AI lunatics. More on AI: Wealthy Tech Guys Can’t Get Dates Because They’re So Widely Hated That Not Even Money Is Making Women Grimace and Deal With Them

items.title: Agentic RAG vs. Plain Hybrid RAG: What My Hydropower Benchmark Revealed
items.summary:
Most RAG applications follow a simple path: Retrieve a few documents → send them to an LLM → generate an answer. That works for straightforward lookup questions. But it becomes fragile when the question spans multiple manuals, needs numerical reasoning, contains tables, or asks for an engineering recommendation grounded in plant documentation. I built an Agentic RAG system for Small Hydropower Plant (SHP) engineering to explore a harder question: Can a multi-agent retrieval workflow improve the quality of answers from private technical documents without depending on paid inference APIs? The answer, based on my evaluation so far, is nuanced: it improves retrieval precision, but comes with a substantial latency cost and does not automatically outperform a well-designed plain RAG pipeline on faithfulness. The complete implementation is available here: Agentic RAG for Small Hydropower . Built for learners: no paid inference APIs required One of my goals was to make this project accessible to students and independent learners who cannot afford recurring API bills. The core RAG pipeline runs locally using Ollama and open-weight models. Document processing, embeddings, retrieval, answer generation, and runtime quality checks do not require paid cloud inference APIs. Once the required models and dependencies are downloaded, you can experiment on compatible hardware without paying per question or per token. For offline benchmarking, I used Gemini and Groq through their available free tiers to evaluate answers against the golden dataset. Those services are optional: evaluation can also use a local Ollama judge. Free-tier quotas and availability may change, so they should not be treated as an unlimited resource. This does not mean running the system has zero cost — hardware, electricity, and inference time still matter. But if you already have a suitable computer, it removes a major barrier to learning: a recurring inference bill. For me, that makes the project useful beyond hydropower. It provides a practical starting point for learning document ingestion, hybrid retrieval, agent orchestration, tool use, and evaluation within a limited budget. The problem: engineering knowledge is not a single-document lookup task Small hydropower projects involve a mix of technical manuals, regulatory guidelines, turbine-selection references, hydrology documents, financial policies, scanned reports, tables, and drawings. A typical question may require several kinds of evidence at once: Which turbine is suitable for a particular head and discharge? What are the applicable regulatory requirements? Which maintenance practices reduce silt erosion? Can the system calculate power output from provided values? Is the answer actually supported by the retrieved documents? A traditional RAG pipeline may retrieve relevant passages, but it usually has no mechanism to decide whether the retrieved context is sufficient, whether a calculation should use a tool, or whether the generated answer contains unsupported claims. That is where the agentic approach becomes useful. Before retrieval: turning engineering documents into usable evidence The first challenge was preparing the documents. Hydropower knowledge arrives in different formats: digital PDFs, scanned reports, Word documents, presentations, spreadsheets, and images. Each format needs a different extraction approach. I built a multi-tier parsing pipeline that converts these files into Markdown before chunking and embedding. Tier 1: Dedicated parsers for Office documents and text For formats with accessible document structure, the pipeline uses dedicated libraries: This avoids sending every file through a more expensive OCR process. Tier 2: Markdown extraction for digital PDFs For PDFs, the pipeline first uses pymupdf4llm to extract text into Markdown, aiming to retain headings and table structure. If the extracted output contains at least 80 characters, the current implementation accepts it. If the output is shorter — or extraction fails — the document moves to the Docling fallback. This is a practical routing heuristic, but it has a limitation: a PDF containing both digital text and scanned pages may pass the threshold even when some pages need OCR. Page-level quality checks would improve this approach. Tier 3: OCR and layout recovery Scanned PDFs and failed PDF extractions are processed with Docling, with OCR and table-structure recovery enabled when the required backend is available. Images also enter the Docling conversion path. The PDF OCR configuration prefers EasyOCR, with RapidOCR as an alternative. It uses CUDA acceleration when available and otherwise falls back to CPU execution. The aim is to recover readable text and useful table structure. Complex drawings, dense tables, and formulas remain difficult, so extracted Markdown should not be assumed to reproduce every detail correctly. Keeping the source traceable Alongside the Markdown, the parser records source information such as the filename, file type, content hash, parsing duration, and page count where available. Parsing failures are recorded explicitly. The content hash also supports caching: an unchanged document can reuse its existing Markdown output, avoiding unnecessary processing. The resulting flow is: Raw documents → format-specific parsing or OCR → Markdown and metadata → chunking → embeddings and indexing This stage directly affects everything that follows. If a table loses its units or OCR misreads a formula, the retrieval and generation stages may work with incorrect evidence. Improving parsing is therefore part of improving answer quality. Binary SHA-256 deduplication is an efficient first line of defense to prevent wasting heavy parsing and OCR compute on identical files, but for the same converted file, Binary deduplication will NOT be applicable — the system will treat them as two completely separate files An actual record saved in data/parsed/metadata.json { "source_path": "D:\GenAi_Code\Agentic_RAG\data\raw\AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf", "file_name": "AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf", "file_type": "PDF", "file_hash": "127653ce9e3151fd6732fd83bfc66e570ab762bdafb22d568fcef524ce0d19bc", "page_count": 0, "parsed_at": 1793168584.5575593, "parse_duration_s": 0.0, "parsed_md_path": "D:\GenAi_Code\Agentic_RAG\data\parsed\AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment__127653ce.md", "error": null } Chunking methodology: preserving structure and source context After parsing, the documents are available as Markdown. The next challenge is dividing them into passages that are useful for retrieval without losing their context. I implemented a Markdown-aware hierarchical chunker. It uses document structure and text length for boundaries, rather than an LLM or embedding-based semantic segmentation model. The chunker uses a 4-pass rule-based pipeline rather than an LLM or arbitrary character slicing: [Raw Markdown Document] │ ▼ ┌─────────┐ │ Pass 1 │ Scan whole document → Divide into Structural Sections └─────────┘ │ Output: `sections` list ▼ ┌─────────┐ │ Pass 2 │ Process all sections → Split into Target-Sized Chunks (1,800 chars) └─────────┘ │ Output: `raw_chunks` list ▼ ┌─────────┐ │ Pass 3 │ Scan all raw chunks → Merge Tiny Leftover Fragments (< 150 chars) └─────────┘ │ Output: `merged_chunks` list ▼ ┌─────────┐ │ Pass 4 │ Enrich all chunks → Inject Citation Banners & Compute Token Counts └─────────┘ │ Output: `final_chunks` list (Written to `chunks.jsonl`) ▼ [Final Output] 1. Split by document structure (Pass 1) Instead of chopping text blindly every NNN characters, the chunker walks through the document line-by-line, tracking markdown headings (#, ##, ###, ####) like a tree or outline. Whenever a heading or a horizontal divider (---) appears, it finishes the current section. It also checks if the heading mentions a slide or page number. When a heading includes a label such as “Slide 12” or “Page 8,” that location is captured as metadata. Page references therefore depend on what the parsing stage preserves; they are not automatically available for every chunk. 2. Split long narrative sections at natural boundaries (Pass 2) Within a section, long text is divided at paragraph boundaries. Oversized paragraphs are further split at sentence boundaries. In simple words: If a text section is too long (>1,800 characters): It first splits cleanly at double newlines (

) to preserve whole paragraphs. If a single paragraph is still too massive, it splits at sentence boundaries (., !, ?). Conditional Overlap: Traditional RAG blindly copies the last N characters (often cutting words in half). Here, the previous paragraph is only carried over if its length is ≤150 characters. The default settings are: The overlap is conditional, rather than a fixed sliding window: the previous paragraph is repeated only when it fits within the overlap allowance. The 1,800-character setting is a target, not a strict maximum. Long individual sentences, table rows, fragment merging, and added source metadata can produce larger chunks. max_chars = 1800 overlap_chars = 150 Imagine a document section with four paragraphs: Paragraph 1 (900 chars): Details about Francis turbine runner design. Paragraph 2 (800 chars): Details about guide vanes and water flow. Paragraph 3 (85 chars): "Cavitation occurs when local water pressure drops below vapor pressure." Paragraph 4 (600 chars): Explaining preventative coatings and blade maintenance. What happens: 1. Building Chunk 1: Adds Para 1 (900 chars) + Para 2 (800 chars) + Para 3 (85 chars) = 1,785 chars. Current chunk is full (≈1800). 2. Along comes Paragraph 4 (600 chars): 1,785+600=2,385 chars (exceeds 1,800!). So Chunk 1 is saved containing: [Para 1 + Para 2 + Para 3]. 3. Now, how should Chunk 2 start? The code looks at the last paragraph of Chunk 1 (Paragraph 3). Paragraph 3 is 85 chars long. Is 85≤150 (overlap_chars)? YES! Because Paragraph 3 is a short, complete sentence, the code carries it over as a natural bridge into Chunk 2: Chunk 2 begins with: "Cavitation occurs when local water pressure drops below vapor pressure. [Paragraph 4 text about coatings and blade maintenance...]" Result: Chunk 2 now has immediate context on why coatings are needed, without cutting any words or sentences in half! What if Paragraph 3 had been huge (e.g. 600 chars)? If Paragraph 3 had been 600 chars, len(current_chunk[-1]) <= 150 would be False. Repeating a massive 600-character block would waste one-third of Chunk 2's capacity. The condition fails, so Chunk 2 starts cleanly with Paragraph 4 alone. 3. Preserve table headers and rows (Pass 2) Tables need different handling from narrative text. In standard chunkers, a long table gets sliced across arbitrary character limits, leaving half the data rows orphaned without column names. This chunker: If a table has 40 rows and exceeds 1,800 characters, it slices it into smaller tables, repeating the top column headers on every slice: Detects Markdown tables (| col1 | col2 |). Slices large tables row-by-row . Repeats the table header and divider row at the top of every chunk slice so the numbers always retain their meaning. Tags the chunk with is_table = True so the agent can run table-specific filtered searches. 4. Attach breadcrumbs and citation metadata (Pass 3) When an embedding model or LLM sees an isolated chunk like “The operating head is 45 meters” , it doesn’t know which plant or turbine that applies to. To fix this, the chunker injects a context banner directly at the top of the chunk’s text: [Source: Turbine_Manual.pdf | Location: Slide/Page 12 | Section: Turbine Manual > Selection Guidelines > Francis Turbines] The operating head is 45 meters... In Pass 2: The chunker fills Chunk 1 up to the target limit (∼1,800 characters). There are 50 characters left over at the end of the section: example:"Refer to Figure 4 for full assembly diagrams." (49 chars) Pass 2 splits this leftover into Chunk 2. The Problem: If left alone, Chunk 2 would be indexed into Qdrant as its own chunk with only 49 characters! If a user searches for something, retrieving that tiny chunk alone is useless. Pass 3 to the rescue: Pass 3 looks at Chunk 2: Size = 49 characters. Is 49<150 (min_chars)? Yes! It appends that 49-character sentence back into Chunk 1. Result: Chunk 1 becomes 1,849 characters (which is completely fine because 1,800 is a soft target), and the tiny orphan chunk is eliminated! Both the raw content and the banner-enriched content are saved. 5. Save chunks for embedding and retrieval (pass 4) Chunks are saved to data/chunks/chunks.jsonl (streaming format for easy reading line-by-line). A high-level statistics file (data/chunks/chunk_summary.json) records total chunks, average tokens, and table counts. tiktoken (cl100k_base) is used for fast token size estimation: These counts help inspect chunk sizes, but they are not exact token counts for the Qwen embedding model because the tokenizers differ. The goal is to create passages that remain understandable after retrieval: a paragraph carries its section context, a table slice retains its headers, and each result can be traced back to its source. # 1. Build the citation context banner banner_parts = [ f"Source: {source_file}", # "HDP_AHN511.ppt" f"Location: Slide/Page {page_or_slide}", # "Location: Slide/Page 1" f"Section: {breadcrumb}" # "Section: HDP_AHN511 > Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing..." ] banner = f"[{' | '.join(banner_parts)}]

" # 2. Prepend banner to the raw text enriched_content = banner + raw_text # 3. Generate structured chunk ID chunk_id = f"{file_stem}__{file_hash[:8]}__c{idx:04d}" # Output -> "HDP_AHN511__9fe0f668__c0002" The chunk is written as a single-line JSON record: { "chunk_id": "HDP_AHN511__9fe0f668__c0002", "source_file": "HDP_AHN511.ppt", "file_type": "PowerPoint (legacy)", "document_title": "HDP_AHN511", "breadcrumb": "HDP_AHN511 > Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing of electrical power", "section_hierarchy": [ "HDP_AHN511", "Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing of electrical power" ], "page_or_slide": 1, "chunk_index": 2, "total_chunks": 37, "is_table": false, "char_count": 531, "token_count": 121, "content": "[Source: HDP_AHN511.ppt | Location: Slide/Page 1 | Section: HDP_AHN511 > Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing of electrical power]

## Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing of electrical power
Based On UI Mechanism 
(Availability Base Tariff)

> **[Slide 1 Image/Diagram OCR]**: HETT", "raw_content": "## Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing of electrical power
Based On UI Mechanism..." } Vector indexing: storing embeddings and evidence in Qdrant After chunking, each passage is embedded locally using qwen3-embedding:0.6b. The indexer expects a 1,024-dimensional vector and stores it in a Qdrant collection named shp_knowledge. Every chunk is represented by a list of 1,024 numbers. Each stored point has three parts: A unique identifier for the chunk: Qdrant requires point IDs to be valid numbers or UUIDs.Instead of generating a random UUID (like uuid4()), it uses uuid5 , which turns the string chunk_id (e.g. Turbine__127653ce__c0001) into the exact same UUID every single time. If you run indexing twice, Qdrant will simply overwrite/update the existing point instead of creating duplicate entries. point_uuid = manager.chunk_id_to_uuid("HDP_AHN511__9fe0f668__c0002") # Returns deterministic UUID5: "877250c9-fe3a-55c0-96a9-89d7d65a689a" An embedding vector for similarity search. Each chunk is converted into a vector using qwen3-embedding:0.6b. Typical chunks are small relative to the configured input limit. However, the chunk-size target is not a strict maximum: long sentences, table rows, merged fragments, and source banners can produce larger inputs. Oversized chunks should therefore be checked using the embedding model’s tokenizer and the input limit configured in the serving runtime. The chunker’s tiktoken counts are estimates, not exact counts for the Qwen model. { "chunk_id": "HDP_AHN511__9fe0f668__c0002", "source_file": "HDP_AHN511.ppt", ... "embedding": [ 0.002478, 0.005229, -0.005374, -0.025804, 0.025764, ... 1024 float numbers total ... ] } A metadata payload containing the text and its source context point = models.PointStruct( # 1. Unique deterministic ID id="877250c9-fe3a-55c0-96a9-89d7d65a689a", # 2. The 1024-dim vector for Cosine similarity search vector=[0.002478, 0.005229, -0.005374, ...], # 3. Payload: Metadata + Context text for LLM retrieval and filtering payload={ "chunk_id": "HDP_AHN511__9fe0f668__c0002", "source_file": "HDP_AHN511.ppt", "file_type": "PowerPoint (legacy)", "is_table": "false", "page_or_slide": 1, "breadcrumb": "HDP_AHN511 > Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing of electrical power", "section_hierarchy": ["HDP_AHN511", "Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing of electrical power"], "token_count": 121, "char_count": 531, "content": "[Source: HDP_AHN511.ppt | Location: Slide/Page 1 | Section: ...]

## Slide 1: ...", "text": "[Source: HDP_AHN511.ppt | Location: Slide/Page 1 | Section: ...]

## Slide 1: ..." } ) The embedding helps locate passages with similar meaning. The payload lets the application read the evidence, apply filters, and identify where it came from. How metadata is generated Metadata is assembled during parsing and chunking, then carried into the index. It is derived from filenames, document structure, extracted location labels, and chunk statistics rather than generated by an LLM. This metadata helps the agents retrieve more selectively. A request for a discharge table can use a table filter, while a document-specific question can constrain retrieval to a source file. How indexing works The indexer reads embedded chunks from JSONL, checks that each vector has the expected dimensions, and uploads points in batches of 128 by default. It converts each chunk ID into a deterministic UUID5 identifier. Re-indexing the same chunk updates the corresponding point instead of creating another copy. That handles repeated indexing of unchanged chunks. Updating a document is a separate concern: changed content can produce new chunk IDs, so removing obsolete document versions requires an explicit cleanup strategy. The collection uses cosine similarity to compare query vectors with stored chunk vectors. Its configuration requests on-disk vectors and payloads, and the indexer creates payload indexes for source_file, file_type, is_table, and page_or_slide. Why I chose Qdrant Qdrant fits three requirements of this project. Local deployment. The application can connect to a Qdrant server inside the organization’s infrastructure. The index manager also supports embedded local disk storage for development, reducing setup requirements for learners. Similarity search with metadata filters. Engineering questions often need both semantic matching and precise constraints. Keeping vectors and source metadata together allows the retriever to combine those requirements. A straightforward indexing workflow. Collections, payloads, deterministic point IDs, and batch upserts map naturally to the project’s document-and-chunk model. These were practical reasons for choosing Qdrant; ChromaDB was also a viable option for local development and metadata-based retrieval. I chose Qdrant for its dedicated vector-search service and configurable payload indexes, which fit my document-filtering requirements. This was an architectural choice, rather than a claim that Qdrant universally outperforms ChromaDB. The project does not benchmark it against other vector databases. Qdrant’s role in hybrid retrieval Qdrant provides the dense retrieval component. A separate local BM25 retriever handles keyword matching, and the application combines their rankings using Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Dense retrieval helps with conceptual similarity. BM25 helps with exact terminology, project names, and document identifiers. Combining the two gives the system complementary ways to find evidence before synthesis and answer generation. The architecture I built The system is designed to run locally with Ollama and Qdrant, making it suitable for document sets that should remain inside an organization. Planner Agent The Planner Agent first classifies the request into one of three routes: Direct answer : Conversational greetings or general questions that do not need documentation. Out-of-scope query : Questions outside small hydropower engineering (e.g. general politics, unrelated code), routed to a polite domain-boundary refusal. RAG-required technical query : Technical questions that proceed to retrieval. For engineering questions, it elaborates domain terms and decomposes broad queries into focused sub-queries with targeted metadata filters (e.g., tagging a discharge inquiry with is_table: true). 2. Orchestrator and specialized workers The Orchestrator dispatches sub-queries to specialized workers using LangGraph’s dynamic Send() API: Narrative retriever : Dense and keyword retrieval over technical principles, manuals, and descriptive text (filter: is_table=false). Tabular retriever : Targeted retrieval over head-flow matrices, turbine efficiency curves, and cost tables (filter: is_table=true). MCP tool worker : Deterministic engineering calculations (power equations P=ηρgQH, specific speed Ns, penstock sizing) and plant telemetry via a dedicated FastAPI Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. You can add multiple workers as you want. For document retrieval, the system combines dense semantic search (Qdrant) and sparse keyword search (BM25) using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) . Exact equipment designations, Indian Standards (IS codes), and plant names receive exact-match boosting. 3. items.summary_html:
Most RAG applications follow a simple path:

Retrieve a few documents → send them to an LLM → generate an answer.

That works for straightforward lookup questions. But it becomes fragile when the question spans multiple manuals, needs numerical reasoning, contains tables, or asks for an engineering recommendation grounded in plant documentation.

I built an Agentic RAG system for Small Hydropower Plant (SHP) engineering to explore a harder question:

Can a multi-agent retrieval workflow improve the quality of answers from private technical documents without depending on paid inference APIs?

The answer, based on my evaluation so far, is nuanced: it improves retrieval precision, but comes with a substantial latency cost and does not automatically outperform a well-designed plain RAG pipeline on faithfulness.

The complete implementation is available here: Agentic RAG for Small Hydropower.
Built for learners: no paid inference APIs required

One of my goals was to make this project accessible to students and independent learners who cannot afford recurring API bills.

The core RAG pipeline runs locally using Ollama and open-weight models. Document processing, embeddings, retrieval, answer generation, and runtime quality checks do not require paid cloud inference APIs. Once the required models and dependencies are downloaded, you can experiment on compatible hardware without paying per question or per token.

For offline benchmarking, I used Gemini and Groq through their available free tiers to evaluate answers against the golden dataset. Those services are optional: evaluation can also use a local Ollama judge. Free-tier quotas and availability may change, so they should not be treated as an unlimited resource.

This does not mean running the system has zero cost — hardware, electricity, and inference time still matter. But if you already have a suitable computer, it removes a major barrier to learning: a recurring inference bill.

For me, that makes the project useful beyond hydropower. It provides a practical starting point for learning document ingestion, hybrid retrieval, agent orchestration, tool use, and evaluation within a limited budget.

The problem: engineering knowledge is not a single-document lookup task

Small hydropower projects involve a mix of technical manuals, regulatory guidelines, turbine-selection references, hydrology documents, financial policies, scanned reports, tables, and drawings.

A typical question may require several kinds of evidence at once:

  • Which turbine is suitable for a particular head and discharge?
  • What are the applicable regulatory requirements?
  • Which maintenance practices reduce silt erosion?
  • Can the system calculate power output from provided values?
  • Is the answer actually supported by the retrieved documents?

A traditional RAG pipeline may retrieve relevant passages, but it usually has no mechanism to decide whether the retrieved context is sufficient, whether a calculation should use a tool, or whether the generated answer contains unsupported claims.

That is where the agentic approach becomes useful.

Before retrieval: turning engineering documents into usable evidence

The first challenge was preparing the documents. Hydropower knowledge arrives in different formats: digital PDFs, scanned reports, Word documents, presentations, spreadsheets, and images. Each format needs a different extraction approach.

I built a multi-tier parsing pipeline that converts these files into Markdown before chunking and embedding.

Tier 1: Dedicated parsers for Office documents and text

For formats with accessible document structure, the pipeline uses dedicated libraries:

This avoids sending every file through a more expensive OCR process.

Tier 2: Markdown extraction for digital PDFs

For PDFs, the pipeline first uses pymupdf4llm to extract text into Markdown, aiming to retain headings and table structure.

If the extracted output contains at least 80 characters, the current implementation accepts it. If the output is shorter — or extraction fails — the document moves to the Docling fallback.

This is a practical routing heuristic, but it has a limitation: a PDF containing both digital text and scanned pages may pass the threshold even when some pages need OCR. Page-level quality checks would improve this approach.

Tier 3: OCR and layout recovery

Scanned PDFs and failed PDF extractions are processed with Docling, with OCR and table-structure recovery enabled when the required backend is available. Images also enter the Docling conversion path.

The PDF OCR configuration prefers EasyOCR, with RapidOCR as an alternative. It uses CUDA acceleration when available and otherwise falls back to CPU execution.

The aim is to recover readable text and useful table structure. Complex drawings, dense tables, and formulas remain difficult, so extracted Markdown should not be assumed to reproduce every detail correctly.

Keeping the source traceable

Alongside the Markdown, the parser records source information such as the filename, file type, content hash, parsing duration, and page count where available. Parsing failures are recorded explicitly.

The content hash also supports caching: an unchanged document can reuse its existing Markdown output, avoiding unnecessary processing.

The resulting flow is:

Raw documents → format-specific parsing or OCR → Markdown and metadata → chunking → embeddings and indexing

This stage directly affects everything that follows. If a table loses its units or OCR misreads a formula, the retrieval and generation stages may work with incorrect evidence. Improving parsing is therefore part of improving answer quality.

Binary SHA-256 deduplication is an efficient first line of defense to prevent wasting heavy parsing and OCR compute on identical files, but for the same converted file, Binary deduplication will NOT be applicable — the system will treat them as two completely separate files

An actual record saved in data/parsed/metadata.json
{
  "source_path": "D:\GenAi_Code\Agentic_RAG\data\raw\AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf",
  "file_name": "AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf",
  "file_type": "PDF",
  "file_hash": "127653ce9e3151fd6732fd83bfc66e570ab762bdafb22d568fcef524ce0d19bc",
  "page_count": 0,
  "parsed_at": 1793168584.5575593,
  "parse_duration_s": 0.0,
  "parsed_md_path": "D:\GenAi_Code\Agentic_RAG\data\parsed\AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment__127653ce.md",
  "error": null
}
Chunking methodology: preserving structure and source context

After parsing, the documents are available as Markdown. The next challenge is dividing them into passages that are useful for retrieval without losing their context. I implemented a Markdown-aware hierarchical chunker. It uses document structure and text length for boundaries, rather than an LLM or embedding-based semantic segmentation model.

The chunker uses a 4-pass rule-based pipeline rather than an LLM or arbitrary character slicing:

[Raw Markdown Document]
       │
       ▼
   ┌─────────┐
   │ Pass 1  │  Scan whole document → Divide into Structural Sections
   └─────────┘
       │  Output: `sections` list
       ▼
   ┌─────────┐
   │ Pass 2  │  Process all sections → Split into Target-Sized Chunks (1,800 chars)
   └─────────┘
       │  Output: `raw_chunks` list
       ▼
   ┌─────────┐
   │ Pass 3  │  Scan all raw chunks → Merge Tiny Leftover Fragments (< 150 chars)
   └─────────┘
       │  Output: `merged_chunks` list
       ▼
   ┌─────────┐
   │ Pass 4  │  Enrich all chunks → Inject Citation Banners & Compute Token Counts
   └─────────┘
       │  Output: `final_chunks` list (Written to `chunks.jsonl`)
       ▼
[Final Output]
1. Split by document structure (Pass 1)

Instead of chopping text blindly every NNN characters, the chunker walks through the document line-by-line, tracking markdown headings (#, ##, ###, ####) like a tree or outline. Whenever a heading or a horizontal divider (---) appears, it finishes the current section. It also checks if the heading mentions a slide or page number.

When a heading includes a label such as “Slide 12” or “Page 8,” that location is captured as metadata. Page references therefore depend on what the parsing stage preserves; they are not automatically available for every chunk.

2. Split long narrative sections at natural boundaries (Pass 2)

Within a section, long text is divided at paragraph boundaries. Oversized paragraphs are further split at sentence boundaries.

In simple words: If a text section is too long (>1,800 characters):

  1. It first splits cleanly at double newlines ( ) to preserve whole paragraphs.
  2. If a single paragraph is still too massive, it splits at sentence boundaries (., !, ?).
  3. Conditional Overlap: Traditional RAG blindly copies the last N characters (often cutting words in half). Here, the previous paragraph is only carried over if its length is ≤150 characters.

The default settings are:

The overlap is conditional, rather than a fixed sliding window: the previous paragraph is repeated only when it fits within the overlap allowance.

The 1,800-character setting is a target, not a strict maximum. Long individual sentences, table rows, fragment merging, and added source metadata can produce larger chunks.

max_chars = 1800
overlap_chars = 150

Imagine a document section with four paragraphs:

Paragraph 1 (900 chars): Details about Francis turbine runner design.
Paragraph 2 (800 chars): Details about guide vanes and water flow.
Paragraph 3 (85 chars): "Cavitation occurs when local water pressure drops below vapor pressure."
Paragraph 4 (600 chars): Explaining preventative coatings and blade maintenance.
What happens:

1. Building Chunk 1:
  Adds Para 1 (900 chars) + Para 2 (800 chars) + Para 3 (85 chars) = 1,785 chars.
  Current chunk is full (≈1800).
2. Along comes Paragraph 4 (600 chars):
  1,785+600=2,385 chars (exceeds 1,800!).
  So Chunk 1 is saved containing: [Para 1 + Para 2 + Para 3].
3. Now, how should Chunk 2 start?
  The code looks at the last paragraph of Chunk 1 (Paragraph 3).
  Paragraph 3 is 85 chars long.
  Is 85≤150 (overlap_chars)? YES!
  Because Paragraph 3 is a short, complete sentence, the code carries it over as a natural bridge into Chunk 2:

Chunk 2 begins with:
"Cavitation occurs when local water pressure drops below vapor pressure.
[Paragraph 4 text about coatings and blade maintenance...]"

  Result: Chunk 2 now has immediate context on why coatings are needed, without cutting any words or sentences in half!

What if Paragraph 3 had been huge (e.g. 600 chars)?
  If Paragraph 3 had been 600 chars, len(current_chunk[-1]) <= 150 would be False.
  Repeating a massive 600-character block would waste one-third of Chunk 2's capacity.
  The condition fails, so Chunk 2 starts cleanly with Paragraph 4 alone.
3. Preserve table headers and rows (Pass 2)

Tables need different handling from narrative text. In standard chunkers, a long table gets sliced across arbitrary character limits, leaving half the data rows orphaned without column names. This chunker: If a table has 40 rows and exceeds 1,800 characters, it slices it into smaller tables, repeating the top column headers on every slice:

  1. Detects Markdown tables (| col1 | col2 |).
  2. Slices large tables row-by-row.
  3. Repeats the table header and divider row at the top of every chunk slice so the numbers always retain their meaning.
  4. Tags the chunk with is_table = True so the agent can run table-specific filtered searches.
4. Attach breadcrumbs and citation metadata (Pass 3)

When an embedding model or LLM sees an isolated chunk like “The operating head is 45 meters”, it doesn’t know which plant or turbine that applies to. To fix this, the chunker injects a context banner directly at the top of the chunk’s text:

[Source: Turbine_Manual.pdf | Location: Slide/Page 12 | Section: Turbine Manual > Selection Guidelines > Francis Turbines]
The operating head is 45 meters...
In Pass 2:
The chunker fills Chunk 1 up to the target limit (∼1,800 characters).
There are 50 characters left over at the end of the section:
 example:"Refer to Figure 4 for full assembly diagrams." (49 chars)
Pass 2 splits this leftover into Chunk 2.

The Problem:
If left alone, Chunk 2 would be indexed into Qdrant as its own chunk with only 49 characters! If a user searches for something, retrieving that tiny chunk alone is useless.

Pass 3 to the rescue:
Pass 3 looks at Chunk 2:
  Size = 49 characters.
  Is 49<150 (min_chars)? Yes!
  It appends that 49-character sentence back into Chunk 1.

Result: Chunk 1 becomes 1,849 characters (which is completely fine because 1,800 is a soft target), and the tiny orphan chunk is eliminated!

Both the raw content and the banner-enriched content are saved.

5. Save chunks for embedding and retrieval (pass 4)
  • Chunks are saved to data/chunks/chunks.jsonl (streaming format for easy reading line-by-line).
  • A high-level statistics file (data/chunks/chunk_summary.json) records total chunks, average tokens, and table counts.
  • tiktoken (cl100k_base) is used for fast token size estimation:

These counts help inspect chunk sizes, but they are not exact token counts for the Qwen embedding model because the tokenizers differ.

The goal is to create passages that remain understandable after retrieval: a paragraph carries its section context, a table slice retains its headers, and each result can be traced back to its source.

# 1. Build the citation context banner
banner_parts = [
    f"Source: {source_file}",                    # "HDP_AHN511.ppt"
    f"Location: Slide/Page {page_or_slide}",     # "Location: Slide/Page 1"
    f"Section: {breadcrumb}"                     # "Section: HDP_AHN511 > Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing..."
]
banner = f"[{' | '.join(banner_parts)}]

"

# 2. Prepend banner to the raw text
enriched_content = banner + raw_text

# 3. Generate structured chunk ID
chunk_id = f"{file_stem}__{file_hash[:8]}__c{idx:04d}"

# Output -> "HDP_AHN511__9fe0f668__c0002"

The chunk is written as a single-line JSON record:
{
  "chunk_id": "HDP_AHN511__9fe0f668__c0002",
  "source_file": "HDP_AHN511.ppt",
  "file_type": "PowerPoint (legacy)",
  "document_title": "HDP_AHN511",
  "breadcrumb": "HDP_AHN511 > Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing of electrical power",
  "section_hierarchy": [
    "HDP_AHN511",
    "Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing of electrical power"
  ],
  "page_or_slide": 1,
  "chunk_index": 2,
  "total_chunks": 37,
  "is_table": false,
  "char_count": 531,
  "token_count": 121,
  "content": "[Source: HDP_AHN511.ppt | Location: Slide/Page 1 | Section: HDP_AHN511 > Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing of electrical power]

## Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing of electrical power
Based On UI Mechanism 
(Availability Base Tariff)

- Prof.Arunkumar                              Harshad D.Patel

Based On UI Mechanism..."
