Vector indexing: storing embeddings and evidence in Qdrant

After chunking, each passage is embedded locally using qwen3-embedding:0.6b. The indexer expects a 1,024-dimensional vector and stores it in a Qdrant collection named shp_knowledge. Every chunk is represented by a list of 1,024 numbers.

Each stored point has three parts:

  • A unique identifier for the chunk: Qdrant requires point IDs to be valid numbers or UUIDs.Instead of generating a random UUID (like uuid4()), it uses uuid5, which turns the string chunk_id (e.g. Turbine__127653ce__c0001) into the exact same UUID every single time. If you run indexing twice, Qdrant will simply overwrite/update the existing point instead of creating duplicate entries.
point_uuid = manager.chunk_id_to_uuid("HDP_AHN511__9fe0f668__c0002")
# Returns deterministic UUID5: "877250c9-fe3a-55c0-96a9-89d7d65a689a"
  • An embedding vector for similarity search. Each chunk is converted into a vector using qwen3-embedding:0.6b. Typical chunks are small relative to the configured input limit. However, the chunk-size target is not a strict maximum: long sentences, table rows, merged fragments, and source banners can produce larger inputs. Oversized chunks should therefore be checked using the embedding model’s tokenizer and the input limit configured in the serving runtime. The chunker’s tiktoken counts are estimates, not exact counts for the Qwen model.
{
  "chunk_id": "HDP_AHN511__9fe0f668__c0002",
  "source_file": "HDP_AHN511.ppt",
  ...
  "embedding": [
    0.002478, 0.005229, -0.005374, -0.025804, 0.025764, 
    ... 1024 float numbers total ...
  ]
}
  • A metadata payload containing the text and its source context
point = models.PointStruct(
    # 1. Unique deterministic ID
    id="877250c9-fe3a-55c0-96a9-89d7d65a689a",

    # 2. The 1024-dim vector for Cosine similarity search
    vector=[0.002478, 0.005229, -0.005374, ...],

    # 3. Payload: Metadata + Context text for LLM retrieval and filtering
    payload={
        "chunk_id": "HDP_AHN511__9fe0f668__c0002",
        "source_file": "HDP_AHN511.ppt",
        "file_type": "PowerPoint (legacy)",
        "is_table": "false",
        "page_or_slide": 1,
        "breadcrumb": "HDP_AHN511 > Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing of electrical power",
        "section_hierarchy": ["HDP_AHN511", "Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing of electrical power"],
        "token_count": 121,
        "char_count": 531,
        "content": "[Source: HDP_AHN511.ppt | Location: Slide/Page 1 | Section: ...]

## Slide 1: ...",
        "text": "[Source: HDP_AHN511.ppt | Location: Slide/Page 1 | Section: ...]

## Slide 1: ..."
    }
)

The embedding helps locate passages with similar meaning. The payload lets the application read the evidence, apply filters, and identify where it came from.

How metadata is generated

Metadata is assembled during parsing and chunking, then carried into the index. It is derived from filenames, document structure, extracted location labels, and chunk statistics rather than generated by an LLM.

This metadata helps the agents retrieve more selectively. A request for a discharge table can use a table filter, while a document-specific question can constrain retrieval to a source file.

How indexing works

The indexer reads embedded chunks from JSONL, checks that each vector has the expected dimensions, and uploads points in batches of 128 by default.

It converts each chunk ID into a deterministic UUID5 identifier. Re-indexing the same chunk updates the corresponding point instead of creating another copy.

That handles repeated indexing of unchanged chunks. Updating a document is a separate concern: changed content can produce new chunk IDs, so removing obsolete document versions requires an explicit cleanup strategy.

The collection uses cosine similarity to compare query vectors with stored chunk vectors. Its configuration requests on-disk vectors and payloads, and the indexer creates payload indexes for source_file, file_type, is_table, and page_or_slide.

Why I chose Qdrant

Qdrant fits three requirements of this project.

Local deployment. The application can connect to a Qdrant server inside the organization’s infrastructure. The index manager also supports embedded local disk storage for development, reducing setup requirements for learners.

Similarity search with metadata filters. Engineering questions often need both semantic matching and precise constraints. Keeping vectors and source metadata together allows the retriever to combine those requirements.

A straightforward indexing workflow. Collections, payloads, deterministic point IDs, and batch upserts map naturally to the project’s document-and-chunk model.

These were practical reasons for choosing Qdrant; ChromaDB was also a viable option for local development and metadata-based retrieval. I chose Qdrant for its dedicated vector-search service and configurable payload indexes, which fit my document-filtering requirements. This was an architectural choice, rather than a claim that Qdrant universally outperforms ChromaDB. The project does not benchmark it against other vector databases.

Qdrant’s role in hybrid retrieval

Qdrant provides the dense retrieval component. A separate local BM25 retriever handles keyword matching, and the application combines their rankings using Reciprocal Rank Fusion.

Dense retrieval helps with conceptual similarity. BM25 helps with exact terminology, project names, and document identifiers. Combining the two gives the system complementary ways to find evidence before synthesis and answer generation.

The architecture I built

The system is designed to run locally with Ollama and Qdrant, making it suitable for document sets that should remain inside an organization.

The high-level workflow is:

        │                         │                  │                         │
       END                        │                  ▼                         │

                                  │        │  Orchestrator Agent   │           │

                                  │        │   Retrieval Grader    │           │

                                  │          │         │Generation Guardail│   │
                                  │          │         │(Gate 2: Post-Gen) │   │

                                  │          │   (Grounded)      │             │

                                  │          │               & retry < max)|   |

                                  │    │  (Diagnoses query gaps & missing terms)│

                                  │
                                  │ (Ungrounded & retry >= max)

                    ┌────────────────────────────┐
                    │       Fallback Agent       │
                    │      (Circuit Breaker)     │
                    │ - Out-of-scope refusal     │
                    │ - Partial answer + warning │
                    └─────────────┬──────────────┘
                                  ▼
                                 END

Each stage has a focused responsibility.

1. Planner Agent

The Planner Agent first classifies the request into one of three routes:

  • Direct answer: Conversational greetings or general questions that do not need documentation.
  • Out-of-scope query: Questions outside small hydropower engineering (e.g. general politics, unrelated code), routed to a polite domain-boundary refusal.
  • RAG-required technical query: Technical questions that proceed to retrieval.

For engineering questions, it elaborates domain terms and decomposes broad queries into focused sub-queries with targeted metadata filters (e.g., tagging a discharge inquiry with is_table: true).

2. Orchestrator and specialized workers

The Orchestrator dispatches sub-queries to specialized workers using LangGraph’s dynamic Send() API:

  • Narrative retriever: Dense and keyword retrieval over technical principles, manuals, and descriptive text (filter: is_table=false).
  • Tabular retriever: Targeted retrieval over head-flow matrices, turbine efficiency curves, and cost tables (filter: is_table=true).
  • MCP tool worker: Deterministic engineering calculations (power equations P=ηρgQH, specific speed Ns, penstock sizing) and plant telemetry via a dedicated FastAPI Model Context Protocol (MCP) server.

You can add multiple workers as you want. For document retrieval, the system combines dense semantic search (Qdrant) and sparse keyword search (BM25) using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). Exact equipment designations, Indian Standards (IS codes), and plant names receive exact-match boosting.

3. Synthesizer Agent

The Synthesizer performs deterministic evidence assembly without an additional LLM call. It gathers worker outputs, removes duplicate chunks, balances evidence across sub-queries, and constructs a context dossier with source references for the generator. This stage still takes processing time, but avoids the inference overhead of another model call.

4. Dual Quality Gates & Self-Correction Loop

To improve answer reliability, the system implements two independent verification gates:

  • Gate 1: Pre-Generation Retrieval Sufficiency (Corrective RAG)
    Before invoking the generator, a retrieval grader checks whether the retrieved evidence actually contains the required formulas, numbers, or parameters. If critical evidence is missing and retry budget remains, the workflow requests another retrieval attempt.
  • The Generator Agent
    The generator drafts an answer when evidence passes Gate 1, or makes a best-effort attempt using available evidence when the retry budget is exhausted.qwen3.5:9b Drafts an engineering response strictly constrained to the synthesized dossier with bracketed source citations.
  • Gate 2: Post-Generation Grounding & Numerical Guardrail
    A local guardrail checks numerical claims against the available evidence. Structure-aware preprocessing reduces false positives from formatting elements such as Markdown headings, list numbers, and citation markers.
  • The Diagnostic Feedback Agent (Self-Correction)
    If either Gate 1 (insufficient context) or Gate 2 (hallucination) fails and retry budget remains, the workflow routes to a Feedback Agent. It analyzes the gap, suggests missing technical synonyms or filters, and loops back to the Planner for a targeted re-retrieval attempt (guarded by a circuit breaker to prevent infinite loops).
  • Circuit Breaker Fallback
    If the post-generation check fails after the retry budget is exhausted, the system returns a fallback response: partial findings, a data-unavailable notice, or a best-effort answer explicitly marked as unverified.
Local-first technology choices
  • Core Framework: Python, LangGraph (stateful graph with MemorySaver thread checkpoints), and LangChain.
  • Local Inference: Ollama running qwen3.5:9b (reasoning/generator) and qwen3-embedding:0.6b (1,024-dim dense vectors).
  • Vector & Keyword Stores: Qdrant (dual-mode: Docker network server or embedded local disk) and custom in-memory BM25 with disk serialization.
  • Deterministic Computation: FastAPI-based MCP tool server for exact formula execution.
  • Document Ingestion: Multi-tier smart parser (pymupdf4llm, Docling GPU vision OCR, RapidOCR, openpyxl, python-docx).
User Interface and FastAPI Backend Architecture

To make the system practical for plant engineers and operators, the user-facing interface is completely decoupled from the underlying agent execution engine.

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              Streamlit Web Frontend (Port 8601)        │
  │  [Engineering Chat]  [Hydro Calculator]  [Citations]   │
  └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                    JSON REST HTTP Requests
           (session_id, query, health probes, uploads)
                              │
                              ▼
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                 FastAPI Server (Port 8600)             │
  │   - Pre-compiles LangGraph Singleton at startup        │
  │   - Manages session threads & MemorySaver checkpointing│
  │   - Probes Ollama, Qdrant, and LangSmith health        │
  └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                [Compiled LangGraph Multi-Agent Engine]
1. Decoupled Client-Server Design

The system decouples the presentation layer from the agent execution engine and calculation services across three dedicated, non-conflicting service ports (8600–8602):

  1. Streamlit Web Portal (Port 8601):
    The interactive engineering interface (ui/app.py). It provides a multi-turn chat window, an evidence citations inspector (revealing source files, section breadcrumbs, and similarity scores), an interactive hydro sizing calculator, and a real-time system health diagnostics sidebar.
  2. FastAPI Agent Backend (Port 8600):
    The FastAPI backend (src/api/app.py)compiles the LangGraph workflow once at startup. It exposes POST /api/v1/chat for agent execution, GET /api/v1/health for diagnostics, and POST /api/v1/documents/upload for saving uploaded documents. Uploaded files require a separate ingestion run before they become searchable.
  3. FastAPI MCP Tool Server (Port 8602):
    A dedicated Model Context Protocol service (src/mcp_server/server.py) exposing deterministic formulas (P=ηρgQH, specific speed Ns​, Sarkaria penstock economic diameter) and SCADA telemetry simulation via JSON-RPC 2.0 and OpenAPI Swagger endpoints (http://localhost:8602/docs).
2. Core API Endpoints

The frontend interacts with the agent engine across three primary endpoints:

  • POST /api/v1/documents/upload: Accepts an uploaded document and saves it to the application’s data directory. The current endpoint does not automatically parse, chunk, embed, or index the file. Those steps run separately.
  • GET /api/v1/health: Real-time diagnostic heartbeat that verifies whether the local Ollama LLM, Qdrant vector database (including indexed point counts), and LangSmith tracing are online.
  • POST /api/v1/upload: Ingestion endpoint that accepts new plant documents (.pdf, .docx, .pptx), immediately passing them through the multi-tier parser and chunker for live vector indexing into Qdrant.
3. Key UI Components

The Streamlit interface organizes engineering workflows into focused tabs:

  • Engineering Assistant: Chat window rendering markdown responses, equations, and active warnings if the fallback circuit breaker was tripped.
  • Citations Inspector: An evidence inspection pane displaying the exact source documents, section breadcrumbs, similarity scores, and text excerpts used to ground each response.
  • Hydro Sizing Calculator: Computes power output and estimated annual energy directly in the Streamlit application using Python. It also provides a rule-based turbine-selection suggestion. This UI calculator operates independently of the MCP tool server used by the agent workflow.
  • System Diagnostics Sidebar: Live status pills displaying the connection health of Ollama and Qdrant, active latency telemetry, and the session ID.
Fully on-prem at runtime

A core design goal of this project is that the RAG system can run fully on-premises without depending on external inference APIs.

At runtime, the architecture uses local components:

  • Ollama for LLM inference and embeddings
  • Qdrant for vector storage and semantic retrieval
  • Local BM25 for keyword retrieval
  • Local document parsing, chunking, indexing, orchestration, and guardrails
  • FastAPI and Streamlit for the application layer

This means that plant manuals, DPRs, maintenance reports, drawings, and operational documents can remain within the organization’s own infrastructure.

External APIs such as Gemini and Groq were used only in the offline evaluation workflow as LLM-as-a-judge providers for scoring the golden dataset. They are not required for the runtime RAG pipeline.

For environments with stricter data policies, the evaluation layer can also be replaced with a local Ollama-based judge. The trade-off is that external judge models can provide an additional independent perspective during benchmarking, while a fully local evaluation setup preserves complete data isolation.

Evaluation: runtime checks and offline benchmarking

I used two evaluation layers: checks inside the running agent workflow, and an offline benchmark against a golden dataset. They answer different questions.

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. Runtime In-Flight Evaluation (Zero External APIs)                   │
│    - Gate 1: Retrieval Sufficiency Grader (qwen3.5:9b)                 │
│    - Gate 2: Faithfulness & Numerical Guardrail (qwen3.5:9b, ≥ 0.90)   │
│    - Feedback Loop & Circuit Breaker (Bounded retry budget)            │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                    │
                                    ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 2. Offline Benchmark: Agentic RAG vs. Plain Hybrid-RAG                 │
│    - 10 Head-to-Head Policy & Licensing Benchmark Cases                │
│    - Multi-provider LLM-as-a-Judge (Google Gemini 2.5 Flash & Groq)    │
│    - Evaluates: Faithfulness, Precision, Recall, Relevancy, Latency    │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Runtime evaluation (In-Flight Quality Gates): checking each response

During execution, the system uses the local qwen3.5:9b model as a judge at two stages.

  1. Retrieval Sufficiency Check (Pre-Gen): The retrieval sufficiency check evaluates whether the assembled context contains the information required to answer the question. When evidence is missing, it identifies the gaps and can trigger feedback and another retrieval attempt. The Pre-Gen Retrieval Sufficiency check (Gate 1) does NOT use a numerical threshold like 0.90. Instead, it uses a semantic boolean decision (is_sufficient: True / False) based on engineering completeness criteria.
  2. Faithfulness & Grounding Check (Post-Gen): The faithfulness check evaluates the generated answer against the available evidence. It returns a groundedness verdict, a faithfulness score, and any statements it considers unsupported. The configured faithfulness threshold is 0.90.

Both checks share a bounded retry budget (cycle_count < MAX_CYCLES). When the budget is exhausted, insufficient retrieval proceeds to best-effort generation; a failed faithfulness check then routes to a fallback response with a warning.

These checks do not require a golden answer or an external inference API. However, an LLM judge is still fallible: passing the check is a probabilistic model assessment, not a mathematical proof of factual truth

Offline evaluation: testing against the golden dataset

For empirical benchmarking, I evaluated the updated Agentic RAG workflow against a standard Plain Hybrid-RAG baseline (single dense vector search + BM25 keyword search without agents or decomposition) across 10 complex Small Hydropower policy and licensing questions from the golden dataset.

Here, “offline” means evaluation outside the live request workflow — not disconnected from the internet. API-based judging sends the evaluation content to those providers. A fully local evaluation setup can instead use an Ollama-based judge. Evaluations were performed using automated LLM-as-a-Judge scoring via Google Gemini 2.5 Flash with automated failover to Groq (openai/gpt-oss-120b).

Metrics used

The first four metrics are LLM-assigned scores on a 0–1 scale in this benchmark. They should be interpreted as judge estimates, rather than exact measurements of factual accuracy.

Hallucination rate is reported separately from average faithfulness; it is not calculated as 1 − faithfulness. Latency is measured from execution, with mean and median used to compare the two pipelines.

Together, these measures help distinguish a grounded but incomplete answer from a comprehensive answer containing unsupported claims — and show how much processing time each architecture requires.

Interpreting the results fairly

The updated head-to-head comparison covers the same ten policy/licensing questions for both systems. It does not establish performance across all engineering tasks.

The benchmark also uses multiple judge models through provider fallback, which can introduce scoring variation. A stronger follow-up would use a fixed judge configuration, repeated runs, and human review of difficult cases, especially calculations, tables, and conflicting evidence.

What the evaluation showed

I compared the updated Agentic RAG workflow with a plain hybrid-RAG baseline across 10 policy and licensing questions.

The result surprised me in a useful way.

  • A Massive Jump in Context Precision (+15.2%):
    Agentic RAG improved context precision from 57.8% to 73.0%. In Plain RAG, a broad query dumps irrelevant chunks into the prompt. In Agentic RAG, the Planner’s sub-query decomposition, the Orchestrator’s targeted worker dispatch (is_table=true/false), and the Synthesizer's deduplication successfully filtered out noise, ensuring the LLM received clearer evidence.
  • Faithfulness Did Not Improve Beyond Baseline (90.0%):
    For straightforward single-hop policy queries, once Plain RAG finds the correct paragraph, a strong generator model (qwen3.5:9b) is already capable of writing an accurate response. Adding multiple agents did not increase factual grounding for these questions.
  • The 3.1× Latency Penalty:
    Running multiple agents on local hardware compounds inference latency. Passing queries sequentially through Planner → Orchestrator → Multiple Workers→ Synthesizer → Grader→ Generator → Guardrail increased average response time from∼2.2 minutes to ∼6.8 minutes.

That is the central lesson from this project:

More agents do not automatically mean more reliable answers.

They add value when they improve retrieval quality, tool selection, and safe failure behavior. But every extra reasoning step adds latency, complexity, and more opportunities for error.

What did not work perfectly?

This project also taught me where Agentic RAG remains difficult.

Guardrails can fail for the wrong reasons

An earlier version of the numerical guardrail incorrectly flagged heading labels such as 3.1 and 4.3 as unsupported engineering claims. That created false failures and unnecessary fallback responses. The fix was not simply “use another LLM.” It required better structure-aware preprocessing before evaluating numbers.

Multi-agent workflows are expensive

Multiple LLM calls, retrieval operations, validation checks, and correction loops add processing overhead. In my local benchmark, this made the agentic workflow substantially slower than a single retrieval-and-generation pipeline.

This latency is not necessarily a fixed limitation. More capable GPUs — either on-premises or cloud-hosted — and an optimized inference engine such as vLLM could reduce model-serving overhead. Prefix caching can avoid reprocessing shared prompt prefixes, while efficient batching can improve throughput when serving concurrent requests. However, higher throughput does not automatically mean a faster answer for an individual user. vLLM optimization documentation

Faithful answers can still be incomplete.

In one benchmark question, the generated answer was grounded in the retrieved content, but the context lacked the expected preference criteria. The system was faithful, but incomplete. This distinction is important:

  • Faithfulness asks: “Did the answer invent claims?”
  • Recall asks: “Did retrieval find the evidence needed to answer fully?”

A trustworthy system needs both.

Future Recommendations: Moving from Prototype to Production

Future improvements should focus on practical reliability, speed, and testing, rather than merely adding more agents.

1. Hardware & Inference Optimization (Tackling the Latency Bottleneck)

The 3.1× latency penalty observed during local testing is a solvable engineering challenge:

  • Hardware upgrades: Higher-memory-bandwidth GPUs, either on-premises or cloud-hosted, could reduce decoding latency when memory access is the limiting factor. Actual gains depend on the model, quantization, context length, available VRAM, and serving configuration. Greater hardware bandwidth does not translate directly into an equivalent end-to-end speedup.
  • Optimized inference engines: Evaluate compatible model configurations with vLLM or TensorRT-LLM to determine whether they improve response latency, throughput, or memory efficiency.
  • Continuous batching: An inference server can batch independent LLM requests that arrive concurrently, improving GPU utilization and serving throughput. This does not automatically parallelize the agent graph or remove dependencies between stages. Deterministic MCP calculations are separate tool operations, not LLM inference requests.
  • Prefix caching: Reusing cached computation for matching prompt prefixes can reduce repeated prompt-processing work. Reuse requires compatible model and cache settings; placing the same evidence after different agent instructions does not necessarily produce a matching prefix. Prefix caching also does not eliminate the time needed to generate new tokens.
  • Smaller models for selected tasks: Test lightweight, quantized models for narrowly defined tasks such as intent classification. Retain a more capable model where evaluation shows it is needed. Retrieval sufficiency checks require particular care because an incorrect verdict can affect the entire answer.
2. Adaptive Query Routing (Plain RAG by Default)

Not every question wants a multi-agent swarm:

  • Simple, single-hop factual questions should route through a fast, low-latency Plain Hybrid-RAG path.
  • The full agentic pipeline (decomposition, tabular workers, and verification loops) should only be activated when a router identifies multi-part questions, table-heavy requests, mathematical calculations, or when initial retrieval confidence is low.
3. Production Ingestion & Asynchronous Jobs
  • Currently, the upload endpoint saves the document without triggering ingestion. A future improvement would connect uploading to an asynchronous job that performs parsing, chunking, embedding, and indexing, with visible progress and failure reporting.
4. Automated Regression Testing & Benchmark Expansion
  • Automated CI/CD Regression Suites: Comprehensive unit and integration assertions testing graph edge routing, circuit breaker trips, regex guardrail numerical filters, citation formatting, and MCP tool parameter validation.
  • Expanded Evaluation Corpus: The current 10-case comparison is a solid pilot, but a comprehensive benchmark should include 50+ diverse engineering scenarios: complex nested tables, OCR-heavy historical plant scans, multi-step hydraulic calculations, and adversarial edge cases.
Final takeaway

Building Agentic RAG is not about making a chatbot appear more intelligent.

It is about deciding when to retrieve, when to calculate, when to retry, when to abstain, and how to show the user what evidence supports an answer.

My current system is not a finished production engineering advisor. It is an evaluated local-first prototype that demonstrates both the promise and the trade-offs of Agentic RAG for domain-specific technical knowledge.

The biggest result was not that Agentic RAG “beat” plain RAG.

It was learning exactly where it helped: retrieval precision and structured workflows — and where it still needs work: latency, recall, testing, and reliable engineering-grade verification.

Agentic RAG vs. Plain Hybrid RAG: What My Hydropower Benchmark Revealed was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: Scientists Made Monkeys Watch Minions to Study Their Brains
items.summary: Welcome back to the Abstract! These are the studies this week that watched movies, made sacrifices, got crafty, and aged backwards. First, scientists learn how primates make meaning out of visuals by peeking into the brains of monkeys as they watch Despicable Me . Then: human sacrifice as climate “crisis rituals,” the fingerprints of prehistoric children, and the longevity secrets of ants. As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens , or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files . Humans watching monkeys watching Minions Raghavan, Vinay S et al. “During natural vision, semantic novelty modulates fixation-related processing in primate cortex.” JNeurosci. Settling down to watch a film is often viewed as a way to relax and shut our brains off for a while. Our brains, however, beg to differ—they are as busy as ever when interpreting videos, according to a new study based on brainwaves of humans and primates as they watch movies and short clips. To better understand how primate brains make meaning out of visual scenes, researchers studied eye movements and electroencephalogram (EEG) readings of neural activity in dozens of humans, as well as two macaques, as they watched videos. “Primate vision relies on eye movements to sample the world, yet how the brain integrates high level meaning across these ‘snapshots’ remains a mystery,” said researchers led by Vinay Raghavan of the City College of New York. The new results hint that “visual processing is not a series of independent glimpses, but a continuous process,” the team said. Human participants with EEG electrodes attached to their scalps (the “scalp movie dataset”) watched a selection of films including The Big Sick , The Peanut Butter Falcon , Whiplash , Room , Me and Earl and the Dying Girl , The Tomorrow Man , Dom Hemingway , Life After Beth , Woodshock , and The Comedian. “Participants were instructed to watch the movie as they would normally watch a movie,” the team said. A different “intracranial dataset” included several human patients and two rhesus macaques, the latter of which had electrodes implanted inside their skulls. This group watched shorter videos, including 10-minute clips of Despicable Me in both English and Hungarian, a 4.3-minute clip of the short film The Present , and three 5-minute clips of documentaries featuring macaques. Taken together, the datasets revealed that the brain responds to “semantic novelty”—meaning new semantic or conceptual information that crops up over the course of a video—which is measured through patterns of short-gaze “fixations.” The study also suggests that many brain regions beyond visual processing are involved in this ability to draw meaning from scenes. “These results challenge traditional vision models that treat fixations as independent snapshots and highlight the importance of considering the temporal dynamics of eye movements and the predictive nature of visual processing,” the team concluded. In addition to opening a new window into the mind, the study raises the irresistible yet unanswerable question of what macaques make of Minions. Alas, here we must confront the limitations of the knowable universe. In other news… Relatively peaceful—apart from the odd mass human sacrifice Snyder, Thomas and Klaus, Haagen. “Pax Lambayeque? Trauma, interpersonal violence, and environment over 3,000 years in the Lambayeque Valley Complex, Peru.” Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. When climate-related disasters struck ancient Peru, some cultures responded with mass human sacrifices to appeal to the cosmos. For example, at least 107 adult men were sacrificed in six closely-timed events at Huaca de la Luna around 550–600 CE, and more than 140 children and 200 juvenile camelids were sacrificed at the Huanchaquito-las Llamas site around 1450 CE. These ritualized killings often coincided with flooding and freak weather related to the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, the natural climate phenomenon in the Pacific Ocean that cycles through a warm “El Niño” phase and a cooler “La Niña” phase. The Huaca de la Luna sacrifice, for instance, occurred during a so-called “mega-Niño.” This connection inspired researchers to determine if environmental conditions were also linked to interpersonal violence outside of these ceremonial “crisis rituals” that were organized by elites. The Lambayeque Valley Complex, its location in Peru, and the sites with human skeletal remains studied in this work. Image: Snyder, Thomas and Klaus, Haagen. The team conducted a meta-analysis of the skeletal remains of 1,633 individuals that lived in Peru’s Lambayeque Valley over the course of 3,000 years before the arrival of Europeans. The remains presented “no strong evidence for an association between environmental factors and interpersonal violence” and suggested “that non-ritual violence in the Lambayeque Valley Complex was rare (1.6%),” according to the study. The mass sacrifices reflect “the sometimes lethal relationships between human behavior, cultural norms, and the environment—and are frequently used as cautionary allegories regarding the ongoing climate crisis,” said authors Thomas Snyder of New York University and Haagen Klaus of George Mason University. Time to add “prevention of ritualized human sacrifice” to the list of reasons to address climate change. Worth a shot? Before Play-Doh, there was clay-doh Davin, Laurent et al. “Modelling symbols among the first-sedentary communities: Emergence of clay figurines in Epipaleolithic Southwest Asia.” PLOS One. The fingerprints of children who lived 15,000 years ago in the southern Levant are preserved on clay artifacts, a discovery that exposes “a rare direct testimony of inter-generational knowledge transmission in a hands-on apprenticeship,” according to a new study. Archaeologists studied 154 clay figurines that were unearthed across three archaeological sites in Israel, including a subset depicting birds, a gazelle, and two human forms. items.summary_html:
Welcome back to the Abstract! These are the studies this week that watched movies, made sacrifices, got crafty, and aged backwards.

First, scientists learn how primates make meaning out of visuals by peeking into the brains of monkeys as they watch Despicable Me. Then: human sacrifice as climate “crisis rituals,” the fingerprints of prehistoric children, and the longevity secrets of ants.

As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens, or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files. 

Humans watching monkeys watching Minions

Raghavan, Vinay S et al. “During natural vision, semantic novelty modulates fixation-related processing in primate cortex.” JNeurosci.

Settling down to watch a film is often viewed as a way to relax and shut our brains off for a while. Our brains, however, beg to differ—they are as busy as ever when interpreting videos, according to a new study based on brainwaves of humans and primates as they watch movies and short clips.

To better understand how primate brains make meaning out of visual scenes, researchers studied eye movements and electroencephalogram (EEG) readings of neural activity in dozens of humans, as well as two macaques, as they watched videos.

“Primate vision relies on eye movements to sample the world, yet how the brain integrates high level meaning across these ‘snapshots’ remains a mystery,” said researchers led by Vinay Raghavan of the City College of New York. The new results hint that “visual processing is not a series of independent glimpses, but a continuous process,” the team said.

Human participants with EEG electrodes attached to their scalps (the “scalp movie dataset”) watched a selection of films including The Big Sick, The Peanut Butter Falcon, Whiplash, Room, Me and Earl and the Dying Girl, The Tomorrow Man, Dom Hemingway, Life After Beth, Woodshock, and The Comedian. 

“Participants were instructed to watch the movie as they would normally watch a movie,” the team said. 

A different “intracranial dataset” included several human patients and two rhesus macaques, the latter of which had electrodes implanted inside their skulls. This group watched shorter videos, including 10-minute clips of Despicable Me in both English and Hungarian, a 4.3-minute clip of the short film The Present, and three 5-minute clips of documentaries featuring macaques. 

Taken together, the datasets revealed that the brain responds to “semantic novelty”—meaning new semantic or conceptual information that crops up over the course of a video—which is measured through patterns of short-gaze “fixations.” The study also suggests that many brain regions beyond visual processing are involved in this ability to draw meaning from scenes.

“These results challenge traditional vision models that treat fixations as independent snapshots and highlight the importance of considering the temporal dynamics of eye movements and the predictive nature of visual processing,” the team concluded.

In addition to opening a new window into the mind, the study raises the irresistible yet unanswerable question of what macaques make of Minions. Alas, here we must confront the limitations of the knowable universe.

In other news…

Relatively peaceful—apart from the odd mass human sacrifice

Snyder, Thomas and Klaus, Haagen. “Pax Lambayeque? Trauma, interpersonal violence, and environment over 3,000 years in the Lambayeque Valley Complex, Peru.” Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.

When climate-related disasters struck ancient Peru, some cultures responded with mass human sacrifices to appeal to the cosmos. For example, at least 107 adult men were sacrificed in six closely-timed events at Huaca de la Luna around 550–600 CE, and more than 140 children and 200 juvenile camelids were sacrificed at the Huanchaquito-las Llamas site around 1450 CE. 

These ritualized killings often coincided with flooding and freak weather related to the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, the natural climate phenomenon in the Pacific Ocean that cycles through a warm “El Niño” phase and a cooler “La Niña” phase. The Huaca de la Luna sacrifice, for instance, occurred during a so-called “mega-Niño.” This connection inspired researchers to determine if environmental conditions were also linked to interpersonal violence outside of these ceremonial “crisis rituals” that were organized by elites.  

The Lambayeque Valley Complex, its location in Peru, and the sites with human skeletal remains studied in this work. Image: Snyder, Thomas and Klaus, Haagen.

The team conducted a meta-analysis of the skeletal remains of 1,633  individuals that lived in Peru’s Lambayeque Valley over the course of 3,000 years before the arrival of Europeans. The remains presented “no strong evidence for an association between environmental factors and interpersonal violence” and suggested “that non-ritual violence in the Lambayeque Valley Complex was rare (1.6%),” according to the study.

The mass sacrifices reflect “the sometimes lethal relationships between human behavior, cultural norms, and the environment—and are frequently used as cautionary allegories regarding the ongoing climate crisis,” said authors Thomas Snyder of New York University and Haagen Klaus of George Mason University.

Time to add “prevention of ritualized human sacrifice” to the list of reasons to address climate change. Worth a shot?

Before Play-Doh, there was clay-doh

Davin, Laurent et al. “Modelling symbols among the first-sedentary communities: Emergence of clay figurines in Epipaleolithic Southwest Asia.” PLOS One.

The fingerprints of children who lived 15,000 years ago in the southern Levant are preserved on clay artifacts, a discovery that exposes “a rare direct testimony of inter-generational knowledge transmission in a hands-on apprenticeship,” according to a new study.

Archaeologists studied 154 clay figurines that were unearthed across three archaeological sites in Israel, including a subset depicting birds, a gazelle, and two human forms. Crafted by the Natufian culture, these artifacts represent “the earliest evidence of a figurative clay tradition in Southwest Asia where it marks an important step in the evolution of human technology,” said researchers led by Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

A Natufian figurine depicting a stylised human body modelled in clay 15,000 years ago, bearing adult and child fingerprints. Image: © Laurent Davin

Because these people sculpted the artifacts by hand, fingerprints are occasionally spotted on the clay, revealing the contributions of children and adults. In some cases, a preserved “succession of gestures on the wet clay suggests that, during the modeling sequence, an adult passed on the figurine to a pre-pubescent child,” the team said. “Therefore, these artefacts could be interpreted as portable figurative mnemotechnic devices related to children’s learning of traditional beliefs and ethno-ornithological knowledge.”

It’s so evocative to see the preserved touch of a child who lived so long ago, capturing a moment of skill-building and, perhaps, play. While we don’t know exactly what these figurines meant to their crafters, their survival is a testament to human creativity and imagination.

The ants are Benjamin-Buttoning

Cole, Blaine J. and Wiernasz, Diane C. “A replaceable soma enables negative senescence in harvester ants.” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

We humans are used to a pretty standard life cycle: Birth, reproductive years, a decline in fertility, and an inevitable slide toward mortality. But a multi-decade study of ants reveals that some colonies operate as “superorganisms” that display increased reproduction and decreased mortality rate with age, reversing the course of normal senescence.

Western harvester ant queen. Image: Blaine J. Cole.

Researchers who gathered 34 years of data on 3,285 colonies of the western harvester ant (Pogonomyrmex occidentalis) discovered that these groups “display reverse aging,” according to their new study. 

“We will show that colonies of P. occidentalis not only have extraordinary longevity, but that their pattern of aging differs dramatically from that of most insects,” said authors Blaine J. Cole and Diane C. Wiernasz of the University of Houston. “Colonies exhibit negative senescence—increased survival and reproduction with greater age.”

This finding does not mean that individual ants are aging in reverse; worker ants live and die normally in these colonies. However, the larger superorganism becomes an unusual “non-senescing form.” While the ants go marching one by one, the colony’s lifespan adds up to a larger sum.  

Thanks for reading! See you next week.

items.title: Ukraine's naval drones made their name attacking Russian warships. Now they're taking the fight onto land.
items.summary: Ukraine uses the Magura drone to hit Russia's navy, and it's increasingly finding new targets in the air and helping operations on land. Ukrinform/Ukrinform/Sipa USA Ukraine's naval drones have been hammering Russian warships. Now, the drones, including UFORCE's Magura, are threatening Russian ground targets. The naval drones "pose a threat to the Russian occupiers on land as well," a commander said. Ukrainian naval drones that have hammered Russia's navy are now coming for Russian targets on land. Magura drones made by Ukrainian-founded defense company UFORCE played an important role in Ukraine becoming a formidable force at sea even without a conventional fleet of warships. Naval drones have damaged and destroyed numerous Russian vessels, pushing Moscow to move much of its Black Sea Fleet away from occupied Crimea. Ukraine's Main Intelligence Directorate, the GUR, revealed in August that it had used Maguras as FPV drone carriers to strike Russian targets on land, leveraging a control vehicle equipped with the "Podlyot" radar complex, which detects aircraft, missiles, and drones, and a Parol-4 IFF interrogator, used to distinguish between friendly and hostile aircraft. The Maguras "pose a threat to the Russian occupiers on land as well," the commander of the GUR's "Group 13" said. "This marks a fundamental shift in the nature of the conflict," said the commander, who uses the call sign "Thirteen." Oleg Rogynskyy, the founder and CEO of UFORCE, told Business Insider that he couldn't comment on the operational specifics, but he said that "it's not hard to imagine" a Magura launching something like the company's heavy Nemesis drone, which could then fly inland to target Russian air defense systems. The Russian air defense systems, he said, were built to take out missiles, not incoming heavy bomber drones flying low at night. In other August wins, the GUR said that drones launched from Maguras destroyed a Russian Pantsir-S1 air defense system, and then later that month, they hit two S-400 launchers and a ground-based antenna used to control Orion drones. A month earlier, a naval drone used by the 123rd Territorial Defense Brigade dropped a ground robot off on the Kinburn Spit for an unusual combat mission. And Ukraine is training for more operations like these. Rogynskyy said that Maguras were used in a September exercise to launch drones, drop off amphibious ground drones for a beach assault, and deliver supplies. He said he expects to see more creative uses as time goes on. In March, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy spotlighted the growing capabilities of Ukraine's naval drones in an address to the UK Parliament. "We started with simple kamikaze sea drones. Then we built drones with turrets that can shoot down helicopters," he said. "Now we have drones that can shoot down Russian fighter jets from the sea. We have developed boats that carry other drones. We also have boats that strike targets on land from the sea." The GUR said in October that after destroying ships in Russia's Black Sea Fleet , "the Magura drone was significantly improved." It explained that now "it is a multifunctional platform capable not only of sinking surface objects, but also of carrying missile weapons, as well as aerial drones for striking ground targets." Before they became drone carriers, Magura drones were armed with alternative weaponry for engaging non-naval targets. In 2024, for instance, one shot down a helicopter with a missile. Last year, the GUR said that Maguras had been used to shoot down Russian fighter jets. Rogynskyy said some of these uses were a surprise to the company. "I didn't expect it. It's the ingenuity of Ukrainian engineers and Ukrainian soldiers that really drives this," he said. UFORCE, which also makes ground drones, AI software, and command-and-control systems, is one of Ukraine's biggest defense companies. Founded in Ukraine and headquartered in London, with major hubs in Kyiv and Washington, DC, it has also attracted significant international interest. The company's Magura drones have been involved in multiple multinational military exercises. UFORCE has also developed a new MV7 model for UK waters and is partnering with RECONCRAFT , an American special-operations boat maker, though no new production runs, customers, or contracts have yet been announced. UFORCE announced on Thursday that it raised $700 million in a Series A funding round from investors, including the UK government and Silicon Valley-based venture capital firms, bringing the company's total valuation to $6 billion. The company wants to scale its manufacturing both in Ukraine and in partner countries to strengthen their defense. Talking about this round of investment, Rogynskyy told Business Insider that "it's time to scale." He said that the future of naval warfare "is all about fully unmanned navies and autonomous patrol presence, et cetera, as well as autonomous standoff." In the near term, he said, many navies want a hybrid approach, coordinating operations between classic crewed assets and drones. He predicted that "pretty much every navy on the planet is going to be scaling itself using cheap, attainable, unmanned assets that are AI-controlled." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Catherine Zeta-Jones says an unexpected career move got her discovered by Steven Spielberg
items.summary: Catherine Zeta-Jones. JC Olivera/Getty Catherine Zeta-Jones recalls how she was discovered by Steven Spielberg in the late 1990s. Spielberg saw her in the CBS miniseries, "Titanic." He had her screen test for "The Mask of Zorro," which he was producing. Catherine Zeta-Jones was in her 20s when she made a decision that would change her career forever. At the time, the Welsh actor was famous to UK audiences for starring in the popular early-'90s British series, "The Darling Buds of May." But she yearned for more, so she decided to move to California and see if she could make it in Hollywood. With six months on a visa, Zeta-Jones had to get work quickly, and auditions were a bit of an ego check. "I'd been in this business since I was 9 years old, professionally in theater and in television, and a few films in Britain at that point," Zeta-Jones told Business Insider . "But I'd go into casting agents, and they'd be asking me what I had done." She ended up taking a role on the 1996 CBS miniseries "Titanic." Though it wasn't a "huge leap" for her, it led to something even better: attention from Steven Spielberg. The director happened to be watching the show one night and liked what he saw. He suggested she screen test for "The Mask of Zorro," which he was producing. A week later, she was "shipped down to Mexico to screen test with Antonio Banderas." The rest is history. See the full clip below: Or read the full interview with Zeta-Jones. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Your Traces Are Evidence: Retention, Legal Hold, and Discovery for Agent Logs
items.summary: The flight recorder you built for debugging has a second reader. Retention policy, legal hold, and what not to write down. Image 01: The Second Reader- When Agent Traces Become Legal Evidence (Image by Author) The discovery request, in this composite drawn from several teams’ first encounters with litigation, was one sentence long: produce all records of automated decision-making concerning the plaintiff, including system logs, for the relevant period. The team’s first reaction was relief. They had the records — of course they had the records. This series had convinced them years earlier: trace everything, don’t sample , keep the full span tree, every prompt, every tool call, every model response. Forty million traces, searchable. If any company could reconstruct exactly what its agent did to one customer on one afternoon, it was them. The relief lasted until someone actually read the traces the way opposing counsel would. There was the agent’s chain-of-thought at step 14, candidly speculating: “the customer’s pattern suggests they may be attempting to exploit the refund window.” There was the quality judge’s verdict on the run, written by their own system: “2/5 — the agent failed to consider the customer’s stated hardship.” There was a behavior-flag rollout note showing the customer had been served the experimental bundle. Their flight recorder had documented, in fluent first-person prose, something that read exactly like a corporation forming an intent, acting on it, and grading itself as negligent — and every line of it was now going to a law firm whose job was to read it that way. Meanwhile the platform’s 90-day TTL had been quietly deleting adjacent traces for three weeks after the preservation letter arrived, because nobody had connected the legal-hold email to the retention config. The thesis of this article: a trace has two readers — the engineer you built it for, and the adversary the law will eventually hand it to — and a logging discipline designed for only the first reader is a liability dressed as an asset. Your traces are business records. They are discoverable, subpoenaable, holdable, and quotable aloud in depositions. That doesn’t mean stop tracing — regulation is busily making tracing mandatory — it means the flight recorder needs what every real flight recorder has: a retention policy someone chose on purpose, a chain of custody, and a design that assumes the tape will someday be played for a room of people who were not the pilot. This is the fifteenth article in the harness series , the second in its law-and-records arc. The previous piece engineered deletion — the deliberate removal of data. This one is its sibling and its tension: the deliberate keeping of data, on a schedule the law respects, in a form you can stand behind. (The standing caveat travels with us: engineering description of the legal landscape, not legal advice — your obligations are jurisdiction- and sector-specific, and counsel scopes them, not a Medium article.) Part 1: Why Agent Logs Are Records — Whether You Meant Them to Be The traces this series taught you to keep are, without exaggeration, among the most complete business records any organization has ever produced. A classical audit log records that something happened: user 4471 was refunded, timestamp, actor. An agent trace records that — plus the entire deliberation: what the system was told, what it retrieved, what alternatives it weighed in visible reasoning, what it almost did, what its own supervisor thought of the result. Companies spent a century learning to be careful in memos and email; the agent stack produces something with the evidentiary density of a wiretap on the company’s own decision-making, generated at machine speed, retained by default. The law is arriving at this pile from two directions at once, and the squeeze between them is the design problem. From one side, regulation increasingly requires the logs to exist. The EU AI Act’s Article 12 mandates that high-risk AI systems “automatically record events over the lifetime of the system” at a traceability level fit for purpose; Articles 19 and 26 then require both providers and deployers to retain those logs for “at least six months” — a floor, not a ceiling, stretched further by sector rules and by any live dispute — with high-risk obligations phasing in through 2027–2028 and non-compliance priced at up to €15M or 3% of worldwide turnover. Deployers, note — the common assumption that logging is the vendor’s problem is specifically wrong. Sector regimes go further: financial-services recordkeeping rules (the SEC’s books-and-records regime and its WORM-storage tradition) treat certain communications as records that must be kept immutably for years. And the SEC’s off-channel communications sweep showed what happens when a channel escapes the record: over $2 billion in penalties across more than 100 firms since 2021 — JPMorgan’s $200 million opener, then wave after wave — for business conducted over WhatsApp where the recordkeeping system couldn’t see it. Read that sweep with agent eyes and a warning surfaces: an agent conducting business through channels your record system doesn’t capture — a side API, a vendor tool with its own logs, a sub-agent whose transcript nobody retains — is a new way to manufacture the same violation. From the other side, litigation makes whatever exists discoverable. The trigger is ordinary: a customer dispute, an employment claim, a regulator’s inquiry. A preservation duty attaches — often before any lawsuit is filed, the moment litigation is reasonably anticipated — and from that moment, the deletion machinery the last article built must stop for the covered material, provably. The doctrine has teeth, and the teeth have a famous recent demonstration we’ll return to: a company whose chat system auto-deleted by design, whose holds didn’t actually suspend the auto-deletion, and whose jury was eventually instructed to assume the destroyed evidence was unfavorable. Hold the two sides together and the shape of the problem is clear. You cannot solve discovery risk by not logging — the regulation floor, your debugging , your attribution , and your evals all forbid it, and selective non-logging during disputes is itself sanctionable. You cannot solve it by keeping everything forever — the deletion article spent five thousand words on why every retained byte is obligation. What remains is the only real option: retention as a designed system — deliberate scope, deliberate clocks, deliberate exceptions — instead of what most agent stacks have today, which is whatever the observability platform’s default TTL happens to be. Part 2: The Trace Through Legal Eyes — A Stratigraphy Before designing the system, read your own trace the way the second reader will. It has layers, and they carry different charges. The conversation layer is personal data wearing a transcript’s clothes — the deletion graph’s concern, and discovery’s starting point. Routine, in both directions. The action layer — tool calls, parameters, results, timestamps — is the closest thing to a classical audit log and usually your friend : it’s the layer that proves what actually happened, in order, with receipts. When your agent behaved correctly, this layer is the defense. This is also why its integrity matters most; more below. The reasoning layer is the dangerous stratum. Chain-of-thought is candid by design — we engineered it to explore, speculate, consider and reject. But juries and regulators read first-person prose as mental state . “The customer may be exploiting the refund window” was, mechanically, one hypothesis in a search process that discarded it two steps later; on a projector in a deposition, it’s the company calling the plaintiff a fraud. The models’ anthropomorphic register makes it worse — reasoning text sounds like an employee thinking, and courts have centuries of practice imputing employees’ thoughts to their employers. You built a system that narrates. The narration is evidence. The judgment layer is the stratum nobody anticipates. This series told you to wire LLM judges over production, score runs, log verdicts. Which means your system now generates contemporaneous written records criticizing its own conduct — “2/5, failed to consider stated hardship” — in exactly the form that, in human organizations, becomes the smoking-gun internal memo. Your traces are business records. They are discoverable, subpoenaable, holdable, and quotable aloud in depositions. The traces this series taught you to keep are, without exaggeration, among the most complete business records any organization has ever produced. Companies spent a century learning to be careful in memos and email; the agent stack produces something with the evidentiary density of a wiretap on the company’s own decision-making, generated at machine speed, retained by default.

The law is arriving at this pile from two directions at once, and the squeeze between them is the design problem.

From one side, regulation increasingly requires the logs to exist. Google’s “history off” era is the canonical spoliation story of the decade: sensitive discussions steered to auto-deleting chats; litigation holds that — per the DOJ — were represented as suspending deletion while employees’ chats kept vanishing on a 24-hour clock; and in Epic v. Google, a judge who put the question to the jury with an instruction to presume the missing evidence unfavorable. Every element has an agent-stack analog: the auto-deleting channel (your TTLs), the hold that didn’t propagate (your retention config), the steering of sensitive topics off the record (your redaction and logging choices, if made for the wrong reasons at the wrong time). The lesson isn’t “never delete” — it’s that the gap between stated policy and actual behavior is the thing courts punish hardest.

The sweep that priced a missing channel. The SEC’s off-channel campaign — $2B+, 100+ firms — established that in regulated sectors, failure to record is a standalone violation needing no underlying misconduct. The agent translation is direct: inventory every channel through which your agents conduct regulable business — every provider, every tool, every sub-agent seam — and confirm each one lands in the record system. “The vendor’s API had logs, but we never ingested them” is the new “it was on the trader’s personal phone.”

The twenty million conversations. The previous article told the NYT v. OpenAI story as a deletion problem; told as a records problem, the moral inverts: a third party held the logs, a court reached them, and 20 million de-identified conversations went into a litigation review environment over objections that de-identification can’t survive free text. Your users’ interactions with your agent are, to some future litigant, exactly this corpus. Design the trace path knowing every party that holds it extends the surface a court can reach.

The deposition test, failed and passed. The cold open’s team, remediated: judge rubrics rewritten against enumerated policy criteria; reasoning prompts steered from motive-speculation to pattern-matching against defined rules; the hold registry wired into both TTL jobs and the erasure sweep, with a quarterly synthetic-hold drill; trace tiers split — full traces 60 days, distilled decision records seven years, WORM. In the actual litigation, the surviving action-layer records showed the agent had applied the refund policy correctly — and could be authenticated. The case settled on terms the team’s counsel attributed, in part, to the other side reading the timeline and folding. The same flight recorder, run through a records discipline, had switched sides.

Part 6: The Landscape

Build: the retention policy document and its enforcing automation; trace tiering (full/distilled/aggregate) with per-tier clocks; the hold registry gating every deletion path, drill included; the deposition-test review habit for harness-authored strings; WORM + hashing for the record tier; the third-party retention map; role-based trace access with logged exports.

Lean on: trace platforms’ retention and deletion APIs (the tools exist — your job is connecting them to policy); cloud object-lock/WORM storage; e-discovery platforms for the production side (they speak legal; your job is an export path that preserves structure and provenance); provider enterprise tiers with contractual retention terms; counsel, early — the retention schedule is a joint deliverable, and the version co-signed by legal is worth double.

My advice on choosing: start with the hold registry, because it’s the piece whose absence is catastrophic and whose cost is a table and two if statements. Then the tier split with real clocks — it forces the conversation about what your record is. The deposition-test lint on rubrics and labels is an afternoon of grep and a standing review question. WORM and signing come when stakes or sector demand. The third-party map is a document sprint, and it's the one most teams have literally never done.

The whole idea in miniature:

def write_trace(run, spans):
    spans = redact_at_ingest(spans)                       # PII masked before storage
    store.append(FULL_TIER, spans, ttl=days(60))          # debugging window, short for cause
    record = distill(spans)                               # actions, policy refs, approvals, outcome
    worm.append(RECORD_TIER, sign(record), ttl=years(7))  # the business record: immutable, provable
    metrics.update(aggregate(spans))                      # forever, and anonymous
def sweep(candidates):                                    # every deletion path, same gate
    for item in candidates:
        if holds.covering(item):                          # the hold beats the sweeper
            log.defer(item, hold=holds.covering(item))    # ...provably
        else:
            delete(item); log.deleted(item, policy=POLICY_VERSION)
    # quarterly: seed a synthetic trace, hold it, verify the TTL bounces. keep the receipt.
Part 7: The Failure Modes Field Guide

The candid chain-of-thought. Speculation about a person’s motives, logged as first-person prose, read as corporate intent. Cure: reason against defined criteria, not characters; deposition-test the prompts.

The self-incriminating judge. Your quality system writes “2/5, unfair to customer” into a permanent record. Cure: rubrics scored against enumerated operational criteria; keep judging, change the vocabulary.

The policy nobody follows. A written 90-day TTL, actually applied sometimes, to some stores. Cure: automated, logged, uniform enforcement — the gap between stated and actual is the sanctionable part.

The hold that didn’t stop the sweeper. Preservation notice sent; TTLs kept running. Cure: holds as registry objects checked by every deletion path; quarterly synthetic-hold drill.

The off-channel agent. Business conducted via a tool or provider whose logs never reach your record system. Cure: channel inventory; every seam ingested or contractually covered.

The unsearchable archive. You kept everything and can produce nothing by deadline. Cure: the distilled tier is structured and queryable; test an export before a court demands one.

The unauthenticatable log. Your exculpatory trace is a mutable database row anyone could have edited. Cure: WORM record tier, hash chains, provenance metadata — evidence needs receipts.

The over-hold. One cautious hold, unscoped, freezes all deletion forever and quietly rebuilds the liability pile. Cure: matter-scoped holds with owners and sunset reviews.

The record about the record. Instructions to keep things off the log, discovered. Cure: never write them; shape records for precision, never for absence.

Part 8: How to Start — A One-Week Plan

Day 1. Read ten of your own production traces as opposing counsel. Bring a highlighter for every line you’d hate to hear read aloud. This exercise recruits every stakeholder you’ll need for the rest of the week.

Day 2. Draft the retention schedule: what exists, its tier, its clock, its statutory floor. Book the counsel review — the schedule matters less than its existence and its co-signature.

Day 3. Build the hold registry — a table, an API, and the if statement in every deletion path, the erasure sweep included. Wire the deferral log.

Day 4. Run the first hold drill: synthetic trace, hold, TTL arrival, bounce, receipt. If it fails, you’ve just had your cheapest possible spoliation incident.

Day 5. Deposition-test the harness’s authored strings — judge rubrics, flag names, error copy. Rewrite the editorials into policy references.

The weekend. Draw the third-party map: every vendor holding trace-path data, their clocks, their hold posture, their subpoena story. Send the three emails the map reveals you need to send.

Conclusion: The Transparency Camp and the Minimalist Camp

One camp holds that the complete record is the best defense — that agents whose every step is logged, judged, and versioned are the most accountable systems ever built, and the org that can replay any decision with receipts wins disputes, audits, and its own engineering arguments. Log everything; sunlight is the strategy.

The other camp has read more depositions. Every byte is a potential exhibit; prose you didn’t need is risk you chose; and the wisest records regime is the one that keeps exactly what the law and the operations require, distilled, and not a token more. Write less down; what doesn’t exist can’t be quoted.

Both camps are right about the failure of the other. The synthesis this article has been building: keep complete records of what happened; be deliberate about records of what was felt — and let every clock, every tier, and every exception be something you chose in daylight, before anyone was angry. The action layer, distilled, immutable, long-lived: that’s the record that acquits correct systems. The speculation, the verbatim wandering, the anthropomorphic narration: operationally short-lived, for documented reasons, uniformly enforced. A trace discipline like that serves both readers — the engineer gets the flight recorder, the second reader gets a record you’re not afraid of — and it converts the question every team eventually faces from “what will they find?” to “here is what we keep, here is why, and here is the proof it’s true.”

Your agent is already testifying. This week decides whether it’s a good witness.

Next in the series: the tools, skills, and servers your agent trusts were written by strangers — The Agent Supply Chain: Provenance for Skills, Tools, and Servers.

items.title: Nearly 9,500 flights were halted across the US after an FAA ground stop. What to do if your trip was affected.
items.summary: People stranded at Miami airport amid the ATC outage on Friday. Giorgio VIERA / AFP via Getty Images Nearly 9,500 flights were canceled or halted after a nationwide air traffic control outage on Friday. This is considered an uncontrollable disruption, so airlines aren't required to provide freebies. Here's what you can do if your flight is delayed or canceled. US airlines are canceling thousands of flights after a rare air traffic control outage affected the US . As of 10:30 p.m. ET, nearly 9,500 flights scheduled to depart the US on Friday and Saturday had been canceled or did not take off, according to data from Cirium, an aviation analytics firm. More than 8,200 of those flights were scheduled for Friday; another 1,200 were Saturday flights. Collectively, nearly 20% of scheduled flights out of the US on Friday and Saturday were canceled, per Cirium. The cancellations came after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop around 3:45 p.m. The stop was lifted around 8:30 p.m., but after so many cancellations, flight chaos is nearly guaranteed to stretch into the weekend. If you're wondering what your options are as the terminals pile up with people frantically trying to get a hotel or food voucher — don't rely on your airline to help out. According to the Department of Transportation, certain delays and cancellations caused by, for example, an ATC outage, are considered "uncontrollable" disruptions. That means airlines are not required to provide freebies such as hotel stays or food vouchers. Don't confuse the rules with the DoT customer service dashboard , which shows passenger compensation for flights disrupted by controllable factors, such as maintenance or crew scheduling. Pilots or flight attendants timing out due to the outage would not fall under crew scheduling. Airlines may offer goodwill vouchers to help out affected customers, but don't bank on it. Customers who book their own hotel or other transportation, such as a rental car or train, may be able to get eligible expenses reimbursed by their credit card. Here's what to do if your flight is disrupted. 1. Know your rights as an airline passenger in the US Airline passengers have some customer rights in the US. Li Rui/Xinhua via Getty Images According to the Department of Transportation, there is no law requiring US airlines to compensate passengers for disruptions caused by uncontrollable events, such as weather. That also includes air traffic control delays. The only rule carriers must follow is to refund customers for cancellations, even in cases of uncontrollable events. And that does not mean travel credits or vouchers — it must be to the original form of payment, and includes any add-ons, such as bags or seats. If you choose to travel but your flight is delayed or canceled, ask the airline for the reason — ideally in writing — so you know what you're entitled to. Airlines have different policies for disruptions they can control. The DoT's Airline Customer Service Dashboard — launched in 2022 — shows what the 10 largest US airlines promise in those cases, including rebookings, meal vouchers, and hotel accommodations. 2. Monitor your airline's app for rebooking options Most airlines allow customers to adjust their flights online. Jaap Arriens/NurPhoto via Getty Images When a flight delay or cancellation is announced, expect people to flock to the nearest customer service line for assistance, and for the phone lines to clog. Wait times can be painfully long, and the best alternatives will likely go quickly. However, some airlines offer the option to rebook on their website or mobile app and waive any fees, making it sometimes easier to make changes online than in person. If all available options are exhausted, have a plan B, such as waiting to speak with a live agent, contacting the airline through social media, or booking a hotel for the night. Direct messaging on Facebook or Twitter can actually serve as a virtual placeholder, and you may hear back via chat before speaking to a live agent. Here are the phone numbers for each airline: Alaska: 1-800-252-7522 or text 82008 Allegiant: 1-702-505-8888 American: 1-800-433-7300 Avelo: 1-346-616-9500 Breeze: No phone number to call, but you can text the airline at 501-273-3931. If you call this number, it'll tell you different ways to contact Breeze, like via email or Facebook Messenger. Delta: 1-800-221-1212 Frontier: No phone number. The best way to contact Frontier is via online chat or email. JetBlue: 1-800-538-2583 Southwest: 1-800-435-9792 United: 1-800-864-8331 3. Ask for a hotel or meal voucher The Hyatt hotel inside Orlando airport. : Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images For controllable delays or cancellations that result in a customer waiting at least three hours for a new flight or requiring an overnight stay, several airlines will offer meal or hotel vouchers . Carriers offering both are Alaska Airlines, Allegiant Air, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, Hawaiian Airlines, JetBlue Airways, Southwest Airlines, and United Airlines, per the DoT dashboard. Frontier Airlines is the only carrier that does not offer accommodations in the event of an overnight delay or cancellation, but it will provide a meal voucher. For US airlines not listed on the dashboard, or in cases where the disruption is uncontrollable (like because of a winter storm), or if the compensation is unclear, simply ask. It never hurts to request a meal or hotel during flight disruptions, and you might get lucky with a goodwill gesture from the carrier. 4. Check if your credit card company offers travel insurance American Express and Chase have travel credit cards. Illustration by Mario Tama/Getty Images Several major banks offer credit cards with travel insurance , such as Chase's Sapphire Reserve and American Express' Platinum Card . Both offer trip protection, meaning customers who purchased their flights with those cards can benefit. For example, during a major storm system, many passengers are likely to end up stranded in random cities across the US. However, banks with travel insurance included can reimburse cardholders for unexpected expenses outside their control, including hotel, meal, and transportation costs. Travel insurance does not apply in all circumstances, like short delays, so be sure to check your policy before making a claim — but it also doesn't hurt to make the claim anyway, even if the answer is no. 5. Know when to walk away Consider renting a car or taking the train. Wang Ying/Xinhua via Getty Images Delays and cancellations are inevitable. Don't spend all day sitting around waiting — set a cutoff time. Once that moment passes, consider alternative ways to reach your destination, such as driving or taking a bus or train (which may also be covered by travel insurance). If you are stuck in another city and have no other option but to stay in a hotel or wait at the airport, decide how you want to spend your time and make a plan. items.title: McKinsey boss Bob Sternfels laid out how companies can prepare for an Nvidia-like crisis
items.summary: Bob Sternfels, global managing partner at McKinsey. Jose Sarmento Matos/Bloomberg via Getty Images The Nvidia scandal holds key reminders for business leaders about how to prepare for a crisis. Boards should imagine and discuss as many scenarios as possible, said McKinsey chief Bob Sternfels. When crisis does strike, thinking about long-term outcomes during the chaos is key, he said. As they watched Nvidia's chaotic week unfold, many board members and executives may have found themselves wondering: "What if our CEO has an affair that gets us embroiled in a reputation-shaking scandal?" Bob Sternfels, global managing partner at McKinsey, has some advice for them. The Nvidia crisis has highlighted the importance of corporate governance, Sternfels said in an interview with Bloomberg on Thursday. It's a reminder to have these discussions and prepare for all imaginable situations so that they're not on the back foot when they arrive, he said. "Having a playbook, even if it's close, is much better than figuring it out in the heat of that moment," Sternfels said. McKinsey, which Sternfels has led since 2021, is one of the world's leading consultancies and advises clients on improving operations, offering guidance on everything from choosing the best technology to implement to handling the unexpected. Sternfels said the best responses to any crisis are long-term rather than knee-jerk reactions to the immediate situation. It's about finding a way to stay steady during the chaos, he said. "There's an immediacy to respond, and you have to cauterize and make a decision, but it also has to be: what are our longer-term objectives? Where are we trying to go?" said Sternfels. On Thursday, Nvidia's board announced Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO. His departure followed days of reports about his personal life, including accusations of a close relationship with someone US officials suspect to be a Chinese intelligence asset and an extramarital affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Huang's downfall will have ripple effects across the AI industry and raises questions about the impact a single leader can have on a company's success. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday. Soeren Stache/picture alliance via Getty Images Since co-founding Nvidia in 1993, Huang has spent more than three decades nurturing the chipmaker into a $4 trillion giant. He is known for embracing a flat leadership model, an approach he has credited as key to the company's success. Also crucial has been his geopolitical reach: Huang's Taiwanese roots and deep personal ties to Taiwan's technology sector have been instrumental in building Nvidia's AI supply chain, and he has the US president on speed dial. Many are now asking how Nvidia will fare without its leather-clad, celebrity leader. Sternfels told Bloomberg that navigating the influence of a well-known, public-facing CEO comes down to leadership development , meaning systematically developing generation after generation of leaders so a company is more robust. McKinsey has found a gap in that kind of planning among clients, he said: "Not many companies are really focused on leadership development. They're focused more narrowly on succession planning." Leadership development doesn't just happen at the CEO level, but at multiple levels in an organization, Sternfels added. Whether the board CEO or the CEO of a top team, it's good practice to have people in leadership who can serve as an independent, objective voice in governance decisions and present a counter viewpoint, he said.
