Sternfels told Bloomberg that navigating the influence of a well-known, public-facing CEO comes down to leadership development, meaning systematically developing generation after generation of leaders so a company is more robust.

McKinsey has found a gap in that kind of planning among clients, he said: "Not many companies are really focused on leadership development. They're focused more narrowly on succession planning."

Leadership development doesn't just happen at the CEO level, but at multiple levels in an organization, Sternfels added.

Whether the board CEO or the CEO of a top team, it's good practice to have people in leadership who can serve as an independent, objective voice in governance decisions and present a counter viewpoint, he said.

items.title: Jensen Huang’s Exit Just Gave AMD and Google Their Biggest AI Opening
items.summary: On the same day that Jensen Huang resigned as NVIDIA’s chief executive after 33 years at the helm of the company he co-founded, another semiconductor company CEO was being celebrated. AMD CEO Lisa Su was named Yahoo Finance’s 2026 CEO of the Year. Su has had quite a triumphant year. AMD shares have been up nearly 139% year-to-date. She signed significant deals with OpenAI and Oracle to deploy its Instinct GPUs. She also surprised investors and AI watchers alike by acquiring Fei-Fei Li’s spatial intelligence startup World Labs for $8.2 billion, in a move that gives her an advantage in guiding future GPU architectures. But the timing is not lost on anyone. Su’s ascension comes at a trying time for NVIDIA. Huang’s abrupt departure has left the world’s most valuable AI chipmaker facing questions about succession, strategy, and its ability to maintain its competitive edge. NVIDIA’s shares fell 4.34% to $166.19 on November 12, following Huang’s resignation, while AMD shares rose 5.86%. The former’s stock has seen a 13.7% correction year-to-date, with shares nosediving 32% from when NVIDIA hit its all-time record on October 6, erasing roughly $1.86 trillion in valuation. Is NVIDIA in Trouble? Huang’s exit raises questions about whether NVIDIA can maintain its strategic direction and industry relationships. Even CFO Colette Kress’ appointment as interim CEO is not enough to calm Wall Street nerves. “Jensen’s role, presence, vision and execution have been central to what NVIDIA and the AI ecosystem are where they are right now,” Neil Shah, Co-founder and Vice President of Research at Counterpoint Research, tells AIM. In the near term, at least, the departure may not cause disruption to NVIDIA’s core operations. Hyperscaler hardware orders are locked in through at least Q3 and Q4 FY27. NVIDIA’s near-term product roadmap, which runs from Blackwell through Vera Rubin and even Feynman generations, is locked in with deep engineering bench strength. However, a leadership exit immediately creates a strategic and diplomatic vacuum. After all, it was Huang who arbitrated GPU allocations and orchestrated multi-billion-dollar circular financing and compute-backed deals. “The immediate challenge for interim leadership under Colette Kress will be maintaining ecosystem trust, managing enterprise relationships, and proving that NVIDIA’s innovation velocity can persist without its visionary founder at the helm, observes Prabhu Ram, VP of Industry Research Group, CyberMedia Research. Huang’s personal relationships that he has carefully curated over three decades across the value chain—from the biggest chip manufacturer TSMC and EMS player Foxconn to players such as SoftBank—have been critical in holding together massive sovereign AI deals, neocloud financing arrangements, and geopolitical lobbying efforts. “Without him at the helm, we will likely see a slowdown in new, aggressive ecosystem-level investments and lucrative bilateral AI infrastructure deals from NVIDIA’s side,” Shah notes. AMD’s Moment Su’s recognition comes after a year of major commercial wins for AMD. The company reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $13.4 billion, up 45% year-on-year. Its data centre business generated $8.5 billion, growing 97% from a year earlier, driven by demand for EPYC server processors and Instinct AI accelerators. AMD’s biggest advantage is no longer simply that it offers an alternative to NVIDIA GPUs. It is increasingly securing large, multi-year infrastructure commitments from some of the biggest AI companies. In October last year, AMD signed a multi-generation agreement with OpenAI to deploy up to 6 gigawatts of its GPUs. Earlier this year, Meta signed another agreement to deploy up to 6 GW of AMD Instinct GPUs . The first deployments for both is expected to begin in the second half of 2026, using custom MI450-based accelerators. Anthropic followed in July with a commitment to deploy up to 2 GW of AMD MI450 GPUs in its Helios rack-scale systems, with the first gigawatt scheduled for the first half of 2027. AMD also committed to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic, including plans to buy $2.5 billion of Anthropic’s non-voting stock during the IPO. But AMD is not the only company on NVIDIA’s coattails. NVIDIA’s next CEO has to hold off OpenAI, Broadcom, Google, Anthropic, Meta, and Amazon chip teams too. In a recent TBPN podcast, Dylan Patel of Seminanalyis said Jensen Huang’s successor could struggle to replicate his influence over NVIDIA’s supply chain. “NVIDIA wants to make aggressive moves, lock up supply and convince suppliers to do things they have never done before, both in terms of technology and supply. That could become a lot harder given that whoever takes over as CEO is unlikely to be as charismatic as Jensen,” he believes. Shah says hyperscalers and sovereign funds will think more about diversification beyond NVIDIA. “A likely leadership transition, combined with tighter US export rules, end-user audits, and post-midterm power and permitting bottlenecks, could give buyers the exact excuse to speed up deployments of custom silicon like Google’s TPUs, AWS Trainium, and AMD accelerators,” he notes. Per Counterpoint Research, custom ASICs were already on track to surpass GPU accelerator unit shipments next year, and this only adds to the uncertainty at NVIDIA, squeezing its inference share and pricing power. Google’s Growing TPU Business Google has spent more than a decade developing its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) to power its own AI workloads, including Gemini. It is now taking the technology beyond its internal infrastructure and turning it into a commercial product. During Alphabet’s third-quarter earnings call, Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian revealed that more than 100 significant TPU customers were using its cloud infrastructure. Google has also started selling complete TPU systems to customers that want to deploy them in their own data centres. In October, Google announced a partnership with Oracle to bring TPUs to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) from 2027. This will make Oracle the first hyperscaler outside Google to offer the chips. That’s significant. Companies were reluctant to bet on ASICs given that NVIDIA GPUs were the only portable option across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and OCI. That lock-in has now weakened. Google recently expanded its eighth-generation (TPU) portfolio with two new systems, TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, to meet the computing requirements of enterprises deploying autonomous AI agents. What’s Next for NVIDIA? Till now, NVIDIA had been using its backstop programme to provide credit support for GPU clusters in exchange for a share of cloud revenue, giving it considerable influence over how computing capacity is distributed between hyperscalers and neocloud providers. This financing model was underpinned by Huang’s credibility and willingness to make bold commitments. His successor may find it harder to take similar risks—espcially as according to reports from The Information and WSJ , Kress repeatedly pushed back internally against Huang’s riskiest financing bets, including paring down OpenAI data centre commitment from $250 billion to $120 billion. “Huang’s exit instantly alters the competitive calculus. Hyperscalers and Big Tech buyers who have long navigated NVIDIA’s ironclad market control will now test for leverage, while chipmaking rivals could see an opening to capture market share,” says Ram. That said, it is not going to be a cakewalk for NVIDIA competitors. Buying an AMD GPU or Google TPU is one thing. Migrating workloads, retraining engineers, and adapting software to a different computing architecture is a different challenge altogether. NVIDIA’s CUDA ecosystem remains deeply embedded in AI development. AMD's ROCm software has been improving, while Google is expanding PyTorch support to make TPUs more accessible to developers. For customers, it is about having more choices, negotiating better prices and avoiding dependence on a single supplier. “For the broader AI investment cycle, this does not mean data centre capex for 2027 and 2028 will collapse as the underlying demand for AI compute remains structurally strong. However, it will trigger a major reallocation of capital and accelerate diversification,” says Shah.

items.title: Forget the 529. These parents are saving for a future without college.
items.summary: Parents are rethinking their 529 savings plans as AI challenges higher education. Nataliya Konovalova; Matthew Crowson Parents are rethinking how to save for their kids' futures, as AI complicates the value of degrees. Some parents are shifting away from tax-advantaged 529 education savings plans. Others keep funding 529 plans, betting the rules will change in an AI future. When Nataliya Konovalova's sons were babies, she set up tax-advantaged 529 savings plans for them. On their birthdays, she'd tell relatives: no gifts, just contributions. As the boys got older — they are now eight and 10 — she began to change her mind about the value of a college education. Konovalova read stories about degree-holders working at McDonald's , and prestigious fellowships that take students straight out of high school . AI was the final straw. Konovalova had long discussions with her husband, who works in tech, about how AI is tightening the entry-level job market. Ultimately, the couple halved their contributions to the boys' 529 plans. "I honestly don't think they will go to a traditional four-year college," she said. For decades, these tax-advantaged plans have been the bread and butter of education savings. Parents can spend investment gains tax-free, provided the money goes toward qualified education expenses like tuition, textbooks, laptops, room and board, and more. The number of 529 plans across the US has grown 80% since 2010, with the average balance more than doubling since then. But AI is putting higher education to the test . Students use it to cheat and currently face an entry-level hiring crisis after graduation, which many blame on AI. Tech execs say chatbots are better than human teachers, and Silicon Valley-types are pitching AI-ified college alternatives . As AI makes the value of a college degree harder to predict, some parents are changing how they save for their children's futures. Business Insider spoke with six families who are reducing their 529 contributions, moving money into more flexible accounts, or continuing to save while questioning whether traditional college will provide the best return on their investment. Of the 921 K-11 parents polled by Intuit Credit Karma/Harris, more than a quarter said they're rethinking how much they need to save for education, and 15% have already reduced their savings. Even AI's biggest names seem unsure. A mom of two asked Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman whether she should save for college in 2025 . "Probably not," he laughed off, before correcting the record. "I don't know. It's really hard to judge." The parents waving goodbye to 529s David Graham thinks college might still be worthwhile by the time his 12-year-old son finishes high school — but not by the time his 8-year-old twin girls graduate. The 52-year-old retired physician from Billings, Montana, set up multiple savings accounts for his kids. Two years ago, he chose to stop funding their 529s entirely. It wasn't an easy decision. Graham thinks that colleges will struggle financially thanks to declining birth rates. He's watched "learn to code" turn from salient advice to an ironic jab. He likes the hybrid Alpha School model, which leans heavily on AI instruction, and believes that AI tutors will drive down the cost of education. At this point, Graham estimates that his son has $50,000 in his 529, and his twin girls have $15,000 each. While he bets that his kids aren't college-bound, he has the money to fund their degrees if they choose otherwise — and is willing to sacrifice the tax benefits. "If he wants to go to school, I'll just write a check," he said. Michael Reynolds, a certified financial planner from Indianapolis, said that about 30% of the parents he worked with were redirecting some funds away from 529s as they doubt the future value of college. "More and more conversations are happening around: Do we put all our eggs in this basket?" he said. Omar Khan is one doubter. Instead of a 529, the millennial father of two is investing for his children via taxable brokerage accounts , knowing he'll pay tax on the gains. He believes the value proposition for brand-name colleges may fade. Khan wants the flexibility to use that money for whatever his kids' futures look like. Should they go into a technical field, buy a house, or bootstrap a company, they'll be set, he said. To save or not to save Matthew Crowson isn't abandoning his 529 — but he's hoping it'll loosen up. The 39-year-old physician is saving for his two sons, aged 3 and 5. He also has a front-row seat to higher education's AI transformation: Crowson is on the faculty at Harvard Medical School. Crowson said some of his best students don't need to show up for class at all; they can learn on their own using AI tools and then come to him with questions. He expected students to start questioning the high cost of tuition, especially compared to the low cost of a chatbot. Should the college-pocalypse come , the government will need to change the 529 rules. Crowson is anticipating this: He hopes the government will expand the definition of "school" by the time his kids grow up (apprenticeships and continuing education are already qualified 529 expenses). Better yet, he's hoping for a "get-out-of-jail-free card" that lets parents draw down all their funds tax-free, no matter where they spend it. "That's a very cautiously optimistic take," he said. The rules have bent before. In 2018, the government allowed parents to use some 529 funds for private high schools . Six years later, the government allowed parents to roll over some money from a 529 into a Roth IRA tax-free. Parents can now use the funds tax-free on post-graduate courses and certificates, too. "Even if you're not saving exactly for college, there are still other ways to be using that money," said Eric Reale, a New York-based financial advisor. Some AI-enmeshed parents still see the value of a 529 plan. Matthew Seeger, who oversees AI strategy for a software company in Chicago, has been saving thoroughly for his three- and five-year-old kids. He wants to spare them the financial burden that college can be. Even so, he's getting worried about AI's longer-term impacts, especially on jobs. But a whole other group of parents are certain AI abundance is coming — and that college is getting the chop. Yet many of their kids loathe the tech. While 9 in 10 kids have used AI, according to a Common Sense Media report , only 26% think the technology will have a mostly positive effect on their lives. While Business Insider spoke with Graham, the Montana dad who had stopped 529 contributions entirely, his 12-year-old son arrived home. Graham asked: Do you use AI? "No," his son responded quickly, before amending his answer to "every once in a while" and running upstairs. "They actually hate AI," Graham said of his kids. "And I don't let them use the H-word." items.summary: Jake Woodson, 34, is one of Goldman's youngest new partners. Goldman Sachs Jake Woodson, a former Rising Star of Wall Street , is one of Goldman's youngest new partners. After a chaotic day, Woodson celebrated with colleagues at a pub and had a quiet dinner with his mom. The trader brought Business Insider inside the big day and shared what he plans to do with the title. Thursday, November 5, was among Jake Woodson's more chaotic days as a trader at Goldman Sachs. AI stocks were plummeting after the midterms, all three benchmark indexes were falling, and, in the middle of it all, Woodson's phone was ringing with one of the most important calls of his career. Everyone on the trading floor went quiet as Woodson, 34, said hello to firm president John Waldron, who congratulated him on being promoted to partner, Goldman's highest-ranking title outside the C-Suite. Woodson, who oversees trading in leveraged corporate debt and loans and was previously one of Business Insider's Rising Stars of Wall Street, is the second-youngest among the 109 executives who earned the promotion this year. "It was high-fives and hugs, and then right back to trading for the rest of the day," Woodson said early the next week, adding that, though his memory of the moment is foggy, he thinks colleagues on the leveraged finance credit desk applauded. His mom was at the center of the day Woodson said he took a few minutes during the work day to call his mom, dad, and brother. He rang his teary-eyed mom first, partly since he'd flown her to New York from his hometown outside of Vancouver, Canada. "I flew my mom out because I figured either I'm not going to make it and I could use a shoulder to cry on, or I really want her there to be a part of it," Woodson said. "I've lived a six-hour flight from my family for 12 years, so it's nice to be able to show them it was worth it." His mom joined Woodson and Goldman's larger credit business that evening in the private room of Monk McGinn's, a pub near the office. She mingled with around 50 internal colleagues and 20 clients who came, meeting some of the people who have defined her son's life for more than a decade. None of Woodson's family works in finance, and he said his mom doesn't know much about his job beyond the fact that it happens at Goldman, so it was special to bring her into his world. The two of them ducked out of the pub earlier than most to have a quiet dinner at Woodson's apartment, FaceTiming his dad and brother in Canada. Woodson celebrated again at a dinner with friends on Friday night, before his mom flew back to Vancouver and he drove to the Catskills alone. He spent Saturday by a lake, breathing air more similar to that of the mountains in British Columbia than of Tribeca. How he got there Woodson didn't always expect to end up at Goldman, even though he studied finance in college. He grew up in a suburb 45 minutes outside of Vancouver and went to the University of British Columbia rather than the Ivy League schools that tend to dot Wall Street resumes. "If you were a betting person, you probably wouldn't bet that there would be a Goldman partner coming from that suburb," Woodson said. He was accepted into UBC's Portfolio Management Foundation, a program that provides hands-on training in investing and finance to a small group of students. That program, with its strong alumni network and ties to Goldman, changed his life more than anything else. Woodson joined Goldman in 2014, starting in investment-grade private credit. He was a distressed credit trader during the pandemic, and, as the head of US distressed credit trading, steered his team through the 2023 banking crisis, before becoming the head of leveraged finance trading this fall. The trader feels some responsibility for representing those who don't start as interns , or come from a target school, or tick most of the other stereotypical finance-kid boxes. He said he's one of many at Goldman who want to ensure that the firm continues to invest in a range of young talent. Continuing to execute When he was one of those younger people, Woodson probably would have expected making partner to feel like a final, grand accomplishment. "It's almost the opposite. It's just the beginning of growing into this role and continuing to operate at a high level," he said, adding that most focused on strengthening his team. Balancing the daily demands of trading and managing people "how they deserve to be managed" will likely become a bigger challenge, Woodson said, and may just demand working more hours . Woodson is one of the rare leaders who is simultaneously respected and liked, a former boss told Business Insider last year. Part of that, Woodson said, comes from treating people, whether internal colleagues or clients, kindly and well, even when it seems disadvantageous in the short term. "It was instilled in me by my mom and maybe Canadian culture that treating people the right way over time is the right thing to do for a number of reasons. It's the right thing to do morally, but it also tends to lead to better outcomes," he said. Beyond setting a good example, his mom also gave him one of the best gifts he received: appropriately cheesy, multicolored, six-foot-tall balloons. Read the original article on Business Insider

His mom was at the center of the day

"I flew my mom out because I figured either I'm not going to make it and I could use a shoulder to cry on, or I really want her there to be a part of it," Woodson said. "I've lived a six-hour flight from my family for 12 years, so it's nice to be able to show them it was worth it."

The two of them ducked out of the pub earlier than most to have a quiet dinner at Woodson's apartment, FaceTiming his dad and brother in Canada. He was accepted into UBC's Portfolio Management Foundation, a program that provides hands-on training in investing and finance to a small group of students. That program, with its strong alumni network and ties to Goldman, changed his life more than anything else.

Woodson joined Goldman in 2014, starting in investment-grade private credit. He was a distressed credit trader during the pandemic, and, as the head of US distressed credit trading, steered his team through the 2023 banking crisis, before becoming the head of leveraged finance trading this fall.

items.title: Stanford Research Open-Sources Memorilla, a Latent Memory Module for Frozen LLMs
items.summary: Stanford researchers have released Memorilla , an open-source memory system for LLMs. The Memorilla memory system reads a whole document collection and hands a frozen LLM just 16 memory tokens. On FactKG, a frozen Qwen3-8B scored 84.33% with Memorilla, against 80.43% with every document in context . It did that with 108x fewer document tokens. Code, training recipes and checkpoints are public under Apache 2.0 . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: 194M-parameter trainable memory module. It always outputs 16 memory tokens, whatever the collection size. The encoder ( Qwen3-Embedding-4B ) and decoder ( Qwen3-8B ) stay frozen. Runs on: Linux with CUDA GPUs and Python 3.11. The quickstart needs 1 GPU with 80 GB (recipes ran on H100 80GB). No quantized variants disclosed. Performance: Highest reported average across 8 benchmarks (49.68), top score on 5 of 8. Best: PersonaMem-v2 accuracy of 44.60%, versus 27.92% for full context. Worst: PubMedQA accuracy of 59.00%, versus 69.00% for LLMLingua-2. What is Memorilla? Memorilla is a memory module that turns a document collection into 16 vectors for a frozen LLM. The work comes from Jure Leskovec’s SNAP group, with co-authors from Toronto, Penn and MIT. A frozen LLM can only use what sits in its context window. Full-context prompting grows slower as history grows. Retrieval pastes the chunks most similar to the question, and can miss weaker clues. Memorilla takes a third route: it learns what each question needs from the whole store. How does Memorilla work? The pipeline has 3 steps: Encode once. A frozen Qwen3-Embedding-4B embeds each document a single time. New documents never force re-encoding of old ones. Read per question. 16 learned slots attend to the question and the full store. The module uses 2 cross-attention layers with 8 heads. Inject. The slots are projected into Qwen3-8B’s input embedding space and prepended to the question. Only the memory module trains: 194,123,776 parameters for the 8B decoder. Training runs in 3 stages. Stage 1 uses about 1.98M Wikipedia paraphrase-reconstruction examples. Stage 2 adds about 1.34M examples from 10 QA and summarization datasets. Stage 3 fine-tunes on all 8 benchmarks. The full recipe takes about 19 hours on 4 H100 GPUs. How does Memorilla perform on benchmarks? All baselines use the same frozen Qwen3-8B, per the paper’s main table. Scores are self-reported by the research team. FactKG: 84.33% accuracy, versus 80.43% full context and 80.38% MemoRAG. PersonaMem-v2: 44.60%, versus 30.90% for xRAG, the next best method. TriviaQA: 57.00 exact match, just ahead of MemoRAG at 56.60. LaMP-4 / LaMP-7: 18.15 and 48.37 ROUGE-L, both the best scores. Average: 49.68, versus 41.92 for xRAG, 40.75 for LLMLingua-2 and 38.02 for Mem0. Memorilla loses on 3 benchmarks. On PubMedQA it scores 59.00%, while LLMLingua-2 reaches 69.00%. Those abstracts total only 324 tokens, so compression has little to gain. MemoRAG leads on PersonalizationV4 (67.88% vs 66.65%) and NarrativeQA ROUGE-L (20.51 vs 19.31). MemoRAG used about 690x and 50x more document tokens there. Compression peaks on NarrativeQA: 16 tokens replace 67,385 document tokens, a 4,212x cut. As agent memory, 8 memory tokens lift a Qwen3-4B TextWorld agent from 18.6% to 24.2% average success. &&& How fast is Memorilla compared to full context? On 1 H100, Memorilla answers in 0.74 s at 512 documents (about 128K tokens). Full context slows from 0.75 s to 19.9 s, which is 27x slower. The memory module itself takes about 2 ms. An optional memory cache precomputes cross-attention keys and values. On 1 B200, a question then takes 8.1 ms at 1M documents and 33 ms at 4M. With torch.compile , the 1M case drops to 5.0 ms. The cache costs 80 GiB at 4M documents. How do you run Memorilla? Install with uv on Linux, then load MemoryVLLM.from_pretrained . The first run downloads about 25 GB of models. Checkpoints live at memorilla/Memorilla-Qwen3-8B as Stage 1, 2, 3, PV4 and PMv2 folders. Each checkpoint must run with the decoder it was trained with ( evaluation docs ). Custom data needs parquet files with collection_id , question , answer and documents columns. The research team also released PersonalizationV4 : 149 synthetic users, 200 conversations each, under CC BY 4.0. Memorilla vs Mem0, MemoRAG and xRAG Benchmark scores come from Memorilla’s paper, which ran every baseline on the same Qwen3-8B. Licenses come from each project’s repository. items.summary_html:
Stanford researchers have released Memorilla, an open-source memory system for LLMs. The Memorilla memory system reads a whole document collection and hands a frozen LLM just 16 memory tokens. On FactKG, a frozen Qwen3-8B scored 84.33% with Memorilla, against 80.43% with every document in context. It did that with 108x fewer document tokens. Code, training recipes and checkpoints are public under Apache 2.0. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension.

TL;DR
  • Size: 194M-parameter trainable memory module. It always outputs 16 memory tokens, whatever the collection size. The encoder (Qwen3-Embedding-4B) and decoder (Qwen3-8B) stay frozen.
  • Runs on: Linux with CUDA GPUs and Python 3.11. The quickstart needs 1 GPU with 80 GB (recipes ran on H100 80GB). No quantized variants disclosed.
  • Performance: Highest reported average across 8 benchmarks (49.68), top score on 5 of 8.
  • Best: PersonaMem-v2 accuracy of 44.60%, versus 27.92% for full context.
  • Worst: PubMedQA accuracy of 59.00%, versus 69.00% for LLMLingua-2.
What is Memorilla?

Memorilla is a memory module that turns a document collection into 16 vectors for a frozen LLM. The work comes from Jure Leskovec’s SNAP group, with co-authors from Toronto, Penn and MIT.

A frozen LLM can only use what sits in its context window. Full-context prompting grows slower as history grows. Retrieval pastes the chunks most similar to the question, and can miss weaker clues. Memorilla takes a third route: it learns what each question needs from the whole store.

How does Memorilla work?

The pipeline has 3 steps:

  1. Encode once. A frozen Qwen3-Embedding-4B embeds each document a single time. New documents never force re-encoding of old ones.
  2. Read per question. 16 learned slots attend to the question and the full store. The module uses 2 cross-attention layers with 8 heads.
  3. Inject. The slots are projected into Qwen3-8B’s input embedding space and prepended to the question.

Only the memory module trains: 194,123,776 parameters for the 8B decoder. Training runs in 3 stages. Stage 1 uses about 1.98M Wikipedia paraphrase-reconstruction examples. Stage 2 adds about 1.34M examples from 10 QA and summarization datasets. Stage 3 fine-tunes on all 8 benchmarks. The full recipe takes about 19 hours on 4 H100 GPUs.

How does Memorilla perform on benchmarks?

All baselines use the same frozen Qwen3-8B, per the paper’s main table. Scores are self-reported by the research team.

  • FactKG: 84.33% accuracy, versus 80.43% full context and 80.38% MemoRAG.
  • PersonaMem-v2: 44.60%, versus 30.90% for xRAG, the next best method.
  • TriviaQA: 57.00 exact match, just ahead of MemoRAG at 56.60.
  • LaMP-4 / LaMP-7: 18.15 and 48.37 ROUGE-L, both the best scores.
  • Average: 49.68, versus 41.92 for xRAG, 40.75 for LLMLingua-2 and 38.02 for Mem0.

Memorilla loses on 3 benchmarks. On PubMedQA it scores 59.00%, while LLMLingua-2 reaches 69.00%. Those abstracts total only 324 tokens, so compression has little to gain. MemoRAG leads on PersonalizationV4 (67.88% vs 66.65%) and NarrativeQA ROUGE-L (20.51 vs 19.31). MemoRAG used about 690x and 50x more document tokens there.

Compression peaks on NarrativeQA: 16 tokens replace 67,385 document tokens, a 4,212x cut. As agent memory, 8 memory tokens lift a Qwen3-4B TextWorld agent from 18.6% to 24.2% average success.

&&&

How fast is Memorilla compared to full context?

On 1 H100, Memorilla answers in 0.74 s at 512 documents (about 128K tokens). Full context slows from 0.75 s to 19.9 s, which is 27x slower. The memory module itself takes about 2 ms.

An optional memory cache precomputes cross-attention keys and values. On 1 B200, a question then takes 8.1 ms at 1M documents and 33 ms at 4M. With torch.compile, the 1M case drops to 5.0 ms. The cache costs 80 GiB at 4M documents.

How do you run Memorilla?

Install with uv on Linux, then load MemoryVLLM.from_pretrained. The first run downloads about 25 GB of models. Checkpoints live at memorilla/Memorilla-Qwen3-8B as Stage 1, 2, 3, PV4 and PMv2 folders.

Each checkpoint must run with the decoder it was trained with (evaluation docs). Custom data needs parquet files with collection_id, question, answer and documents columns. The research team also released PersonalizationV4: 149 synthetic users, 200 conversations each, under CC BY 4.0.

Memorilla vs Mem0, MemoRAG and xRAG

Benchmark scores come from Memorilla’s paper, which ran every baseline on the same Qwen3-8B. Licenses come from each project’s repository.

  • FactKG: 84.33% vs 80.43% full context, with 108x fewer tokens.
  • Highest reported 8-benchmark average: 49.68.
  • Weak spot: PubMedQA at 59.00% and fine-grained facts.
  • Apache 2.0 code; 194M-parameter checkpoints on Hugging Face.

items.title: Runway's open-source Praxis-1 turns video AI into a robot controller
items.summary: Runway releases its robotics model Praxis-1 with open weights and source code under the Apache 2.0 license. The model uses knowledge from video training for robot control and leads the World Action Model category on Nvidia's RoboLab-120 benchmark. items.title: ‘It’s like the wild west’: how AI has rocked the literary world
items.summary: With authors losing lucrative deals and writers removed from prize shortlists, accusations of AI use are sending shock waves through the publishing industry. Is it too late to turn the tide on machine writing? T he romance novelist Coral Hart got her break writing books for Mills & Boon, the publisher of bodice-ripper paperbacks. In 2012, she decided to dip her toe in self-publishing. She felt drawn to dark romance, a subgenre featuring twisted, toxic love stories that was taking off online but that publishers didn’t want to touch. Three years later, things were going well enough that she decided to self-publish full-time. Kindle Unlimited, where Hart sells her books, rewards prolific writers: the algorithm favours those who can produce a new book at least once a month. Hart says she knows of authors who hire more than a dozen ghostwriters to keep pace. By herself, Hart can write 10,000 words a day, but AI could help her produce many more. Since 2025 she has written 370 novels under 21 pen names using AI, earning herself “high six figures”.

items.title: Scale Dominates AI Research. A 14-Year Microsoft Veteran Just Walked Away.
items.summary: Originally reported by IT之家 In 2019, I was on a call where a senior engineering lead told our team to stop exploring alternative training approaches. "Scaling will solve it," they said flatly. We folded. Six months later, some of those same problems still weren't solved — but the budget for new ideas had evaporated. If that sounds familiar, you're not alone. And you might understand exactly why John Langford just left Microsoft. After 14 years at the company and as co-founder of the Microsoft AI Frontiers Lab, Langford departed citing a fundamental frustration: research innovations couldn't find paths to production, and cost-optimization research wasn't taken seriously. His ~50-person team was merged into Mustafa Suleyman's new Microsoft AI department this September. The cultural and strategic mismatch, according to Langford, proved irreconcilable. For those who haven't followed the ML theory side closely, Langford isn't a casual presence. He's one of the researchers who advanced Contextual Bandits — the framework behind recommendation systems, adaptive UIs, and any system that learns from incomplete feedback in real time. That line of work connects directly to how your application might decide which model architecture to use at inference time, or how to allocate compute dynamically. Microsoft (and much of industry) has bet heavily on the scaling hypothesis: bigger models, more data, more tokens, diminishing-but-still-positive returns. The questions shift from first principles to marginal optimization. That's important work — but it's not the work Langford signed up for. "Cost reduction" becomes the mandate without intellectual honesty. Let's be clear: spending less on existing approaches matters enormously at production scale. But when the narrative becomes exclusively about squeezing more out of current models rather than questioning whether current models are the right tool, you lose the researchers who joined specifically to ask different questions. Acquisition-driven org restructuring creates friction. Langford's team landed inside Suleyman's organization. Different backgrounds, different incentives — Suleyman comes from DeepMind and enterprise AI products; Langford comes from theoretical ML. Merger noise is inevitable. items.title: The Researcher's Trap: Why Scale Is Winning (And What We're Losing)
items.summary: Originally reported by IT之家 I once watched a colleague spend six months building a clever algorithm that could cut training costs by 40%. It got one slide in a leadership deck and never saw production. Meanwhile, a team shipped a slightly larger model two weeks later and got celebrated. This isn't a Microsoft story — it's every large tech org's story. But it just got a lot more personal. John Langford, a 14-year Microsoft veteran and co-founder of their AI Frontiers lab, just left. By his own account, the breaking point wasn't salary or stock options. It was the slow realization that the most interesting problems in his field had no clear path to resolution inside the company. His research — grounded in contextual bandits, exploration theory, and offline policy evaluation — represents some of the most intellectually honest work in machine learning. And he couldn't get traction on the idea that there are better ways forward than just scaling up. Let me be clear: scaling works. Langford explicitly acknowledges this. Bigger models improve predictions. The return profile is clearer for engineering leadership. You can roadmap it. You can allocate compute budgets with confidence. But treating scale as the only strategy isn't just boring — it's actively dangerous for the field. Here's what most people miss about Langford's departure. He's not complaining that his ideas weren't implemented. He's describing a structural problem where ideas about whether we should be doing this aren't being seriously considered at all. Cost-reduction research, alternative paradigms, methods that don't fit the "bigger is better" narrative — these get politely acknowledged and strategically deprioritized. That's a different failure mode than "my code didn't ship." The context matters. In September, his roughly 50-person team was folded into Mustafa Suleyman's Microsoft AI division. On paper, this consolidates talent. In practice, it shifts power centers and recalibrates priorities. When your organizational home changes hands, the things your former champions valued lose their sponsorship. New leaders bring different mental models about what counts as progress. This isn't unique to Microsoft. I've seen it at companies across the industry. The pattern is almost comically predictable: A research group proves something interesting Leadership recognizes the publication value Leadership declines the implementation cost The researchers are reassigned to projects with clearer ROI timelines Everyone tells themselves it's pragmatic decision-making The quiet cost? The people who stay become good at picking problems that will win, not good at solving problems that matter. This is how entire subfields go dormant while generating impressive quarterly reports. So what should a senior ML researcher do when they recognize this pattern? Langford's situation suggests three hard truths: First, scale your influence before you scale your ideas. Building a coalition that outlasts reorganizations is more valuable than any single project. If your work survives leadership changes, you have leverage. Second, know the difference between "not ready" and "not wanted." Some innovations genuinely need infrastructure or market conditions to mature. Others are being killed because they threaten an existing investment thesis. Reading this distinction correctly determines whether you wait or leave. Third, document the opportunity cost. When you watch a team pivot from exploratory work to shipping yet another scaled model, record what's being abandoned. Not for the performance review — for the next time someone asks whether alternatives exist. Langford's work on contextual bandits and offline policy evaluation isn't going anywhere. Those are foundational problems that will keep maturing regardless of whether any particular lab prioritizes them. The question is whether the people shaping industry direction are incentivized to ask harder questions about efficiency, or whether the reward structure only celebrates those who push parameters harder. I've been on both sides of this equation — the researcher watching ideas stall and the engineer deciding which ones to greenlight. The honest answer is that most of these decisions feel reasonable in the moment. They only look tragic in retrospect. What do you think — is there a way to structurally protect exploratory research inside a scale-up organization, or is this tension fundamentally unresolvable at anyone above startup size?

items.title: Why Great ML Researchers Leave Big Tech (It's Not About Money)
items.summary: Originally reported by IT之家 After 14 years at Microsoft, renowned ML researcher John Langford walked away. His reason? Innovation couldn't land. Cost-saving research wasn't taken seriously. Sound familiar? Let's talk about what actually happens when world-class researchers join tech giants—and why so many eventually bail out. The Scale Trap Is Real Langford acknowledged something important publicly: yes, scaling models improves predictions. Yes, it gives enterprises predictable ROI. But treating scale as the only path kills exploratory research. This isn't new. It's the classic tension between "let's build the best model" and "let's figure out why we need bigger models at all." Contextual bandits, offline policy evaluation, exploration algorithms—these are the unglamorous foundations that make systems actually work in production. They don't win blog posts. They win at inference time, where cost matters more than accuracy points. What Actually Breaks Inside Big Labs Two things tend to happen: First , reorganizations merge teams for strategic alignment—not technical coherence. Langford's ~50-person AI Frontiers group got folded into Mustafa Suleyman's AI division in September 2026. Mergers sound efficient. They're rarely neutral for research culture. Second , "innovation" gets redefined. Ideas that can't ship within quarters lose funding. Research becomes roadmap-driven instead of curiosity-driven. And suddenly, your life's work looks like a feature request. The Hard Truth Nobody Posts On LinkedIn Scaling-focused research pays off visibly. Papers get cited, models get deployed, stock prices move. Exploratory work? Its value compounds silently over years. When leadership rewards the visible, the invisible starves. Langford didn't leave because Microsoft stopped valuing research. He left because the type of research valued shifted toward incremental optimization rather than foundational progress. That's a difference every ML engineer should understand before joining—or staying at—a big lab. Practical Takeaways If you're building ML teams (or considering joining one): Protect exploratory budget lines. Not everything needs quarterly ROI. Some projects exist to prevent organizational blindness. Resist conflating R&D with product roadmaps. They serve different masters. Mixing them quietly kills both. Watch for reorg signals. When research groups merge without technical rationale, ask who benefits and what gets dropped. Celebrate inference-efficient wins. Better context handling, cheaper offline evaluation, tighter exploration—these matter when deployment scales. ## The Open Question We keep hearing that "AI research talent is scarce." But maybe the problem isn't scarcity—it's retention. We're losing researchers not to competitors, but to their own organizations' priorities. What's your experience? Have you seen great ML researchers leave companies over research direction, not compensation? How do you balance scale pragmatism with exploratory ambition? Share below. 👇

items.title: The Scaling Monoculture Is Breaking Out Its Best Researchers
items.summary: Originally reported by IT之家 I spent three years at a company that told me "we scale everything." Every new model, every system redesign, the question wasn't "what's the right approach?" — it was "how much bigger can we make it?" A year later, two senior engineers left because they couldn't reconcile their actual beliefs about the field with what the company would fund. Sound familiar? John Langford, Microsoft's longest-tenured AI scientist, just exited after 14 years. And his parting message cuts through all the press release noise: the organization doesn't take his research seriously enough, and the narrow focus on scaling models is crowding out real innovation. What Langford Actually Does Matters Langford isn't some fringe researcher. He's the person behind Contextual Bandits — the theoretical framework that lets machines make smarter decisions with incomplete feedback. That's not incremental ML. That's foundational work that underpins recommendation systems, ad bidding, resource allocation, and any system where you learn by doing rather than by having all the data upfront. His collaborators published papers on exploration algorithms, problem reduction techniques, and offline policy evaluation that are cited constantly in production ML circles. This is people building the tools that let systems improve without infinite labeled datasets or compute budgets. The Real Story Isn't About Ego Most coverage frames this as another high-profile AI researcher walking away. But read Langford's actual statements carefully and the picture is sharper: Scaling does improve predictions. He says so directly. The returns are predictable, measurable, and appeal to executives who want roadmaps with Gantt charts. What he disagrees with is making scaling the only credible research direction — which systematically defunds everything else. When your organization rewards only one thesis about how intelligence emerges, you don't get better research. You get compliance research: people telling you what you want to hear so they keep their budgets. This happens everywhere, not just at big tech. I've watched teams pivot from interesting side projects to "here's what the VP wants to see" — and the smartest engineers on those teams tend to leave within 18 months. Why This Should Make You Pause If you're leading a machine learning team or deciding where to invest your research time, here's the uncomfortable truth Langford's departure reveals: Convergence thinking gets promoted. Divergence thinking gets managed down. The scaling argument wins meetings because it sounds definitive. Alternative approaches — efficient learning, offline evaluation, structured exploration — sound speculative until someone publishes results nobody expected. Then everyone suddenly has interest again. The teams worth investing in are the ones that let researchers pursue questions that might fail. Because the ones that do succeed are often the ones nobody saw coming. The Open Question Nobody's Asking Microsoft absorbed Langford's 50-person AI Frontiers lab into Mustafa Suleyman's division in September. The restructuring reportedly created friction around research direction and how seriously different visions were treated. Langford left. Other researchers have left similar situations quietly. So here's my question for anyone running ML teams: How do you actually measure whether your organization treats unconventional research paths as serious options or just things to survive until the next round? Because the answer to that predicts retention far better than salary bands ever will. I'd love to hear how others have navigated this — the companies that got it right and the ones that pushed their best people out the door by ignoring them.

items.title: Why I Stayed at My Startup When Everyone Said "Just Build Faster"
items.summary: Originally reported by IT之家 In 2018, my CTO told me our model architecture problem wasn't an engineering problem — it was a data problem. "More data will fix this," he said, spreading a spreadsheet that showed we needed ten times our current training set. Three months later, after spending $200K on data collection, we had slightly better accuracy on things that didn't matter to users. Meanwhile, the elegant little contextual bandit approach my lead engineer proposed got buried because it didn't fit the growth narrative. John Langford just left Microsoft after 14 years, and this tiny story from my past keeps replaying in my head. Not because I think I'm John Langford — absolutely not. But because the dynamic is universal: somewhere between a company's first AI hires and its tenth act of corporate optimization, someone decides that the way to innovate is to scale harder instead of think deeper. And nobody notices they've crossed that line until the good researchers start leaving. Langford co-founded Microsoft AI Frontiers and built one of the most respected teams in industry ML research. His work on contextual bandits, offline policy evaluation, and exploring algorithm design genuinely shaped how production recommendation and decision systems work today. This isn't abstract academia — this is infrastructure-level ML thinking that moves products. Microsoft folded his roughly 50-person team into Mustafa Suleyman's new AI division this past September. The official reason? Strategic realignment. The personal reason, as Langford stated plainly, is that his team's research couldn't find a path to real application. Innovation ideas weren't being taken seriously. Scaling got funding; thinking differently got deferrals. Here's what I wish every engineering leader would sit with: scaling IS legitimate. Langford himself acknowledged this — bigger models improve prediction quality, and the return path is clearer for executives. The question isn't whether scaling works. The question is whether treating scaling as the only lever changes what kind of company becomes. When I worked on ML system design at previous companies, I saw two patterns repeat: Pattern A: Every bottleneck gets framed as a compute problem. The expensive query? "Throw GPUs at it." The slow pipeline? "Scale horizontally." The archaic feature store? "Migrate to a vector database." Somewhere along the way, rethinking the problem stopped happening. Nobody asked if the problem was worth solving the same way. Pattern B: The researchers who kept asking those questions either adapted and started shipping incrementally useful work, or they left. Langford clearly fell into the second camp, and honestly, I respect that choice enormously. It's easier to pretend you're changing the organization from within. It's also, more often than not, exhausting and futile. The practical takeaway here isn't "leave your job when things feel wrong." The takeaway is organizational: if your AI strategy conversation is exclusively about compute budgets and dataset sizes rather than about problem formulation and alternative approaches, you already made the decision to optimize for velocity over direction. You don't need to announce that. People notice. Companies like DeepMind and Google Brain survived this tension for decades because they institutionalized separation — research teams with protected time and different success metrics than product teams. Microsoft's AI Frontiers existed in exactly that spirit. Removing that separation without explicitly addressing what replaces it doesn't make the org stronger. It makes it honest about what it values, which is sometimes worse. If you're building AI teams, ask yourself: when was the last time a rejected research idea actually improved the product, even partially? If you can't answer that, you might be managing for efficiency rather than optionality. What does your organization do when a well-reasoned alternative approach challenges the dominant scaling hypothesis? Does anyone actually listen, or do they just file it under "not enough compute"?

This isn't some disgruntled engineer posting vague complaints on Hacker News. This is someone who helped build the mathematical foundations for how recommendation systems, ad auctions, and countless real-world ML pipelines make decisions under uncertainty. And he's pointing at something most of us feel but rarely articulate. The Scale Trap No One Wants to Admit Let's be clear about what happened technically. Langford's research area — contextual bandits, offline policy evaluation, exploration strategies — sits at the intersection of theory and practice. These are the mechanisms that let systems learn from historical data without requiring expensive online experimentation. Think: should this user see this feature? Should we try this pricing strategy? Which model architecture deserves another shot given limited compute? These problems are hard . They require new mathematical tools, not just bigger transformers. And they're precisely the kind of problems that get squeezed when the dominant narrative becomes "scale until it works." The team was restructured this past September, folded into Mustafa Suleyman's consolidated AI division. From what Langford has said publicly, there were fundamental disagreements about research direction and whether the organization would genuinely invest in alternative approaches beyond scaling. He acknowledges that scaling models does improve predictive performance. Yes. That's empirically true. But treating it as the primary or sole research vector means other dimensions of the problem — efficiency, robustness, sample complexity, the kinds of questions his bandit research addresses — become secondary. Or invisible. What This Means for Us as Practitioners Here's where this hits home for anyone building production ML systems: 1. Your company probably has the same tension. The executives want benchmarks that move and demos that impress. The researchers want to solve harder, messier problems. Both are valid. The tragedy happens when one side gets zero budget. If you're in a position to influence resource allocation, fight for at least a slice of the pie to go toward non-scaling research. Even 10% matters. 2. Contextual bandits aren't going away — they're getting priced out. Offline policy evaluation alone is critical for any org running A/B tests at scale. Yet how many engineering teams have dedicated researchers working on this versus teams working on making existing architectures slightly larger? The imbalance is real and it's visible in hiring patterns across the industry. 3. "Innovation difficulty" is a structural problem, not a people problem. Langford didn't leave because Microsoft ran out of smart people. He left because the incentive structure rewards shipping incremental improvements to the dominant paradigm over pursuing genuinely different approaches. Until leadership changes how they measure and reward research impact, this pattern repeats. The Uncomfortable Question We talk a lot about AI safety, alignment, and capability risk. But there's a quieter failure mode: when the organization makes it impossible for the right questions to even be asked. Langford spent 14 years at one of the best-resourced AI labs on the planet. His core grievance wasn't lack of resources — it was that the resources weren't being directed toward the problems he thought mattered most. That should terrify every engineering leader reading this. Because the next person with his insight and track record might look at your organization and reach the same conclusion. What do you think? Are companies actually investing meaningfully in non-scale AI research, or is it just rhetorical support? Have you experienced this tension firsthand — and if so, how did you navigate it? Drop a comment. I want to hear your stories.

items.title: Weight-space programming at 50 forward passes: Qwen hit 48.1%, Gemma 7.0%
items.summary: GPT-6 Astra edited 131,072 of Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights with no training. Its MATH-500 score went from 7.9% to 48.1%. On the same budget of 50 forward passes, Gemma 3 270M went from 6.8% to 7.0%. It fixed a bug. It did not teach math. The work is by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab at MIT CSAIL, published Nov 2, 2026. The logs are public, so you can check the numbers without running a model. Pull the numbers Run this and you get the score and the share of answers cut at the token limit, for each Qwen run: base = https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/main/exp8_math for run in unedited p10c p25c p50c ; do curl -s " $base /eval/ $run /merged.json" \ | jq -c --arg run " $run " '[$run, .math500.acc, .math500.cut_share]' done ["unedited",0.079,0.93] ["p10c",0.1235,0.8725] ["p25c",0.141,0.8635] ["p50c",0.481,0.3305] The matched-budget table Forward passes Qwen MATH-500 Qwen cut at token limit Gemma MATH-500 Unedited 7.9% 93.0% 6.8% 10 12.3% 87.2% 7.6% 25 14.1% 86.4% 7.7% 50 48.1% 33.1% 7.0% One pass is up to 512 generated answers or 1,024 texts read for Qwen. Gemma's generation pass is larger, at 2,048. Limits: Each budget is one run, and each run chose a different edit. The 10-pass run changed 30 matrices. The 25-pass run zeroed one attention head. The 50-pass run edited 64 MLP columns in each of layers 15 and 19. Gemma's setup differs : no thinking mode, 8,192 tokens, temperature 1.0 and format-agnostic grading. Read the columns separately. The Gemma gain isn't established. Four other runs , told a stricter grading rule, scored 6.1% to 6.7% on the same scale. No model was rerun for this post. akhaliq's re-run of the 50-pass checkpoint got 51.0% with 31.6% cut off. Its base-model check was a 25-problem smoke test. The edit The rules banned backward passes, autograd, optimizers and iterative fitting. Astra had a CPU Python kernel over the weights and could only run the model through the forward-pass tool. The arithmetic: 2 layers × 64 columns × 1,024 = 131,072 weights. Against a nominal 0.8 billion, that's 0.016384%. The report rounds it to 0.016%. Astra traced the loops to one direction written by those MLPs, then subtracted it. A steering vector works on the same idea at inference time, by adding a contrast direction to activations. Here the direction went into the weights. On Hacker News, yurimo , who says part of their research is in weight-space learning, reads the fix as close to that established technique. Split the gain From the same table : 93.0 − 33.1 = 59.9 points fewer answers cut off. 48.1 − 7.9 = 40.2 points more answers correct. Those compare shares, so they don't show which answers changed. Astra's confirmation run gets closer, on 1,152 held-out practice problems: 579 answers went from wrong to right, and 576 of them had been cut off. Accuracy on finished answers didn't change. Those are Astra's own numbers, on practice data. Gemma has no such bug. Only 8.5% of its answers reach its limit, and Astra found ordinary arithmetic and algebra errors. You can split any score jump this way. Count the answers cut off at the limit first, then compare only the ones that finished. Check the brief Astra was told what to look for, as one example: curl -s " $base /runs/p50c/turns/t001/prompt.txt" | grep -o "if the model often fails[^.]* \. " if the model often fails because it repeats itself and never finishes, finding and fixing what drives that repetition counts. That brief runs to 10,315 bytes. It names no layer or direction. Astra still needed 158 turns, 80 Python runs and 20.3 hours , including a 4.7-hour wait when the model could not be reached. Qwen's model card also warns this model is prone to thinking loops. The limit The authors write that editing could remove an obstacle hiding an ability, but could not add one the model lacked. In experiments 5 and 6, Astra wrote small game networks from scratch, so that limit is about language models that already exist. A third of Qwen's answers still hit the limit. My reading, not theirs: one AI can now debug another. Teaching it something new still takes training. The maintained version, with the chart and the comment thread, is on argbe.tech .
items.summary_html:
GPT-6 Astra edited 131,072 of Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights with no training. Its MATH-500 score went from 7.9% to 48.1%. On the same budget of 50 forward passes, Gemma 3 270M went from 6.8% to 7.0%.

It fixed a bug. It did not teach math.

The work is by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab at MIT CSAIL, published Nov 2, 2026. The logs are public, so you can check the numbers without running a model.

Pull the numbers

Run this and you get the score and the share of answers cut at the token limit, for each Qwen run:

base=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/main/exp8_math
for run in unedited p10c p25c p50c; do
  curl -s "$base/eval/$run/merged.json" \
    | jq -c --arg run "$run" '[$run, .math500.acc, .math500.cut_share]'
done

["unedited",0.079,0.93]
["p10c",0.1235,0.8725]
["p25c",0.141,0.8635]
["p50c",0.481,0.3305]
The matched-budget table
Forward passes Qwen MATH-500 Qwen cut at token limit Gemma MATH-500 Unedited 7.9% 93.0% 6.8% 10 12.3% 87.2% 7.6% 25 14.1% 86.4% 7.7% 50 48.1% 33.1% 7.0%

One pass is up to 512 generated answers or 1,024 texts read for Qwen. Gemma's generation pass is larger, at 2,048.

Limits:

  • Each budget is one run, and each run chose a different edit. The 10-pass run changed 30 matrices. The 25-pass run zeroed one attention head. The 50-pass run edited 64 MLP columns in each of layers 15 and 19.
  • Gemma's setup differs: no thinking mode, 8,192 tokens, temperature 1.0 and format-agnostic grading. Read the columns separately.
  • The Gemma gain isn't established. Four other runs, told a stricter grading rule, scored 6.1% to 6.7% on the same scale.
  • No model was rerun for this post. akhaliq's re-run of the 50-pass checkpoint got 51.0% with 31.6% cut off. Its base-model check was a 25-problem smoke test.
The edit

The rules banned backward passes, autograd, optimizers and iterative fitting. Astra had a CPU Python kernel over the weights and could only run the model through the forward-pass tool.

The arithmetic: 2 layers × 64 columns × 1,024 = 131,072 weights. Against a nominal 0.8 billion, that's 0.016384%. The report rounds it to 0.016%.

Astra traced the loops to one direction written by those MLPs, then subtracted it. A steering vector works on the same idea at inference time, by adding a contrast direction to activations. Here the direction went into the weights. On Hacker News, yurimo, who says part of their research is in weight-space learning, reads the fix as close to that established technique.

Split the gain

From the same table:

  • 93.0 − 33.1 = 59.9 points fewer answers cut off.
  • 48.1 − 7.9 = 40.2 points more answers correct.

Those compare shares, so they don't show which answers changed. Astra's confirmation run gets closer, on 1,152 held-out practice problems: 579 answers went from wrong to right, and 576 of them had been cut off. Accuracy on finished answers didn't change. Those are Astra's own numbers, on practice data.

Gemma has no such bug. Only 8.5% of its answers reach its limit, and Astra found ordinary arithmetic and algebra errors.

You can split any score jump this way. Count the answers cut off at the limit first, then compare only the ones that finished.

Check the brief

Astra was told what to look for, as one example:

curl -s "$base/runs/p50c/turns/t001/prompt.txt" | grep -o "if the model often fails[^.]*\."

if the model often fails because it repeats itself and never finishes, finding and fixing what drives that repetition counts.

That brief runs to 10,315 bytes. It names no layer or direction. Astra still needed 158 turns, 80 Python runs and 20.3 hours, including a 4.7-hour wait when the model could not be reached. Qwen's model card also warns this model is prone to thinking loops.

The limit

The authors write that editing could remove an obstacle hiding an ability, but could not add one the model lacked. In experiments 5 and 6, Astra wrote small game networks from scratch, so that limit is about language models that already exist. A third of Qwen's answers still hit the limit.

My reading, not theirs: one AI can now debug another. Teaching it something new still takes training.

The maintained version, with the chart and the comment thread, is on argbe.tech.

items.title: How I check a WordPress site for hidden casino spam (5-minute checklist)
items.summary: Last week I was checking a small business website in Delhi before pitching SEO work. The homepage looked normal. But the site had more than 2,000 hidden posts, and almost all of them were about casinos and betting. The owner had no idea. This kind of hack is common on WordPress sites that nobody updates. So now I run a quick check on every site before I talk to the owner. You only need a browser. 1. Count the posts through the REST API Open this in your browser: https://example.com/wp-json/wp/v2/posts?per_page=10 You will see the latest posts as JSON. Open DevTools > Network, click the request and look for the X-WP-Total header. That is the total number of posts. A local shop or clinic site usually has 0 to 50 posts. If you see 2,000, something is wrong. 2. Search the site for spam words Try the built-in WordPress search: https://example.com/?s=casino Also try betting , slot and loan . A clean small business site should return nothing. 3. Check what Google can see Search Google for: site:example.com casino If spam pages show up here, Google has already found them. 4. Read robots.txt and the sitemap Open /robots.txt , then /wp-sitemap.xml or /sitemap_index.xml . Look for sitemaps you did not create, or lines that point to a different domain. 5. Check the canonical tag View the page source and search for rel="canonical" . It should point to your own domain. On another site I checked, the canonical tag, robots.txt and sitemap all pointed to a different company's domain. Google was being told the pages belonged to someone else. What to do if you find spam Take a full backup first. Don't just delete the posts. Find how they got in: old plugins, old themes, weak passwords or admin users you don't know. Update WordPress, the theme and all plugins. Remove anything you don't use. Change every password and check the Users list for unknown admins. Remove the spam pages, then submit a clean sitemap in Google Search Console. Why this matters A hacked site quietly loses trust and rankings, and the owner usually finds out last. A five-minute check every few months is worth it. I'm Shiv, founder of Team Elivate , a small web design and SEO studio in Rohini, New Delhi. Questions? Leave a comment.

Last week I was checking a small business website in Delhi before pitching SEO work. The homepage looked normal. But the site had more than 2,000 hidden posts, and almost all of them were about casinos and betting.

The owner had no idea.

This kind of hack is common on WordPress sites that nobody updates. So now I run a quick check on every site before I talk to the owner. You only need a browser.

1. Count the posts through the REST API

Open this in your browser:

https://example.com/wp-json/wp/v2/posts?per_page=10

You will see the latest posts as JSON. Open DevTools > Network, click the request and look for the X-WP-Total header. That is the total number of posts.

A local shop or clinic site usually has 0 to 50 posts. If you see 2,000, something is wrong.

2. Search the site for spam words

Try the built-in WordPress search:

https://example.com/?s=casino

Also try betting, slot and loan. A clean small business site should return nothing.

3. Check what Google can see

Search Google for:

site:example.com casino

If spam pages show up here, Google has already found them.

4. Read robots.txt and the sitemap

Open /robots.txt, then /wp-sitemap.xml or /sitemap_index.xml.

Look for sitemaps you did not create, or lines that point to a different domain.

5. Check the canonical tag

View the page source and search for rel="canonical". It should point to your own domain.

On another site I checked, the canonical tag, robots.txt and sitemap all pointed to a different company's domain. Google was being told the pages belonged to someone else.

What to do if you find spam
  • Take a full backup first.
  • Don't just delete the posts. Find how they got in: old plugins, old themes, weak passwords or admin users you don't know.
  • Update WordPress, the theme and all plugins. Remove anything you don't use.
  • Change every password and check the Users list for unknown admins.
  • Remove the spam pages, then submit a clean sitemap in Google Search Console.
Why this matters

A hacked site quietly loses trust and rankings, and the owner usually finds out last. A five-minute check every few months is worth it.

I'm Shiv, founder of Team Elivate, a small web design and SEO studio in Rohini, New Delhi. Questions? Leave a comment.

items.title: JavaScript Promises vs Async/Await — Explained Simply
items.summary: I'm Safdar Ali , a frontend engineer in Bengaluru. "Promises vs async await" is not a rivalry — async/await is syntax sugar on top of Promises. You still need both mental models for React, Next.js Server Components, and every fetch call. This guide uses BEFORE/AFTER pairs from production code, not toy timers. Async JavaScript is why frontend engineers touch backends without changing jobs — fetch, auth, file uploads, AI streams. Promises formalised callbacks; async/await made them readable. Search "promises vs async await" and forums still debate syntax preference. In production the debate is error handling and parallelism. Get those right and either syntax works; get them wrong and both fail silently on slow networks in India. Mental model — pending, fulfilled, rejected Every Promise is in one of three states. await only pauses inside async functions until fulfillment or rejection. The event loop keeps running other tasks — your loading spinner can animate while fetch waits. Same async operation — Promise chain vs async/await type User = { id: string; name: string }; // Promise style function loadUserPromise(id: string): Promise { return fetch("/api/users/" + id) .then((res) => { if (!res.ok) throw new Error("HTTP " + res.status); return res.json() as Promise ; }); } // async/await style — identical behavior async function loadUserAsync(id: string): Promise { const res = await fetch("/api/users/" + id); if (!res.ok) throw new Error("HTTP " + res.status); return res.json() as Promise ; } Under the hood, async function always returns a Promise. await pauses that function until the Promise settles — it does not block the main thread. fetch returns a Promise immediately — the HTTP response arrives later. await does not make fetch synchronous; it only pauses your async function until the Promise settles. Other UI keeps updating because the browser event loop is free. That distinction is what interviewers test when they ask about blocking vs non-blocking I/O. BEFORE / AFTER — escaping callback hell // BEFORE — nested callbacks (hard to read, easy to miss errors) getUser(id, (err, user) => { if (err) return handle(err); getOrders(user.id, (err2, orders) => { if (err2) return handle(err2); render(user, orders); }); }); // AFTER — async/await linear flow async function showDashboard(id: string) { try { const user = await loadUserAsync(id); const orders = await loadOrders(user.id); render(user, orders); } catch (err) { handle(err); } } Error handling — try/catch vs .catch() Style When I use it try/catch around await Most async functions .catch() on chain Fire-and-forget analytics Promise.allSettled Partial failures OK // BEFORE — forgot await, try/catch never runs on rejection async function bad() { try { const data = fetch("/api/data"); // missing await — bug return data; } catch (e) { console.error(e); } } // AFTER async function good() { try { const res = await fetch("/api/data"); if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Failed"); return await res.json(); } catch (e) { console.error(e); throw e; // rethrow for UI error boundary } } Parallel fetch — Promise.all vs sequential await Sequential await is slow when requests are independent. Dashboard needs user + orders + notifications — run together. // BEFORE — 3 round trips in series (~900ms total on 300ms each) async function loadSlow() { const user = await fetchUser(); const orders = await fetchOrders(); const notes = await fetchNotifications(); return { user, orders, notes }; } // AFTER — parallel (~300ms + overhead) async function loadFast() { const [user, orders, notes] = await Promise.all([ fetchUser(), fetchOrders(), fetchNotifications(), ]); return { user, orders, notes }; } // One failure should not kill all — allSettled const results = await Promise.allSettled([ fetchUser(), fetchOrders(), ]); const user = results[0].status === "fulfilled" ? results[0].value : null; Promise.race is useful for timeouts — reject if fetch exceeds eight seconds on flaky mobile data. Document timeout values in API client modules so the whole app behaves consistently. Sequential await is correct when order matters: create user, then create profile with user id — parallelising those two calls would be a bug. Next.js Server Components — async by default // app/dashboard/page.tsx type Stats = { users: number; revenue: number }; async function getStats(): Promise { const res = await fetch(" https://api.example.com/stats ", { next: { revalidate: 60 }, }); if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Stats unavailable"); return res.json(); } export default async function DashboardPage() { const stats = await getStats(); return ; } Server Components are async functions — no useEffect fetch. See RSC vs client components . Client pitfalls — useEffect and race conditions // BEFORE — no abort, stale response overwrites new search useEffect(() => { fetch("/api/search?q=" + query).then((r) => r.json()).then(setResults); }, [query]); // AFTER — AbortController useEffect(() => { const ctrl = new AbortController(); (async () => { try { const res = await fetch("/api/search?q=" + query, { signal: ctrl.signal }); const data = await res.json(); setResults(data); } catch (e) { if ((e as Error).name !== "AbortError") console.error(e); } })(); return () => ctrl.abort(); }, [query]); Promises vs async/await — quick comparison Topic Promises (.then) async/await Readability Chains indent right Linear top-to-bottom Error handling .catch() at end try/catch around await Parallelism Promise.all([...]) await Promise.all([...]) Return type Always Promise async fn returns Promise Debugging Stack in .then Stack at await line When I keep raw Promises Utility libraries returning Promises, combining with Promise.race for timeouts, or .then() in non-async callbacks. async/await is for readable control flow; Promises are the underlying contract. Creating Promises — wrap legacy callbacks once function readFileAsync(path: string): Promise { return new Promise((resolve, reject) => { readFile(path, "utf8", (err, data) => { if (err) reject(err); else resolve(data); }); }); } // Prefer promisify utilities in Node; in browser wrap once at module boundary Async iterators — streams beyond one JSON blob async function* lineChunks(stream: ReadableStream ) { const reader = stream.getReader(); const decoder = new TextDecoder(); let buffer = ""; while (true) { const { done, value } = await reader.read(); if (done) break; buffer += decoder.decode(value, { stream: true }); const lines = buffer.split("\n"); buffer = lines.pop() ?? ""; for (const line of lines) yield line; } } Large CSV exports and AI streaming responses use async iteration. Promises handle single results; iterators handle sequences. Both compose with await in for-await-of loops. Unhandled rejections — the production alert you want // Node / edge — log unhandled rejections in API routes process.on("unhandledRejection", (reason) => { console.error("Unhandled rejection:", reason); }); // Always return Response from route handlers — never floating promise export async function GET() { try { const data = await loadData(); return Response.json(data); } catch (e) { return Response.json({ error: "Server error" }, { status: 500 }); } } Floating promises in server actions and API routes caused silent 500s on a client project until we wrapped every async entry point. Treat await like a return statement — every path must settle. Practice pattern Rewrite one sequential useEffect fetch as Promise.all. Add try/catch and rethrow. Measure network tab — the win is immediate on slow Indian mobile networks. Async literacy is the bridge between UI work and API design. When you read backend OpenAPI docs, you already think in Promises — negotiating timeout and retry policies with your team gets easier. The syntax debate ends when you debug: stack traces from async/await point at your await line; Promise chains point at the nearest .then. Pick whichever makes the failure obvious to your future self. Server Actions in Next.js return Promises to the client when you call them from forms — same mental model, different wire format. Always handle rejection in UI with error boundaries or toast messages; unhandled rejections in the browser console are user-facing failures you never measured. Next: JavaScript array methods .
