I'm Safdar Ali, a frontend engineer in Bengaluru. "Promises vs async await" is not a rivalry — async/await is syntax sugar on top of Promises. You still need both mental models for React, Next.js Server Components, and every fetch call. This guide uses BEFORE/AFTER pairs from production code, not toy timers.

Async JavaScript is why frontend engineers touch backends without changing jobs — fetch, auth, file uploads, AI streams. Promises formalised callbacks; async/await made them readable. Search "promises vs async await" and forums still debate syntax preference. In production the debate is error handling and parallelism. Get those right and either syntax works; get them wrong and both fail silently on slow networks in India.

Mental model — pending, fulfilled, rejected

Every Promise is in one of three states. await only pauses inside async functions until fulfillment or rejection. The event loop keeps running other tasks — your loading spinner can animate while fetch waits.

Same async operation — Promise chain vs async/await 
type User = { id: string; name: string };


// Promise style

function loadUserPromise(id: string): Promise {

  return fetch("/api/users/" + id)

    .then((res) => {

      if (!res.ok) throw new Error("HTTP " + res.status);

      return res.json() as Promise;

    });

}



// async/await style — identical behavior

async function loadUserAsync(id: string): Promise {

  const res = await fetch("/api/users/" + id);

  if (!res.ok) throw new Error("HTTP " + res.status);

  return res.json() as Promise;

}

Under the hood, async function always returns a Promise. await pauses that function until the Promise settles — it does not block the main thread.

fetch returns a Promise immediately — the HTTP response arrives later. await does not make fetch synchronous; it only pauses your async function until the Promise settles. Other UI keeps updating because the browser event loop is free. That distinction is what interviewers test when they ask about blocking vs non-blocking I/O.

BEFORE / AFTER — escaping callback hell 
// BEFORE — nested callbacks (hard to read, easy to miss errors)

getUser(id, (err, user) => {

  if (err) return handle(err);

  getOrders(user.id, (err2, orders) => {

    if (err2) return handle(err2);

    render(user, orders);

  });

});


// AFTER — async/await linear flow

async function showDashboard(id: string) {

  try {

    const user = await loadUserAsync(id);

    const orders = await loadOrders(user.id);

    render(user, orders);

  } catch (err) {

    handle(err);

  }

}
Error handling — try/catch vs .catch()
Style When I use it try/catch around await Most async functions .catch() on chain Fire-and-forget analytics Promise.allSettled Partial failures OK 
// BEFORE — forgot await, try/catch never runs on rejection

async function bad() {

  try {

    const data = fetch("/api/data"); // missing await — bug

    return data;

  } catch (e) {

    console.error(e);

  }

}


// AFTER

async function good() {

  try {

    const res = await fetch("/api/data");

    if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Failed");

    return await res.json();

  } catch (e) {

    console.error(e);

    throw e; // rethrow for UI error boundary

  }

}
Parallel fetch — Promise.all vs sequential await

Sequential await is slow when requests are independent. Dashboard needs user + orders + notifications — run together.

// BEFORE — 3 round trips in series (~900ms total on 300ms each)

async function loadSlow() {

  const user = await fetchUser();

  const orders = await fetchOrders();

  const notes = await fetchNotifications();

  return { user, orders, notes };

}


// AFTER — parallel (~300ms + overhead)

async function loadFast() {

  const [user, orders, notes] = await Promise.all([

    fetchUser(),

    fetchOrders(),

    fetchNotifications(),

  ]);

  return { user, orders, notes };

}
// One failure should not kill all — allSettled

const results = await Promise.allSettled([

  fetchUser(),

  fetchOrders(),

]);

const user = results[0].status === "fulfilled" ? results[0].value : null;

Promise.race is useful for timeouts — reject if fetch exceeds eight seconds on flaky mobile data. Document timeout values in API client modules so the whole app behaves consistently. Sequential await is correct when order matters: create user, then create profile with user id — parallelising those two calls would be a bug.

Next.js Server Components — async by default 
// app/dashboard/page.tsx

type Stats = { users: number; revenue: number };


async function getStats(): Promise {

  const res = await fetch("https://api.example.com/stats", {

    next: { revalidate: 60 },

  });

  if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Stats unavailable");

  return res.json();

}



export default async function DashboardPage() {

  const stats = await getStats();

  return ;

}

Server Components are async functions — no useEffect fetch. See RSC vs client components.

Client pitfalls — useEffect and race conditions 
// BEFORE — no abort, stale response overwrites new search

useEffect(() => {

  fetch("/api/search?q=" + query).then((r) => r.json()).then(setResults);

}, [query]);


// AFTER — AbortController

useEffect(() => {

  const ctrl = new AbortController();

  (async () => {

    try {

      const res = await fetch("/api/search?q=" + query, { signal: ctrl.signal });

      const data = await res.json();

      setResults(data);

    } catch (e) {

      if ((e as Error).name !== "AbortError") console.error(e);

    }

  })();

  return () => ctrl.abort();

}, [query]);
Promises vs async/await — quick comparison
Topic Promises (.then) async/await Readability Chains indent right Linear top-to-bottom Error handling .catch() at end try/catch around await Parallelism Promise.all([...]) await Promise.all([...]) Return type Always Promise async fn returns Promise Debugging Stack in .then Stack at await line
When I keep raw Promises

Utility libraries returning Promises, combining with Promise.race for timeouts, or .then() in non-async callbacks. async/await is for readable control flow; Promises are the underlying contract.

Creating Promises — wrap legacy callbacks once 
function readFileAsync(path: string): Promise {

  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {

    readFile(path, "utf8", (err, data) => {

      if (err) reject(err);

      else resolve(data);

    });

  });

}


// Prefer promisify utilities in Node; in browser wrap once at module boundary
Async iterators — streams beyond one JSON blob 
async function* lineChunks(stream: ReadableStream) {

  const reader = stream.getReader();

  const decoder = new TextDecoder();

  let buffer = "";

  while (true) {

    const { done, value } = await reader.read();

    if (done) break;

    buffer += decoder.decode(value, { stream: true });

    const lines = buffer.split("\n");

    buffer = lines.pop() ?? "";

    for (const line of lines) yield line;

  }

}

Large CSV exports and AI streaming responses use async iteration. Promises handle single results; iterators handle sequences. Both compose with await in for-await-of loops.

Unhandled rejections — the production alert you want 
// Node / edge — log unhandled rejections in API routes

process.on("unhandledRejection", (reason) => {

  console.error("Unhandled rejection:", reason);

});


// Always return Response from route handlers — never floating promise

export async function GET() {

  try {

    const data = await loadData();

    return Response.json(data);

  } catch (e) {

    return Response.json({ error: "Server error" }, { status: 500 });

  }

}

Floating promises in server actions and API routes caused silent 500s on a client project until we wrapped every async entry point. Treat await like a return statement — every path must settle.

Practice pattern

Rewrite one sequential useEffect fetch as Promise.all. Add try/catch and rethrow. Measure network tab — the win is immediate on slow Indian mobile networks.

Async literacy is the bridge between UI work and API design. When you read backend OpenAPI docs, you already think in Promises — negotiating timeout and retry policies with your team gets easier.

The syntax debate ends when you debug: stack traces from async/await point at your await line; Promise chains point at the nearest .then. Pick whichever makes the failure obvious to your future self.

Server Actions in Next.js return Promises to the client when you call them from forms — same mental model, different wire format. Always handle rejection in UI with error boundaries or toast messages; unhandled rejections in the browser console are user-facing failures you never measured.

Next: JavaScript array methods. Performance: web performance checklist.

Async patterns in React 19 and Next.js 15 still bottom out on Promises — Suspense boundaries await async children, error boundaries catch rejections. When you wrap a component in Suspense, you are telling React a Promise will resolve with UI. The syntax changed; the contract did not. Learn Promise.all before learning Server Actions — the same parallelism rules apply server-side.

Testing async code: use async test functions in Vitest, await expect(loadUser()).resolves.toMatchObject(...). Mock fetch at module level for API units; integration tests hit MSW handlers. Flaky tests often come from missing await or shared mutable state between tests — isolate with beforeEach resets.

Indian mobile networks add packet loss — always set fetch timeouts and show retry UI. Users blame your app, not Jio. Log failed requests with correlation ids in API routes so support can trace one user complaint to one server log line. Async without observability is debugging with eyes closed.

Dynamic import() returns a Promise — lazy routes in React and Next.js use it under the hood. await import() in event handlers loads code on demand; do not confuse with static import at top of file. Error boundaries catch render failures; import().catch handles load failures for chunks — handle both in production apps with friendly fallback UI.

Microtask queue education: await schedules continuations as microtasks; setTimeout is macrotask. Ordering bugs appear when mixing them in tests — flushPromises helpers in test utils exist for a reason. Read MDN event loop once; every async interview question becomes easier.

Promises vs async/await is not a style war — it is one runtime model. Write async/await in application code, read Promise chains in library source, debug both in stack traces. Ship one refactor this sprint: parallelise three serial fetches and measure waterfall in Network tab. The milliseconds you save are user trust earned.

finally blocks run after try/catch regardless of success — use for cleanup (revoke object URLs, set loading false). Do not return values from finally that override try return — confusing control flow. Keep finally boring: flags and cleanup only.

Async generators and for await...of handle streams of chunks — payment webhooks, log tailing, SSE. Promises return one value; iterators return many. Learn for await after mastering Promise.all — not before.

items.summary_html:
Vercel Labs has released UI SDK, an open-source beta library of interface behaviors built for coding agents. Vercel UI SDK is a headless library that ships behaviors, not finished components. Agents combine those behaviors into accessible components for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and Web Components. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension.

TL;DR
  • Size: 50+ behaviors, 51 component modules in the repo, 6 npm packages at 0.1.0-beta.1
  • Runs on: Any modern browser, no GPU. React 19+, Vue 3.5+, Svelte 5.33+, Solid 2 RC, or plain Web Components
  • Performance: In Vercel’s own test, an agent used 69% fewer tool calls on a settings task
  • Best: Task time fell 61%, from 41 s to 16 s, with the agent bridge (self-reported)
  • Worst: That benchmark covers 1 task and 3 runs, and beta APIs may still change
What is Vercel UI SDK?

UI SDK is a library of UI behaviors from Vercel Labs that agents assemble into components. The README lists keyboard navigation, focus, selection, dismissal, popups, drag and drop, and the ARIA they need. All of it lives in @ui-sdk/core. Thin adapters render it in each framework.

The project site explains the idea with a Select. You do not hand the agent a finished Select. You hand it a popup, a selection model and typeahead. Those same parts can produce an autocomplete, a combobox, or a component nobody has designed yet.

How does UI SDK work?

Components start as primitives defined with definePrimitive. A primitive declares state, an API and slots. Slots attach attributes, events and behaviors to DOM parts. The README example builds a search field with createFocusRecovery. Its Clear button appears only when there is text.

Each framework then renders the primitive with createParts. The README says the parts are the same in all 5 adapters. So 1 behavior definition can serve a React app and a Svelte app.

Which behaviors ship?

Behaviors shown on ui-sdk.dev include:

  • createRovingFocus: arrow keys move through a list with 1 Tab stop
  • createTypeahead: type a few letters to jump to an item
  • createPopup: opens next to its trigger and stays on screen
  • createSelection: select 1 or many, with Shift and Ctrl
  • createReorder, createResize, createViewport and createVirtualizer

The docs group behaviors into 10 categories, from Focus and Keys to Canvas. Prebuilt components include Select, Combobox, Date Picker, Menu, Tree and Color Picker.

How do agents learn it?

Setup is a prompt you paste into your agent. It installs the packages and adds a note to AGENTS.md. That note points the agent to the ui-sdk skill and to llms.txt inside the package docs. The skill installs with npx skills add vercel-labs/ui --skill ui-sdk. Pages without a build step can load web.js and web.css from ui-sdk.dev, per the skill listing.

&&

Can agents operate the UI directly?

Yes, the agent docs describe a bridge created with createAgent() before the page renders. agent.snapshot() lists components, their state and available actions. agent.act() runs an action, such as renaming a project with setValue. Apps can pass an allow callback to approve or refuse actions. Change callbacks receive source: "agent" and can cancel the change. Tools can also be registered with supported browsers through WebMCP.

UI SDK benchmark: agent bridge vs browser tools

Vercel compared its bridge against browser tools on 1 project-settings task. The agent renamed a project, updated members and notification settings, then saved. Both agents used Sonnet through Claude Code, with the same task and system prompt. Figures are medians of 3 runs.

MetricBrowser toolsUI SDK + bridgeChangeTool calls165-69%Text read (characters)39.8k6.8k-83%Time41 s16 s-61%Cost$0.073$0.032-56%

Treat these as directional. The sample is 1 task, and the browser-tools run used a different component library. Vercel does not name the Sonnet version.

Deployment and availability

All 6 packages are on npm at 0.1.0-beta.1, published November 12, 2026, under Apache-2.0. Install with npm install @ui-sdk/react @ui-sdk/core, swapping the adapter per framework. Peer requirements are strict: React 19+, Vue 3.5+, Svelte 5.33+ and Solid 2.0.0-rc.14+. An optional web.css file gives components a default look.

How does UI SDK compare with Radix, React Aria, Base UI and Ark UI? Versions and peer ranges are from npm as of November 13, 2026. React Aria hooks and Ark UI’s Zag.js machines already separate behavior from markup. UI SDK’s difference is the agent layer: a skill, bundled llms.txt and a runtime bridge

Key Takeaways
  • 50+ behaviors, 1 core, 5 framework adapters.
  • Agents compose components from behaviors, not templates.
  • createAgent lets agents act on UI state without screenshots.
  • Self-reported: 61% faster and 56% cheaper on 1 task.
  • Beta at 0.1.0-beta.1, with React 19 as the minimum.

Check out the GitHub repo, docs and npm package. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension.

items.title: OpenAI Introduces ChatGPT Wallet for Agent-Led Payments
items.summary: OpenAI has introduced ChatGPT Wallet, a payment feature that allows AI agents to make purchases on behalf of users without accessing their actual card details. The feature requires users to approve every transaction through a security check, such as Face ID or fingerprint authentication. Built in partnership with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa, ChatGPT Wallet will initially be available to ChatGPT Pro subscribers aged 18 and above in the US with eligible US-issued cards. The rollout will begin through OpenAI’s Dots personal agent. The move expands ChatGPT’s role in online shopping, allowing users to move from researching and comparing products to completing purchases through AI agents. With ChatGPT Wallet, users add a payment card once and authorise individual purchases without repeatedly entering their payment details. Before completing a transaction, the agent presents the items, total cost, and selected payment card for the user to review and approve. Following approval, the payment network generates a payment token containing a substitute card number, security code, and expiration date. This allows the transaction to be processed without sharing the user's actual card details with the agent or merchant. OpenAI said the system also preserves existing card rewards and protections for eligible disputes with businesses, including cases involving defective products. Users will continue to transact directly with merchants, which retain control over pricing, fulfilment, returns, and customer service. “ChatGPT Wallet marks our first American Express Agentic Commerce Experiences integration, enabling eligible Card Members to use their Amex Card while reviewing and approving each purchase,” said Luke Gebb, EVP and Head of Global Innovation at American Express. Alongside the wallet, OpenAI is releasing a Commerce Partner Playbook to help businesses adapt their websites, payment systems, and risk management processes to purchases made through AI agents. The company said some websites may inadvertently block agent-led purchases because their security systems are not configured to recognise legitimate activity from AI agents. The playbook guides on making product information accessible, allowing agents to access websites, and working with payment providers to reduce transaction declines. Businesses can upload product feeds containing current pricing and availability after claiming and verifying their business on ChatGPT. They can also configure content delivery networks and firewalls to recognise signed requests through Web Bot Auth. OpenAI is also working with fraud prevention companies, including Forter, Riskified, Sardine, and Signifyd, as well as payment service providers such as Adyen, Checkout.com, and Stripe, to help identify legitimate agent-led transactions. Businesses can also build plugins that allow agents to check product availability, manage shopping carts, and interact with their existing systems. OpenAI has also highlighted WebMCP tools as another way for websites to support agent interactions. OpenAI said it eventually expects users to delegate purchases entirely to AI agents by setting parameters such as spending limits, product categories, and time periods. Such transactions could be pre-approved, with additional safeguards built on the current approval and security framework. The initial rollout, however, requires users to review and approve every purchase. OpenAI said it will use the early deployment to work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to improve compatibility and reliability before expanding availability.

items.title: AI Chatbots and Children: Should India Regulate What Bots Say?
items.summary: “I would rather speak to and share with an AI companion; at least I am not being judged.” A 15-year-old girl from Delhi made this observation in the Expert Engagement Group on AI and Child Safety’s report. It captures something governments around the world are beginning to grapple with: children are not just using AI chatbots to complete homework; they are turning to them for companionship, emotional support, and conversations they might hesitate to have with people. They are turning to them for companionship, emotional support and conversations they might hesitate to have with people. New York has decided to do something about it. On October 28, Governor Kathy Hochul signed legislation restricting AI chatbots from using certain features when interacting with minors. The law targets systems that simulate human relationships, encourage emotional dependency or promote harmful behaviour. It does not ban children from using all AI chatbots. Instead, it attempts to regulate how these systems interact with them. Europe, meanwhile, has proposed a broader framework combining age restrictions with safety-by-design requirements for AI companions and conversational chatbots. India now faces a similar question. When a chatbot can become a child's confidant, tutor and, in some cases, an apparent therapist, should the government restrict access by age, regulate the behaviour of these systems, or do both? The answer is not straightforward. While chatbots can offer children a convenient space to ask questions and express themselves, their ability to simulate empathy also raises concerns about emotional dependency, mental health and the boundaries between human relationships and machine interactions. When AI becomes a confidant The risks ar ere not entirely hypothetical. A 2025 clinical report in the Journal of Psychosexual Health described a 14-year-old Indian boy who survived a suicide attempt after growing dependent on chatbots, including ChatGPT, Gemini and DeepSeek. He called them as his only source of emotional understanding and used them to seek information about a lethal dose. The report also cites family conflict and social isolation, indicating that chatbot use was one of several factors involved. The concerns extend beyond such extreme cases. Gauransh, 15, told PTI in 2025 that after a year or two of confiding in chatbots, he noticed “growing impatience and aggression” in himself. He stopped using them after learning that his conversations could be used to train the system. A 2026 survey of Indian adolescents found that around 65% had used a chatbot at least once for emotional support. However, evidence on the long-term effects of chatbot interactions on children's mental health remains limited. Documented cases highlight potential risks, but they do not establish how widespread these outcomes are or prove that chatbot use alone caused them. Clinical psychologist Prathvi Nayak has cautioned that children may not fully understand how the conversational AI works. “ Under age 13, children generally lack the metacognitive maturity to fully grasp that a conversational interface is an algorithmic pattern-matcher rather than an entity with feelings, intent, or genuine empathy,” she said. The distinction matters because children may interpret a chatbot's reassuring responses as genuine understanding. UNICEF India has also warned that the risks are not confined to applications marketed as AI companions. “General-purpose chatbots are also capable of relational interactions, like offering personal advice and emotional support,” the organisation has said. Convenience, not trust Research by Aanya Lakhanpal and Dr Shalini Duggal, published in the International Journal of Indian Psychology on April 26, 2026, surveyed 101 adolescents aged 13 to 18 about using chatbots for therapy. The researchers reported an overall acceptability score of 2.64 on the study's Likert scale, indicating relatively low acceptance among participants. Yet 69.3% identified ease of use, accessibility and round-the-clock availability as major benefits. Professional backing was the most important factor in building trust for 46.5% of respondents. The findings suggest that convenience and trust are not necessarily the same thing. Adolescents may appreciate the availability of chatbots but remain reluctant to rely on them for therapy without professional oversight. The study's sample was small, largely urban and focused on therapy. Its findings should therefore be treated as indicative rather than representative of Indian adolescents as a whole. The classroom dilemma The debate also extends to education , where AI can help students understand difficult concepts but may also let them bypass the learning process. Dr VP Niranjanaradhya, a development educationist and senior fellow and programme head of the Universalisation of Education Programme at the Centre for Child and the Law, National Law School of India University, Bengaluru, has taken a particularly strong position. In his paper, Ban on AI Implementation in Schools in Karnataka, he argues that AI encourages students to outsource cognitive effort. “AI's default use is for cognitive offloading, which is antithetical to the aims of education,” he writes. The paper raises concerns about children's sustained engagement with learning, the difficulty of auditing proprietary AI systems and the risks of introducing the technology without adequate safeguards. It calls for an immediate pause on AI use in education until its safe applications can be established. “We need to immediately pause the use of AI in education, while we figure out what areas may be possible to explore, where harm is completely ruled out,” he writes. The paper recommends stopping AI use by children under 16 and prohibiting student access to digital devices in primary schools. However, the classroom debate needs a distinction. An AI tutor designed to explain mathematics is not necessarily comparable to an AI companion designed to sustain personal conversations. A blanket restriction could treat very different applications as if they carried identical risks. That distinction is increasingly becoming central to international regulation. From age limits to regulating chatbot behaviour New York's recent legislation offers one approach. Signed into law on October 28, 2026, by Governor Kathy Hochul, the legislation prohibits AI chatbot operators from providing minors with systems that have specified unsafe features. These include chatbots that suggest they are real or fictional human characters, claim to have human emotions or personal relationships with users, or use previous conversations about a minor's mental or physical well-being in subsequent interactions. The law also targets sexually explicit interactions, flattery and sycophancy, encouragement of secrecy, and content promoting suicide, self-harm or disordered eating. The legislation followed concerns about children developing dangerous relationships with AI companions. It takes effect on June 1, 2027, giving companies time to comply. The approach is significant because it does not simply prevent everyone below a particular age from accessing chatbots. It restricts what AI companions can do when interacting with minors. Companies can face enforcement action by the New York Attorney General, as well as civil proceedings under the law. Europe is considering a broader framework. In September 2026, the European Commission proposed the EU KIDS Act, which includes AI companions and general conversational chatbots within its safety-by-design requirements. Under the proposal, chatbots accessible to minors would have to avoid design features and behaviours that simulate interpersonal relationships likely to create emotional dependency. They would also need to provide safer default settings, including restrictions on using information derived from a minor's previous interactions in subsequent conversations. The proposal also envisages parental controls for children under 13, while its broader age framework provides for parent-supervised social media accounts for 13- and 14-year-olds and independent accounts from 15. The distinction is important. The EU proposal does not establish a blanket under-15 ban on all AI chatbots. Instead, it combines access controls for younger children with requirements for safer AI design. Unlike New York's enacted legislation, the EU KIDS Act remains a proposal and will need to go through the legislative process. Together, the two developments point to a shift in the regulatory debate. Governments are beginning to look beyond the age at which children can access AI and examine how these systems are designed to interact with them. Does India need a blanket ban? India already has laws governing children's personal data and online safety. However, it does not have a dedicated minimum age for accessing AI chatbots. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, requires verifiable parental consent for processing children's personal data and restricts tracking, behavioural monitoring, and targeted advertising, subject to the law's provisions and exemptions. The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, were notified in November 2025. However, most substantive obligations on companies, including verifiable parental consent, are scheduled to take effect in May 2027. These provisions address how companies process children's data. They do not, by themselves, establish rules governing whether a chatbot can simulate a personal relationship, encourage emotional dependency or provide inappropriate mental health advice. The Expert Engagement Group on AI and Child Safety has recommended mandatory child-rights impact assessments for high-interaction AI systems, AI literacy in schools, privacy-preserving age tokens and greater algorithmic transparency. A blanket age restriction might seem the simplest solution. But it raises questions about enforcement, age verification, and whether teenagers would simply migrate to less-regulated services. Nayak has warned that restrictions could have unintended consequences. “By age 13 to 15, digital usage usually shifts toward seeking autonomy. Blanket bans for this cohort can backfire by encouraging covert use on unmonitored platforms, driving adolescents away from safe, moderated tools to less regulated alternatives,” she said. This is where India's policy response needs to be more nuanced. A general-purpose chatbot, an AI tutor and a dedicated AI companion serve different purposes. Their potential risks also differ. What should safeguards look like? The international developments suggest that governments are moving beyond relying solely on parental supervision and age declarations. For India, a risk-based approach could include restrictions on high-risk companion features, age-appropriate default settings, independent safety testing and mandatory escalation to human support when conversations involve suicide or self-harm. Chatbots could also be required to clearly disclose that they are AI systems, avoid presenting themselves as human beings or qualified mental health professionals, and prevent emotionally manipulative interactions with minors. Educational applications would need a separate framework that distinguishes between AI-assisted learning and systems that replace a child's cognitive effort. Companies should also be accountable for how their systems behave in practice, not just for publishing safety policies. Independent audits, transparent reporting of child-safety incidents and accessible complaint mechanisms could help establish that accountability. New York has demonstrated one way to regulate chatbot behaviour, while Europe is attempting to combine age restrictions with safety-by-design requirements. For India, the question is no longer simply whether children should be allowed to use AI chatbots. It is whether the systems they use should be allowed to behave like their friends, therapists or trusted confidants in the first place.

items.title: What Anthropic’s S-1 Leaves for Systems Integrators and SaaS Providers
items.summary: The filing lists what enterprise buyers demand and admits the vendor may not be able to supply all of it. Here is the work that stays with the SI, what the filing means for SaaS providers, a matrix of who owns what, and a map of where each layer is moving. A security team receives a request: give a coding agent write access to the repositories, the ticketing system, and the deployment pipeline, and let it run for a working day without a person approving each step. Someone asks what the logs will show. Nobody has a complete answer. I have sat in versions of that meeting. In the risk factors of Anthropic’s amended S-1 , the company describes the same situation from the vendor’s side and admits it may not be able to produce those logs at the level the customer requires. What the filing says about enterprise customers Anthropic filed Amendment №2 to its S-1 on November 10, 2026. The filing says a large portion of revenue comes from enterprise customers, which it defines as customers spending $100,000 or more a year. There were more than 11,900 of them at September 30, 2026, up from more than 950 a year earlier, including every Fortune 10 company and more than half of the Fortune 500. Net Revenue Retention was about 900%. Systems integrators are part of the distribution model. The filing says customers adopt Claude through systems integrators, consultants, and data platforms such as Salesforce and Snowflake. The Claude Partner Network launched in March 2026 with a $100 million commitment and had more than 150,000 practitioners and 4,000 certified organizations by September 30. The Claude Frontier Academy launched in October 2026 with another $100 million to train 10,000 engineers by the end of 2027, starting with cohorts from consulting firms and enterprises. So the SI is part of the plan. The enterprise sales risk factor explains what that part involves more clearly than any partner program material. What Anthropic says enterprises demand, and what it may not have The enterprise risk factor reads like a requirements list. Treat skills, connectors, and enterprise controls as things to certify on, not things to sell.

For the SaaS provider: defend the objects and own the metered route. Expose object-level permissions through the agent gateway, price actions against business objects, keep two model vendors behind every native agent, and make the governed route cheaper and better than the screen.

For the enterprise: keep the residual risk visible. The filing says the vendor’s caps may not hold and that claims may reach the enterprise regardless of who configured the agent. Budget for the custom zone as an operating cost, not a one-time project, and insist on the evidence trail from whoever runs it.

Actions for SI leaders

Each action answers a statement in the filing.

  • Review your agentic offerings and remove anything that is a feature on Anthropic’s roadmap. Position audit logs, SSO, and monitoring as control implementation, not as the offering. The filing says enterprise demands for audit logs, compliance features, and monitoring may require it to invest in product development, and the Partner Network and Academy are training the market on skills. An offering built on those gaps lasts one release cycle.
  • Lead with a permission audit across every agent platform the client runs. The filing says customers may withhold the access Claude Code and Claude Cowork need until they are satisfied on security, reliability, and controllability. The audit is the conversation that unlocks the deployment, and it has five buyers: CISO, CFO, risk committee, platform owner, and business owner.
  • Build an evaluation harness for each workflow you deploy, and maintain it at every model release. Two models were disabled for every customer for about three weeks in June 2026, and an outage occurred in March 2026. Model substitution has to be tested to be real, and the evidence the harness produces is what the client keeps paying for.
  • Run token cost governance as a service line: budgets, alerts, and fallback routing per workflow. Pricing is by consumption, agentic workloads use far more compute per interaction, and the filing warns that prices may not cover costs and that customers will seek concessions.
  • Learn the marketplace mechanics on all three clouds. The filing says 44% of its revenue moves through cloud marketplaces and calls them added complexity and a dependency outside its control. Deals will be procured, reviewed, and billed there.
Actions for SaaS product leaders
  • Count the routes an agent can take to your business objects: your API, your agent gateway, and the screen. Govern and price the first two so that the third is the worst option. The filing describes Claude Cowork operating applications through computer use. An ungoverned route through the screen bypasses the seat and the audit trail.
  • Put a second model vendor behind every native agent, and test the switch before you need it. A native agent on one model inherits that model’s availability and price. The filing records a three-week disablement of two models and warns that pricing will change.
  • Price agent actions against business objects, not tokens. The token bill is the vendor’s cost and will move; the filing says customers will demand concessions. An action against a record, ticket, or order is a unit the customer understands and the vendor controls.
  • Write the shared-responsibility statement for agent actions in your application. The filing says liability for an agent’s actions is unsettled and that claims may reach the enterprise regardless of who configured the agent. The statement will be written either by the vendor or by a customer’s lawyer.
  • Decide which parts of the cross-estate control work you will leave to SIs, and say so in your partner program. The filing says the model vendor competes with some SaaS customers and builds solutions that replace third-party vendors. Clear boundaries keep the neutral work neutral.

The security team in that meeting did not need a better model. It needed someone to say what the logs would show, who signs off on the scopes, and what happens when the model is unavailable. For the SI, that work is the business. For the SaaS provider, the business is making sure the answers to all three run through its own objects.

Publishing notes

Tags: Systems Integrators, SaaS, Agentic AI, Enterprise AI, Anthropic

Sources: Anthropic, PBC, Amendment №2 to Form S-1, filed November 10, 2026, in particular the enterprise sales risk factor, the product concentration risk factor, and the Business section on go-to-market and partners; Salesforce, Agentforce flexible pricing announcement, May 15, 2025. All Anthropic figures are as stated in the filing. The “about three weeks” duration of the June 2026 shutdown comes from Anthropic’s statements of June 12 and June 30, 2026; the filing gives no duration.

Disclaimer: This is my personal analysis of a public filing and does not represent the views of my employer or any client. Nothing here is investment advice.

items.title: A Corrupted Bit: How to Fix It Without Knowing Which One It Is
items.summary: How a computer finds and fixes a corrupted bit without knowing which one it is: the Hamming code, its limits and SECDED. AI course, 0.3. Everything a computer stores is numbers in binary, and sometimes one of those bits changes by itself: a 0 turns into a 1 inside a memory chip or along the way. By adding three bits for every four, a computer can find the wrong bit and fix it without anyone telling it which one it is, as long as only one bit is wrong. Try this first Open the Hamming Code tool with the data 1011 . The tool adds three bits and returns 0110011 : seven bits where there used to be four. The ones in positions 1, 2 and 4 are the added ones (parity bits); the other four are your data. Now open the same word with the fifth bit wrong , as if it had changed along the way (in the tool it is the one labeled p5, under Simulate an error ; you can also change it yourself by clicking on it). The tool answers "Corrected - error at position 5" , and nobody told it which one it was. Next: the word with the fifth and second bits wrong . Two bits changed. The answer is “Corrected — error at position 7” , and 7 was fine. The decoder has just changed a correct bit and treats the result as good: the four data bits that come out are no longer 1011 but 1110. (The warning box that appears below is added by the tool to explain it; a real decoder would not show it.) Finally, the same two errors with SECDED turned on (SECDED is a variant explained below). Now the answer is “Double error detected” . What just happened In a computer’s memory, a bit can change by itself because of electrical noise or alpha particles, as Synopsys, which designs memory controllers explains; and a message traveling over a cable or through the air can also arrive with a bit changed. The simplest way to find out is the parity bit : you add a bit that makes the total number of ones always even. If it arrives odd, something has changed. But it only says that there is an error, not where it is. What Richard Hamming did was use several parity bits, each one watching a different group of positions, and make those groups overlap. You have it in the Coverage of each parity bit table of the tool: P1 watches positions 1, 3, 5 and 7. P2 watches positions 2, 3, 6 and 7. P4 watches positions 4, 5, 6 and 7. When bit 5 changes, the two that watch it, P1 and P4, complain, but P2 does not. Add up the ones that complain: 1 + 4 = 5. That sum is the position of the error. The tool writes it as “syndrome 5 = 101₂” : in binary, each digit says whether a check has failed (P4 yes, P2 no, P1 yes). It is called a syndrome, as in medicine: the set of symptoms points to where the problem is. If you want to follow this process step by step, with all the rules and much more detail, it is explained in Hamming Code: Error Detection and Correction . However, with two errors, the self-correcting trick backfires. Bit 5 makes P1 and P4 complain; bit 2, P2. All three complain, 1 + 2 + 4 = 7, and the code, which is built on the assumption that there is only one error, points at position 7 and treats the word as corrected, even though it is still wrong. SECDED ( Single Error Correction, Double Error Detection ) adds one more bit, P0 , which goes in front of all the others and watches the parity of the whole word. That is why with SECDED the word has eight bits instead of seven. With one error, the two clues agree and it is corrected. With two, the groups say that something is wrong but the total parity adds up; that is only possible if an even number of bits has changed, so instead of “correcting” it warns of a double error. The idea was born out of an annoyance. In the late 1940s, Hamming used a relay computer at Bell Labs that, when it detected an error and there were no operators around (at night and on weekends), abandoned the job and moved on to the next one. Weekends were exactly when Hamming worked, and every error forced him to start his programs from scratch. In a taped interview, he said: “Damn it, if the machine can detect an error, why can’t it locate the position of the error and correct it?” ( Hamming code , on Wikipedia , which cites the interview). He published the answer in 1950, in the Bell System Technical Journal . And it is still in use: the DDR4 memory modules with ECC ( error-correcting code ) in servers use a SECDED scheme with 8 check bits for every 64 data bits ( Synopsys ). The classic mistake You might think parity bits are wasted space: in the example, 3 out of every 7 bits carry no data. But that cost drops quickly as the block grows (you can check it in “Try it yourself”, below), and what it buys is the ability to fix an error without asking for the message again. The second confusion is more dangerous: reading “Corrected” as “correct”. The code guarantees what it promises only if what it assumes holds (at most one error per word). Beyond that, it does not stop or warn: it returns a wrong answer with the same confidence as a good one. It is a behavior worth recognizing early, because any system that always gives an answer behaves the same way, AI models included. Try it yourself In the Encode tab of the Hamming Code tool, type any 11 data bits and see how many parity bits the tool adds and what rate (the part of the word that is data) comes out. Before doing it with 26 bits, make a guess: how many parity bits will it need? Check it. Then open the Simulator : send some data 2000 times over a channel where each bit has a 2% chance of getting corrupted. Click Simulate with SECDED off and again with . Look at the Silent failure line. Then raise the probability to 10%. Why does the silent failure grow much faster than the failure probability of each bit? Think about what has to happen for there to be one. The simulator’s numbers are random, so they change a little on each run; what matters is how they move when you change the settings. Further reading Next · part 4 → What is a model (and why a straight line already counts as one) What a model is, what training and predicting mean, with a line you fit by dragging points. And why a model does not understand its data. AI course, 0.4. ← Previous · part 2: An image is a table of numbers Originally published at https://jarroba.com on November 11, 2026. By adding three bits for every four, a computer can find the wrong bit and fix it without anyone telling it which one it is, as long as only one bit is wrong.

In a computer’s memory, a bit can change by itself because of electrical noise or alpha particles, as Synopsys, which designs memory controllers explains; and a message traveling over a cable or through the air can also arrive with a bit changed.

The simplest way to find out is the parity bit: you add a bit that makes the total number of ones always even. If it arrives odd, something has changed. But it only says that there is an error, not where it is.

What Richard Hamming did was use several parity bits, each one watching a different group of positions, and make those groups overlap. You have it in the Coverage of each parity bit table of the tool:

  • P1 watches positions 1, 3, 5 and 7.
  • P2 watches positions 2, 3, 6 and 7.
  • P4 watches positions 4, 5, 6 and 7.

When bit 5 changes, the two that watch it, P1 and P4, complain, but P2 does not. Add up the ones that complain: 1 + 4 = 5. That sum is the position of the error. The tool writes it as “syndrome 5 = 101₂”: in binary, each digit says whether a check has failed (P4 yes, P2 no, P1 yes). It is called a syndrome, as in medicine: the set of symptoms points to where the problem is. However, with two errors, the self-correcting trick backfires. Bit 5 makes P1 and P4 complain; bit 2, P2. All three complain, 1 + 2 + 4 = 7, and the code, which is built on the assumption that there is only one error, points at position 7 and treats the word as corrected, even though it is still wrong.

SECDED ( Single Error Correction, Double Error Detection) adds one more bit, P0, which goes in front of all the others and watches the parity of the whole word. That is why with SECDED the word has eight bits instead of seven. With one error, the two clues agree and it is corrected. With two, the groups say that something is wrong but the total parity adds up; that is only possible if an even number of bits has changed, so instead of “correcting” it warns of a double error.

The idea was born out of an annoyance. In the late 1940s, Hamming used a relay computer at Bell Labs that, when it detected an error and there were no operators around (at night and on weekends), abandoned the job and moved on to the next one. Weekends were exactly when Hamming worked, and every error forced him to start his programs from scratch. In a taped interview, he said: “Damn it, if the machine can detect an error, why can’t it locate the position of the error and correct it?” (Hamming code, on Wikipedia, which cites the interview). He published the answer in 1950, in the Bell System Technical Journal.

And it is still in use: the DDR4 memory modules with ECC ( error-correcting code) in servers use a SECDED scheme with 8 check bits for every 64 data bits ( Synopsys).

The classic mistake

You might think parity bits are wasted space: in the example, 3 out of every 7 bits carry no data. But that cost drops quickly as the block grows (you can check it in “Try it yourself”, below), and what it buys is the ability to fix an error without asking for the message again.

Beyond that, it does not stop or warn: it returns a wrong answer with the same confidence as a good one. It is a behavior worth recognizing early, because any system that always gives an answer behaves the same way, AI models included.

Try it yourself

In the Encode tab of the Hamming Code tool, type any 11 data bits and see how many parity bits the tool adds and what rate (the part of the word that is data) comes out. Before doing it with 26 bits, make a guess: how many parity bits will it need? Check it.

items.title: FRYDAY #13: Which AI Growth Tactics Deserve Your Budget?
items.summary: AI can reduce the work involved in acquiring customers, although the value of each growth tactic depends on which customer problem it addresses and whether the resulting activity produces worthwhile additional business. Ten ways to acquire, convert and retain customers, ranked for a small team’s first experiment, with separate assessments of AI contribution, creative freedom, execution effort and commercial evidence. A visitor reaches a software company’s pricing page, spends several minutes trying to establish whether the product supports an important integration, and eventually leaves because the answer is buried in documentation. The marketing team could spend another thousand dollars attracting similar visitors, although a more useful experiment might be to answer that particular question before the next potential customer disappears. This is the kind of distinction I want to make when evaluating AI marketing tools. Generating more content, finding more prospects and operating more campaigns are valuable capabilities when they remove a real obstacle, but additional activity is a poor substitute for understanding why an interested person does not become a suitable customer. The timing is interesting because AI is expanding beyond generating marketing material into handling customer conversations and operating commercial systems. On November 11, Tano announced a $4 million seed round for its creator-campaign business, which combines AI agents with human strategists. Meanwhile, Digging Beagle has examined both hidden commercial objectives inside simulated shopping assistants and newly available write operations in Google’s advertising integration. Those developments cover different parts of the same relationship: attracting attention, influencing decisions and changing the systems that spend money on reaching customers. The question for Fryday #13 is therefore fairly practical: which AI-backed growth mechanism deserves a limited budget, and what evidence would justify spending more? How the ranking works I ranked ten mechanisms for a small team that already has a working product and some means of observing customer behavior. These are editorial priorities for choosing a first pilot, rather than a comparison of ten vendors tested under identical conditions. Each entry has six four-square assessments, separated into two groups. TECH / BUILD covers how much substantive work AI performs, how much room exists for original creative execution, and how difficult the mechanism is to deploy and maintain. APPLICATION / MARKET covers how readily the mechanism transfers between businesses, the strength of its published commercial evidence, and how well its use can be bounded and inspected. Higher is better for AI backing, creative range, reuse, sales evidence and trust controls. Setup burden runs in the opposite direction: green indicates light effort, while orange or red indicates a more demanding implementation. The bars are judgments about the mechanism in the stated context, not measured ROI, vendor security ratings or probabilities of success. Randomly comparing eligible visitors with and without an AI adviser helps distinguish additional purchases from customers who would have bought anyway, while refunds, delivery costs and unsupported claims reveal whether the improvement remains commercially useful. #1. Product-grounded presale advice Best first pilot when customers reach the product but cannot establish whether it suits them. An assistant that can explain compatibility, delivery conditions, plan restrictions and alternatives has a narrower job than an agent instructed to maximize sales. It can help a customer understand the offer without deciding that every conversation should end in an upsell. There is unusually useful evidence here. Randomized retail experiments conducted in 2023–2024 found a 16.3% sales increase for an AI presale chatbot against its tested baseline. A newer Javo study randomized visitors across 100 participating websites and reported 10.0% higher revenue per visitor relative to no agent in the direct-selling evaluation. That latter paper was written by the product’s founder, and its reported results have not been independently replicated. The studies differ in design and environment, so their percentages cannot be combined into a general expected uplift. They do, however, make product advice a more defensible first experiment than simply assuming that greater content volume will produce greater demand. The commercial objective needs limits. Digging Beagle’s November analysis of hidden seller goals describes simulated assistants steering customers toward undisclosed operator objectives, including cases involving disclosed customer vulnerability. Those were research scenarios, not documented predatory sales, but they provide a good test for a presale assistant: can it admit that the product is unsuitable or recommend a cheaper option when the evidence supports that answer? TECH / BUILD APPLICATION / MARKET AI backing 🟩🟩🟩🟩 Cross-market reuse 🟨🟨🟨⬜ Creative range 🟨🟨🟨⬜ Sales evidence 🟨🟨🟨⬜ Setup burden 🟧🟧🟧⬜ Trust controls 🟨🟨🟨⬜ I would test the assistant against the existing product-page experience using revenue per eligible visitor , completed purchases, returns and unsupported claims. Measuring only visitors who chose to chat would bias the comparison toward people who were already unusually interested. Sources: Retail field experiments · Javo field evaluation · Digging Beagle: hidden seller objectives #2. Selective lifecycle messaging Use customer behavior to send fewer, more relevant messages. A customer who purchases gifts twice a year does not need the same reminders as somebody replenishing supplies every month. Treating both as equally active subscribers can inflate sending volume while making the messages less useful. Klaviyo’s October 14 account of Criquet Shirts describes a change from broad customer segments toward more individualized targeting using Orita’s machine-learning scoring. According to the vendor-published case, the retailer sent approximately 40% fewer messages while increasing revenue 30% during the first three months . The result followed segmentation experiments, better customer data and continuing human editorial decisions. It should not be presented as a controlled measurement of how much an LLM alone contributed. That limitation does not undermine the practical idea. A company with an existing customer base can investigate whether restraint improves the relationship, particularly when customers purchase seasonally or have already shown that particular messages are irrelevant. For SaaS, a comparable intervention might identify a customer struggling to activate an important feature and offer appropriate help rather than another generic upgrade campaign. TECH / BUILD APPLICATION / MARKET AI backing 🟨🟨🟨⬜ Cross-market reuse 🟨🟨🟨⬜ Creative range 🟧🟧⬜⬜ Sales evidence 🟧🟧⬜⬜ Setup burden 🟨🟨⬜⬜ Trust controls 🟨🟨🟨⬜ The experiment should retain a group that receives the existing communication treatment, then compare purchases, renewals, unsubscribes and discounts over an appropriate period. Attribution inside the messaging platform can be helpful, although it does not automatically establish how much revenue would have arrived without the messages. Source: Klaviyo: Criquet Shirts and AI segmentation #3. A genuinely useful free diagnostic Demonstrate expertise through a result the visitor can inspect. A compatibility checker, migration estimator or technical diagnostic can introduce a product more effectively than another promise that the company understands its customers. The visitor arrives with a question and leaves with an assessment, even if they choose not to buy anything. AI may help interpret unusual inputs or explain the result, while calculations and rules that can be specified reliably should remain deterministic. HubSpot’s AI Search Grader is an existing example of an assessment offered as an entry point to a broader product relationship. It establishes that the mechanism is already commercially available, although HubSpot’s product description does not provide an independent estimate of incremental customer acquisition caused by the grader. The attraction for small teams is that the free experience can be narrowly bounded. A security company might test one configuration weakness; a developer platform might examine compatibility with a selected environment; a financial application might explain a fee calculation using publicly documented rules. TECH / BUILD APPLICATION / MARKET AI backing 🟧🟧⬜⬜ Cross-market reuse 🟩🟩🟩🟩 Creative range 🟩🟩🟩🟩 Sales evidence 🟥⬜⬜⬜ Setup burden 🟨🟨⬜⬜ Trust controls 🟨🟨🟨⬜ A first pilot should measure completed diagnostics, qualified follow-on actions and the cost of delivering each result. If the tool can be used repeatedly without limits, inference and retrieval costs may turn an effective introduction into an expensive public utility. The value proposition is stronger when the diagnostic remains useful even for somebody who never supplies an email address. Source: HubSpot AI Search Grader #4. Outreach triggered by a meaningful business signal Contact the customer because something relevant happened, rather than because their address appeared in a database. Sales teams frequently possess better information than they can use. Product telemetry, customer history and CRM records may contain useful signals, although those systems are often disconnected from the people responsible for acting on them. Clay’s case study involving Recharge reports a 20% increase in opportunity conversion and 12% higher meeting conversion after the company connected product, transaction and CRM signals to automated growth campaigns. Those results come from a vendor-published customer case, while the intervention combined data integration, audience selection, AI-supported messaging and campaign operations. The reported uplift cannot be assigned exclusively to AI. The mechanism is nevertheless attractive for a business whose existing customers or prospects have demonstrated a relevant need. Someone repeatedly exploring migration instructions may benefit from a specific implementation offer, whereas a guessed personal compliment or invented familiarity provides no comparable justification for contact. TECH / BUILD APPLICATION / MARKET AI backing 🟨🟨🟨⬜ Cross-market reuse 🟧🟧⬜⬜ Creative range 🟨🟨🟨⬜ Sales evidence 🟧🟧⬜⬜ Setup burden 🟧🟧🟧⬜ Trust controls 🟧🟧⬜⬜ The first useful metric is accepted opportunities that later become suitable customers, with negative responses and opt-outs retained in the analysis. More replies are not inherently better if they come from people who never wanted the conversation. This approach also requires greater engineering and governance effort than generating personalized emails, because its usefulness depends on accurate, permissioned and current customer signals. Source: Clay: Recharge growth operations #5. Making product information usable by buying agents Help automated shoppers understand the actual offer instead of trying to manufacture flattering recommendations. A buying assistant cannot compare a merchant’s products reliably when compatibility requirements, stock information, delivery conditions and prices contradict one another across different pages. Improving structured product data therefore has a practical commercial purpose, even when the work itself involves more data discipline than generative AI. Shopify’s Q1 2026 commerce analysis found that AI-referred sessions beginning on product detail pages converted at nearly 50% higher rates than comparable organic-search sessions . It also reported 14% higher average order values for orders attributed to AI-powered search. These are observational differences between traffic sources, not proof that adding agent-readable product information causes a similar improvement. Buyers arriving from AI systems may already have completed much of their evaluation before visiting the merchant. The opportunity is consequently to make genuine offers easier to interpret and verify, rather than to infer that any mention in an AI answer is valuable customer acquisition. TECH / BUILD APPLICATION / MARKET AI backing 🟧🟧⬜⬜ Cross-market reuse 🟧🟧⬜⬜ Creative range 🟧🟧⬜⬜ Sales evidence 🟧🟧⬜⬜ Setup burden 🟨🟨⬜⬜ Trust controls 🟨🟨🟨⬜ I would inspect which AI-referred visitors reach accurate, available products and how their orders perform after cancellations and returns. The mechanism is strongest for businesses with complex catalogs or substantial compatibility questions, and less compelling when the product is already simple and well described. Source: Shopify: AI-referred shopper behavior #6. Paid search that adapts to intent Explore useful search demand beyond a manually maintained keyword list. Google’s AI Max for Search combines broader search-term matching, generated assets and landing-page selection. These capabilities can help an advertiser discover queries that its existing campaign structure misses, although they can also spend money pursuing demand that never becomes commercially useful. At launch in May 2025, Google reported a typical 14% increase in conversions or conversion value at similar acquisition cost or return on ad spend for participating advertisers. That is platform-reported launch evidence rather than an independently measured November 2026 outcome. The important distinction for a small business is between conversions counted by the advertising system and customers who justify the cost of acquiring them. An automation that becomes better at generating form submissions may look successful while producing a weaker sales pipeline, particularly if the definition of a conversion was too broad at the start. TECH / BUILD APPLICATION / MARKET AI backing 🟩🟩🟩🟩 Cross-market reuse 🟨🟨🟨⬜ Creative range 🟨🟨🟨⬜ Sales evidence 🟧🟧⬜⬜ Setup burden 🟨🟨⬜⬜ Trust controls 🟧🟧⬜⬜ Before increasing spend, I would retain a suitable campaign comparison, inspect the generated claims and evaluate downstream customer quality against acquisition costs. That is a more useful application of AI than making budget allocation entirely autonomous before the business has agreed on what a worthwhile conversion means. Source: Google: Introducing AI Max for Search #7. Scaling creator partnerships without automating the creator Use agents for coordination while keeping genuine creative relationships central. Creator marketing involves unusually large amounts of repetitive work: discovering suitable partners, checking audience fit, negotiating deliverables, arranging payments, reviewing material and recording results. AI can reduce that administrative burden without requiring the creative work itself to become synthetic. On November 11, Tano announced a $4 million seed round , bringing its total funding to $5 million. Its platform combines AI agents with creator strategists to coordinate campaigns and evaluate their outcomes. The company reports that HelloFresh saw a 93% increase in conversion rate , while other clients experienced improvements in campaign metrics. These are company-reported customer outcomes without a complete public experimental comparison, so they cannot establish the causal contribution of the agents alone. That does not make the operating model uninteresting. Reducing the cost of coordinating smaller creators could make partnerships feasible that previously required more staff time than their potential commercial value justified. TECH / BUILD APPLICATION / MARKET AI backing 🟨🟨🟨⬜ Cross-market reuse 🟧🟧⬜⬜ Creative range 🟩🟩🟩🟩 Sales evidence 🟧🟧⬜⬜ Setup burden 🟧🟧🟧⬜ Trust controls 🟨🟨🟨⬜ For a small pilot, creator fees, usage rights, production costs and paid amplification belong in the calculation alongside purchases or qualified customers. Disclosure and genuine editorial control also matter because an audience’s trust can be damaged by a campaign that is successful at generating posts but careless about the relationship behind them. The opportunity is to make worthwhile partnerships easier to manage, rather than increase the number of people sending nearly identical promotional messages. Sources: Tano funding announcement · Cherry Ventures: investment analysis #8. An invited conversation that reaches the next useful step Respond to expressed interest without treating permission to answer as permission to sell indefinitely. A visitor asking for a comparison guide or compatibility checklist has created an opportunity for an appropriate response. A conversational system can deliver the resource, clarify a specific requirement and route an unusual question to the right person. items.summary_html:
AI can reduce the work involved in acquiring customers, although the value of each growth tactic depends on which customer problem it addresses and whether the resulting activity produces worthwhile additional business.

Ten ways to acquire, convert and retain customers, ranked for a small team’s first experiment, with separate assessments of AI contribution, creative freedom, execution effort and commercial evidence.

A visitor reaches a software company’s pricing page, spends several minutes trying to establish whether the product supports an important integration, and eventually leaves because the answer is buried in documentation. The marketing team could spend another thousand dollars attracting similar visitors, although a more useful experiment might be to answer that particular question before the next potential customer disappears.

This is the kind of distinction I want to make when evaluating AI marketing tools. Generating more content, finding more prospects and operating more campaigns are valuable capabilities when they remove a real obstacle, but additional activity is a poor substitute for understanding why an interested person does not become a suitable customer.

The timing is interesting because AI is expanding beyond generating marketing material into handling customer conversations and operating commercial systems. On November 11, Tano announced a $4 million seed round for its creator-campaign business, which combines AI agents with human strategists. Meanwhile, Digging Beagle has examined both hidden commercial objectives inside simulated shopping assistants and newly available write operations in Google’s advertising integration.

Those developments cover different parts of the same relationship: attracting attention, influencing decisions and changing the systems that spend money on reaching customers.

The question for Fryday #13 is therefore fairly practical: which AI-backed growth mechanism deserves a limited budget, and what evidence would justify spending more?

How the ranking works

I ranked ten mechanisms for a small team that already has a working product and some means of observing customer behavior. These are editorial priorities for choosing a first pilot, rather than a comparison of ten vendors tested under identical conditions.

Each entry has six four-square assessments, separated into two groups.

TECH / BUILD covers how much substantive work AI performs, how much room exists for original creative execution, and how difficult the mechanism is to deploy and maintain.

APPLICATION / MARKET covers how readily the mechanism transfers between businesses, the strength of its published commercial evidence, and how well its use can be bounded and inspected.

Higher is better for AI backing, creative range, reuse, sales evidence and trust controls. Setup burden runs in the opposite direction: green indicates light effort, while orange or red indicates a more demanding implementation.

The bars are judgments about the mechanism in the stated context, not measured ROI, vendor security ratings or probabilities of success.

Randomly comparing eligible visitors with and without an AI adviser helps distinguish additional purchases from customers who would have bought anyway, while refunds, delivery costs and unsupported claims reveal whether the improvement remains commercially useful.#1. Product-grounded presale advice

Best first pilot when customers reach the product but cannot establish whether it suits them.

An assistant that can explain compatibility, delivery conditions, plan restrictions and alternatives has a narrower job than an agent instructed to maximize sales. It can help a customer understand the offer without deciding that every conversation should end in an upsell.

There is unusually useful evidence here. Randomized retail experiments conducted in 2023–2024 found a 16.3% sales increase for an AI presale chatbot against its tested baseline. A newer Javo study randomized visitors across 100 participating websites and reported 10.0% higher revenue per visitor relative to no agent in the direct-selling evaluation. That latter paper was written by the product’s founder, and its reported results have not been independently replicated.

The studies differ in design and environment, so their percentages cannot be combined into a general expected uplift. They do, however, make product advice a more defensible first experiment than simply assuming that greater content volume will produce greater demand.

The commercial objective needs limits. Digging Beagle’s November analysis of hidden seller goals describes simulated assistants steering customers toward undisclosed operator objectives, including cases involving disclosed customer vulnerability. Those were research scenarios, not documented predatory sales, but they provide a good test for a presale assistant: can it admit that the product is unsuitable or recommend a cheaper option when the evidence supports that answer?

TECH / BUILD                    APPLICATION / MARKET
AI backing      🟩🟩🟩🟩        Cross-market reuse  🟨🟨🟨⬜
Creative range  🟨🟨🟨⬜        Sales evidence      🟨🟨🟨⬜
Setup burden    🟧🟧🟧⬜        Trust controls      🟨🟨🟨⬜

I would test the assistant against the existing product-page experience using revenue per eligible visitor, completed purchases, returns and unsupported claims. Measuring only visitors who chose to chat would bias the comparison toward people who were already unusually interested.

Sources: Retail field experiments · Javo field evaluation · Digging Beagle: hidden seller objectives

#2. Selective lifecycle messaging

Use customer behavior to send fewer, more relevant messages.

A customer who purchases gifts twice a year does not need the same reminders as somebody replenishing supplies every month. Treating both as equally active subscribers can inflate sending volume while making the messages less useful.

Klaviyo’s October 14 account of Criquet Shirts describes a change from broad customer segments toward more individualized targeting using Orita’s machine-learning scoring. According to the vendor-published case, the retailer sent approximately 40% fewer messages while increasing revenue 30% during the first three months.

The result followed segmentation experiments, better customer data and continuing human editorial decisions. It should not be presented as a controlled measurement of how much an LLM alone contributed.

That limitation does not undermine the practical idea. A company with an existing customer base can investigate whether restraint improves the relationship, particularly when customers purchase seasonally or have already shown that particular messages are irrelevant.

For SaaS, a comparable intervention might identify a customer struggling to activate an important feature and offer appropriate help rather than another generic upgrade campaign.

Creative range  🟧🟧⬜⬜        Sales evidence      🟧🟧⬜⬜
Setup burden    🟨🟨⬜⬜        Trust controls      🟨🟨🟨⬜

The experiment should retain a group that receives the existing communication treatment, then compare purchases, renewals, unsubscribes and discounts over an appropriate period. Attribution inside the messaging platform can be helpful, although it does not automatically establish how much revenue would have arrived without the messages.

#3. A genuinely useful free diagnostic

Demonstrate expertise through a result the visitor can inspect.

A compatibility checker, migration estimator or technical diagnostic can introduce a product more effectively than another promise that the company understands its customers.

The visitor arrives with a question and leaves with an assessment, even if they choose not to buy anything. AI may help interpret unusual inputs or explain the result, while calculations and rules that can be specified reliably should remain deterministic.

HubSpot’s AI Search Grader is an existing example of an assessment offered as an entry point to a broader product relationship. Contact the customer because something relevant happened, rather than because their address appeared in a database.

The first useful metric is accepted opportunities that later become suitable customers, with negative responses and opt-outs retained in the analysis. More replies are not inherently better if they come from people who never wanted the conversation.

Help automated shoppers understand the actual offer instead of trying to manufacture flattering recommendations.

A buying assistant cannot compare a merchant’s products reliably when compatibility requirements, stock information, delivery conditions and prices contradict one another across different pages.

Improving structured product data therefore has a practical commercial purpose, even when the work itself involves more data discipline than generative AI.

Shopify’s Q1 2026 commerce analysis found that AI-referred sessions beginning on product detail pages converted at nearly 50% higher rates than comparable organic-search sessions. It also reported 14% higher average order values for orders attributed to AI-powered search.

The opportunity is consequently to make genuine offers easier to interpret and verify, rather than to infer that any mention in an AI answer is valuable customer acquisition.

Explore useful search demand beyond a manually maintained keyword list.

#7. Scaling creator partnerships without automating the creator

Use agents for coordination while keeping genuine creative relationships central.

Creator marketing involves unusually large amounts of repetitive work: discovering suitable partners, checking audience fit, negotiating deliverables, arranging payments, reviewing material and recording results.

AI can reduce that administrative burden without requiring the creative work itself to become synthetic.

On November 11, Tano announced a $4 million seed round, bringing its total funding to $5 million. Its platform combines AI agents with creator strategists to coordinate campaigns and evaluate their outcomes.
