items.title: Semantic Models: What They Are, the Types Available, and When to Use Which
items.summary: The same question, three different queries Ask “What was net revenue last quarter?” through three consumers that share one warehouse, and you can get three answers. A finance report filters on ship_date, excludes tax and subtracts refunds. A BI dashboard filters on created_at and sums amount. An LLM-generated query joins orders to refunds and sums amount again, so any order with two refunds is counted twice and cancelled orders stay in. All three queries run without errors, and each is internally consistent. They disagree because the definition of net revenue lives in each consumer’s own query logic, not in one shared place. A semantic model moves it out of the queries and into a single governed object. The metric, its filters, its time dimension, the join path and the grain are declared once, and every consumer compiles its SQL from that declaration. On the left, each consumer carries its own logic. On the right, all three request the metric from one model. The rest of this article covers what a semantic model contains, why raw schemas break LLM-generated SQL, the main types of semantic model, how each is consumed, and how to choose among them. The short rule is to pick the one that lives where your data and your queries already live, and to define every metric once. What a semantic model is A semantic model is a governed description of your data in business terms: entities, metrics, dimensions, relationships and rules. People write it once, and both humans and software read it. Think of it as the glossary and rulebook that sits between raw tables and everyone who asks questions of them. The term has a second meaning in AI work: an embedding model that maps text to vectors so that similar meanings land close together. That powers semantic search over documents and is a separate topic. This article covers the analytics meaning. What a semantic model encodes A semantic model turns database structure into business meaning. It typically defines six kinds of things. The examples are illustrative. The important property is that each definition exists once and every consumer shares it. A dashboard, a notebook and an LLM agent all compute net revenue the same way, because none of them redefines it. Why raw schemas fail LLMs The most dangerous failure of text-to-SQL is not an error message. It is a query that runs and returns a plausible, wrong number. The model may join tables incorrectly or misread a column’s meaning, and nothing sits between the question and the generated SQL to catch it. Five causes recur in practice. Ambiguous columns. status, amount and date mean different things in different tables. Which date is the order date, and which is the ship date? Undefined metrics. “Revenue”, “active user” and “churn” each have several defensible definitions, and the schema holds none of them. Hidden join paths. Several routes may connect two tables, and only one is correct for the question asked. Fan-out and grain errors. Joining a one-to-many table before aggregating duplicates rows and inflates totals without any warning. Implicit filters. Test accounts, cancelled orders and soft-deleted rows are excluded by convention, not by structure. Better models help but cannot fully fix these, because the missing information is not in the schema. It lives in people’s heads and in old dashboards. Types of semantic models Semantic models differ mainly in where they live, because that decides who can use them and how portable they are. Six types cover most of what you will meet. Read the picture from the bottom. Tables sit in the data platform, a semantic model of one of four kinds sits above them, and consumers ask for metrics by name. Three notes on the table. Warehouse-native objects are structured definitions. A Snowflake semantic view describes logical tables, relationships, facts, dimensions and metrics, and it can also carry verified queries and instructions for AI-generated SQL. A Databricks metric view separates measure definitions from dimensions, so the engine computes the right aggregation for whatever grouping a user asks for, and it can carry synonyms for AI accuracy. OSI is about portability. It is a vendor-neutral, open-source format for datasets, metrics, dimensions and relationships, backed by several data and analytics vendors. Treat it as something to watch rather than something to depend on today. Verification scope. The Snowflake, Databricks, Microsoft and OSI details were checked against current vendor documentation. The Looker, Cube, AtScale, code-defined and ontology rows describe the general design and were not benchmarked here. Product names and features change quickly, so confirm against current docs before choosing. How semantic models are consumed A semantic model is only useful when something reads it. Five consumption patterns are common, and one model can serve several of them at once. All five patterns read the same model, and the model generates the SQL that the warehouse runs. The fourth and fifth patterns are where semantic models matter most for AI. Fabric IQ, for example, answers questions over governed models while respecting role-based access and row-level security, so the assistant cannot see more than the user could. items.summary_html:
The same question, three different queries

Ask “What was net revenue last quarter?” through three consumers that share one warehouse, and you can get three answers. A finance report filters on ship_date, excludes tax and subtracts refunds. A BI dashboard filters on created_at and sums amount. An LLM-generated query joins orders to refunds and sums amount again, so any order with two refunds is counted twice and cancelled orders stay in. All three queries run without errors, and each is internally consistent.

They disagree because the definition of net revenue lives in each consumer’s own query logic, not in one shared place. A semantic model moves it out of the queries and into a single governed object. The metric, its filters, its time dimension, the join path and the grain are declared once, and every consumer compiles its SQL from that declaration.

On the left, each consumer carries its own logic. On the right, all three request the metric from one model.

The rest of this article covers what a semantic model contains, why raw schemas break LLM-generated SQL, the main types of semantic model, how each is consumed, and how to choose among them. The short rule is to pick the one that lives where your data and your queries already live, and to define every metric once.

What a semantic model is

A semantic model is a governed description of your data in business terms: entities, metrics, dimensions, relationships and rules. People write it once, and both humans and software read it. Think of it as the glossary and rulebook that sits between raw tables and everyone who asks questions of them.

The term has a second meaning in AI work: an embedding model that maps text to vectors so that similar meanings land close together. That powers semantic search over documents and is a separate topic. This article covers the analytics meaning.

What a semantic model encodes

A semantic model turns database structure into business meaning. It typically defines six kinds of things. The examples are illustrative.

The important property is that each definition exists once and every consumer shares it. A dashboard, a notebook and an LLM agent all compute net revenue the same way, because none of them redefines it.

Why raw schemas fail LLMs

The most dangerous failure of text-to-SQL is not an error message. It is a query that runs and returns a plausible, wrong number. The model may join tables incorrectly or misread a column’s meaning, and nothing sits between the question and the generated SQL to catch it.

Five causes recur in practice.

  • Ambiguous columns. status, amount and date mean different things in different tables. Which date is the order date, and which is the ship date?
  • Undefined metrics. “Revenue”, “active user” and “churn” each have several defensible definitions, and the schema holds none of them.
  • Hidden join paths. Several routes may connect two tables, and only one is correct for the question asked.
  • Fan-out and grain errors. Joining a one-to-many table before aggregating duplicates rows and inflates totals without any warning.
  • Implicit filters. Test accounts, cancelled orders and soft-deleted rows are excluded by convention, not by structure.

Better models help but cannot fully fix these, because the missing information is not in the schema. It lives in people’s heads and in old dashboards.

Types of semantic models

Semantic models differ mainly in where they live, because that decides who can use them and how portable they are. Six types cover most of what you will meet.

Read the picture from the bottom. Tables sit in the data platform, a semantic model of one of four kinds sits above them, and consumers ask for metrics by name.

Three notes on the table.

  • Warehouse-native objects are structured definitions. A Snowflake semantic view describes logical tables, relationships, facts, dimensions and metrics, and it can also carry verified queries and instructions for AI-generated SQL. A Databricks metric view separates measure definitions from dimensions, so the engine computes the right aggregation for whatever grouping a user asks for, and it can carry synonyms for AI accuracy.
  • OSI is about portability. It is a vendor-neutral, open-source format for datasets, metrics, dimensions and relationships, backed by several data and analytics vendors. Treat it as something to watch rather than something to depend on today.
  • Verification scope. The Snowflake, Databricks, Microsoft and OSI details were checked against current vendor documentation. The Looker, Cube, AtScale, code-defined and ontology rows describe the general design and were not benchmarked here. Product names and features change quickly, so confirm against current docs before choosing.
How semantic models are consumed

A semantic model is only useful when something reads it. Five consumption patterns are common, and one model can serve several of them at once.

All five patterns read the same model, and the model generates the SQL that the warehouse runs.

The fourth and fifth patterns are where semantic models matter most for AI. Fabric IQ, for example, answers questions over governed models while respecting role-based access and row-level security, so the assistant cannot see more than the user could. A later section walks through how an LLM consumes a model step by step.

Which semantic model to use when

Start from where your data lives and where your people already ask questions. The table maps common situations to a starting point.

Read the path from the top and stop at the first yes. It is a starting point, not a rule, because many teams combine types.

Four questions settle most choices.

  1. Where does the data live? Prefer a model that sits next to it.
  2. Where do people already ask questions? Prefer the tool they already use.
  3. Who owns the definitions? Prefer a home where that team can review and version them.
  4. What must be portable? If the answer is “everything”, favor an independent layer or an open format.

These types are not exclusive. A common arrangement is one metric layer for numbers plus an ontology for relationships between concepts.

Deep dive: consuming a semantic model from an LLM

The semantic model shrinks the LLM’s job from writing SQL to choosing from a menu of defined terms.

Questions the model describes flow left to right. Anything it does not describe stops at the semantic layer with an explicit refusal.

In a typical design, the LLM decomposes a question into the right combination of metrics and dimensions, and the semantic engine generates the SQL deterministically. If the model picks the right metric and dimensions, the query is correct, and it cannot return numbers that differ subtly from run to run. The trade-off is coverage: only questions the model describes can be answered.

A grounded pipeline has five stages.

  1. Interpret. The LLM maps the question to metrics, dimensions, filters and a time range, using the names, descriptions and synonyms in the model.
  2. Validate. The request is checked against the model. An unknown metric or an invalid combination is rejected.
  3. Compile. The semantic engine generates SQL using the defined joins, filters and grain.
  4. Execute and explain. The warehouse runs the query, and the answer comes back with the definitions that produced it.
  5. Fall back. If the question is not modeled, the system says so clearly and routes it to a guarded alternative or a person.
Worked example: one question, two routes

This example is illustrative. The tables, columns and definitions are invented. The question is “What was net revenue by region last quarter?”, asked in October 2026.

Route 1: raw schema. Given tables orders, refunds and customers, a model might plausibly write this.

SELECT c.region, SUM(o.amount) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.created_at >= '2026-07-01' AND o.created_at < '2026-10-01'
GROUP BY c.region;s

It runs and returns numbers, and it is wrong in four ways: it counts cancelled orders, includes tax, filters on creation date instead of ship date, and the join to refunds duplicates any order with more than one refund. It never subtracts a refund at all.

Route 2: semantic layer. The model defines net_revenue once: order amount excluding tax and cancelled orders, minus refunds, recognized on ship date. The LLM then only has to produce a structured request.

{
  "metrics": ["net_revenue"],
  "group_by": ["customer__region"],
  "time": { "grain": "quarter", "range": "2026-Q3" }
}

The engine compiles the correct SQL from the definition. The LLM had no opportunity to get the logic wrong, and every consumer of net_revenue gets the same number.

How to measure the impact on your own data

Accuracy depends on the dataset, the question set and the model, so measure the effect on your own data instead of borrowing someone else’s figure. A repeatable evaluation needs five things:

  1. Write a golden set of real questions with verified answers.
  2. Run each question several times, since consistency is part of trust.
  3. Score three outcomes separately: correct, wrong but plausible, and correctly declined.
  4. Track coverage, meaning the share of real questions the semantic model can answer.
  5. Record cost and latency alongside accuracy.
Pitfalls and design guidance
  • Coverage is the price of determinism. A semantic layer answers only what it models. Grow it from the questions people actually ask, using query logs and declined requests as the backlog.
  • Start small. Model the dozen metrics people argue about first.
  • Keep a fallback, and label it. For exploratory questions, guarded text-to-SQL is reasonable, but mark its answers as unverified. Prefer the semantic layer first and text-to-SQL second for ad hoc work.
  • Give every metric an owner. A definition nobody owns drifts, and drift brings back the inconsistency you built the layer to remove.
  • Version it. Metric changes alter historical numbers, so record when and why a definition changed.
  • Write good descriptions and synonyms. The LLM selects terms by reading them. Vague names produce wrong selections.
  • Do not model everything. An oversized model slows interpretation and invites the same ambiguity you are removing.
Takeaways
  1. A semantic model states what your data means once, in business terms, so people and LLMs share one definition instead of guessing.
  2. Six types exist: warehouse-native, BI-platform, code-defined, independent, ontology-based and interchange formats. They differ mainly in where they live.
  3. Choose by where your data lives and where your people already ask questions, then check who owns the definitions and what must be portable.
  4. Dashboards, SQL, APIs, built-in assistants and your own LLM agent can all consume the same model.
  5. For LLMs, a semantic layer fails loudly with a clear refusal, while raw-schema text-to-SQL can fail quietly with a plausible wrong number.
  6. Start with the dozen contested metrics, give each an owner, version every change, and measure on your own questions.

In the layered architecture described later in this series, the semantic model grounds what the system knows, and a decision model governs what it does next.

items.title: How Modern Web Guidance Helps Coding Agents Choose Browser APIs
items.summary: Illustration generated with AI. How to give an agent current browser guidance, with a Codex dialog refactor that uncovered a focus regression in WebKit. Modern Web Guidance is a skill from the Chrome team that gives coding agents a searchable library of web-platform guides and browser compatibility data. The team built it because agents can fall back on familiar JavaScript patterns even when HTML or CSS can handle the same job. The guides help an agent choose an API based on the browsers a project actually supports. Chrome announced the stable 1.0 release on November 10, 2026, with Firefox and Edge joining the project. Chrome’s release announcement To use it with a compatible agent such as Codex or Claude Code, run npx modern-web-guidance@latest install from your project directory. Record your browser requirements in the project’s agent instructions, such as AGENTS.md in Codex. You can name minimum browser versions or set a target like Baseline 2025, which covers features that became interoperable across major browsers by the end of that year. Installation and browser targets Then give the agent a concrete task, such as simplifying a settings dialog while preserving its keyboard behavior. The skill tells the agent to search for the relevant UI pattern and retrieve a guide before editing. The guide supplies implementation advice and helps the agent decide whether a feature needs a fallback for older browsers. How the guide library works Eight rewrites of one dialog Browser capture of the first guided version for current browsers, Playwright WebKit 27.2, November 12, 2026. What does access to those guides change in a refactor? The test started with a small notification-settings page. Its custom dialog used 46 nonblank lines of JavaScript to open and close the overlay, keep the background inactive, manage keyboard focus, and apply or discard a change. The task was to simplify the code while preserving those behaviors. Within each pair, two fresh Codex sessions got the same prompt, starting files, and browser requirements. Both ran GPT-5.6 Terra at low reasoning effort. One had Modern Web Guidance 1.0 installed. Two pairs targeted Safari 26.2 and newer and set a Baseline 2025 target. The other two required support back to Safari 18.4 and asked for a fallback or a supported alternative when an API was too new. The finished pages went through six scenarios in Chrome 157, Firefox 159, and Playwright WebKit 27.2. The older-target pages also had to pass in Playwright WebKit 18.4. These are specific test environments. The Safari versions describe project requirements, while the WebKit versions describe the test builds. Two guided sessions reached the outer time limit after writing their changes. Their saved pages went through the same checks. Every run chose a native . Codex reached for that element even with no guidance installed. The change showed up one step later, in how the button opened it. The browser takes over opening the dialog All four unguided versions called showModal() from JavaScript. The two guided versions for current browsers handed the opening action to the button itself. The button from the first guided run shows both attributes. commandfor="delivery-editor" command="show-modal">Edit delivery commandfor names the dialog by ID. command="show-modal" tells the browser what to do when the button is activated. The app still uses JavaScript to restore the saved form value on opening and apply a change on Save. The browser now handles the act of opening the modal. MDN’s Invoker Commands reference Author-created chart from the November 12, 2026 experiment. “Passed” means all six scenarios passed in the test environments for that pair. The focus regressions were observed in WebKit after opening by mouse. In the current-browser pairs, the guided code came in at 15 nonblank JavaScript lines each, compared with 20 and 21 without the guides. Those counts cover the entire rewrite, including changes to focus and form handling. Under the older-browser requirement, both guided versions kept showModal(). The difference shrank to one line in each pair. In an extra check outside the current-browser target, the buttons that relied on the HTML command did nothing in WebKit 18.4. Safari added support for those commands in 26.2. Browser support for Invoker Commands The opener and the previously focused element All four unguided versions passed all six scenarios in their test environments. One of the four guided versions did. All eight passed in Chrome and Firefox. In WebKit, three guided versions left focus off Edit delivery after a mouse opening followed by Escape, Cancel, or Save. One of those versions still used showModal(). The same symptom appeared with either way of opening the dialog. The effect was easy to reproduce in the first pair. Click Edit delivery , press Escape, then press Enter. In WebKit 27.2, both dialogs closed on Escape. Enter reopened the unguided version, where focus had returned to the button. The guided version stayed closed. Focus had landed on the page’s body. The dialog guide in version 1.0.0 advises against writing focus restoration code and says, “The browser returns it to the invoker.” The logs show all four guided sessions retrieved that guide. The reason Codex kept or removed any particular line remains unknown. Version 1.0.0 dialog guide The HTML Standard describes a more precise rule. When a modal opens, the browser records the element that was focused immediately beforehand and attempts to restore that focus when the modal closes. In Safari, clicking a button generally leaves it unfocused. The element that opened the dialog and the element that previously held focus can therefore be different. HTML Standard · MDN on clicking and focus The same generated page makes that difference visible. In the WebKit 27.2 probe, opening with Enter from the focused button and closing with Escape returned focus to the button. Opening with a mouse click and closing with Escape left body as the active element in the three affected versions. The passing guided version for the older target kept editSettings.focus() in its close handler. It gave the application an explicit destination for focus, as all four unguided versions did. For a pull request like this, make the expected behavior explicit. Open the modal with a click and with the keyboard. After Escape, Cancel, and Save, check that focus lands back on the opener in a browser the project supports. The button should still be ready for the user’s next Enter, even when HTML handled the opening. items.title: Trump's transportation chief demands $50 billion to prevent another huge FAA fiasco
items.summary: US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said that Congress needs to Homeland Security $50 billion to fix the matter at the root. Alex Wong/Getty Images Trump's transportation chief wants $50 billion to replace aging tech blamed for Friday ground stop. Markwayne Mullin and Sean Duffy cited old routers overloading for the repeated failures. Nationwide FAA halt delayed about 10,000 flights, and led to over 6,000 cancellations. The Department of Transportation says it wants $50 billion to replace aging technology that led to Friday's ground stop . In a press conference on Friday evening, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that the US has "old switches, old routers" that became overloaded with data and failed, disrupting communications at multiple air-route traffic-control centers. "We should talk to our senators and our members of Congress to say 'we don't deserve this, America,'" Duffy said. "This is the greatest country — by the way, with the greatest president — let's give the money to fix this very real problem." "How many times does this have to happen before Congress gives the money to fix it?" Duffy added. During the press conference, Duffy repeatedly said the administration needs $50 billion to replace the hardware and software that has been around since the 1980s. He added that the system can no longer handle the volume of data moving through it. "We need one complete system. We need someone to come in and build the whole system. Doing it — nickel-and-diming it together — does not work. This is what happens when that takes place, " Mullin said. On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration halted departures across the US as a safety precaution, while aircraft already in the air continued toward their destinations or were diverted as needed. US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said that Congress needs to Homeland Security $50 billion to fix the matter at the root.

Alex Wong/Getty Images

  • Trump's transportation chief wants $50 billion to replace aging tech blamed for Friday ground stop.
  • Markwayne Mullin and Sean Duffy cited old routers overloading for the repeated failures.
  • Nationwide FAA halt delayed about 10,000 flights, and led to over 6,000 cancellations.

The Department of Transportation says it wants $50 billion to replace aging technology that led to Friday's ground stop.

In a press conference on Friday evening, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that the US has "old switches, old routers" that became overloaded with data and failed, disrupting communications at multiple air-route traffic-control centers.

"We should talk to our senators and our members of Congress to say 'we don't deserve this, America,'" Duffy said. "This is the greatest country — by the way, with the greatest president — let's give the money to fix this very real problem."

"How many times does this have to happen before Congress gives the money to fix it?" Duffy added.

During the press conference, Duffy repeatedly said the administration needs $50 billion to replace the hardware and software that has been around since the 1980s. He added that the system can no longer handle the volume of data moving through it.

"We need one complete system. We need someone to come in and build the whole system. Doing it — nickel-and-diming it together — does not work. This is what happens when that takes place," Mullin said.

On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration halted departures across the US as a safety precaution, while aircraft already in the air continued toward their destinations or were diverted as needed.

The ground stop was lifted around 8:15 pm ET on Friday, but the disruption left airlines scrambling to reposition planes and crews. Roughly 10,000 flights were delayed and nearly 5,000 canceled, according to Business Insider's count.

The officials said they have seen no evidence that the failure was caused by a cyberattack or system failures linked to artificial intelligence, but added that they are still investigating the precise cause of the outage.

items.title: Photos show trouble at airports nationwide as FAA grounds all flights
items.summary: A passenger walks past a board displaying delayed flights at JFK International in New York City after the FAA issued a national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety" on Friday. Angelina Katsanis/Reuters Passengers are being taken off planes nationwide. The FAA ordered all planes grounded. The Transportation Secretary cited a "communications" issue at all air-traffic control centers. It's a bad night to be traveling. Passengers are being deplaned, and flights are delayed after the FAA grounded every flight nationwide because of what it called "extraordinary circumstances." Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the ground stop was ordered because of a "communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers." Officials have not yet said what caused the communication issue. As the ground stop became a multi-hour ordeal, passengers have begun to crowd boarding areas, have been asked to leave flights, and are scrambling to find their luggage. 'All flights have been halted' Passengers wait at McGhee Tyson Airport after the FAA issued a ground stop for all flights across the U.S. on Nov. 13. Adam Sparks/News Sentinel/Reuters Boarding areas began to fill up at airports across the country. On Friday afternoon, the FAA said in a post on X that there has been a temporary telecommunications outage. "Out of an abundance of caution, all flights have been halted," said the FAA. "Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis." The exact cause remains unclear A person stands in front of a departures board at Logan international airport after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety." Brian Snyder/Reuters Flight boards are flashing red and orange across all major airports. Transportation officials have not yet said why they issued the ground stop. The FAA is prepared to make a system update Passengers wait inside the main terminal after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety" following the agency's earlier report of serious air traffic control communications issues at Dulles International Airport, in Dulles, Virginia, US, November 13, 2026. REUTERS/Daniel Heuer Daniel Heuer/Reuters In some airports, stranded passengers are congregating in terminals as security check lines grow longer. The outage occurred the same day the FAA rolled out SMART , a new AI-powered tool designed to help manage air traffic. Air Space Intelligence, the company behind SMART, said Friday's disruption was not "based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC." Lines are growing in many airports Queues are forming at the Salt Lake City airport after passengers were told to disembark a flight to Chicago. Jon Lett Jon Lett, a passenger who was traveling from the Salt Lake City Airport to Kansas City, told Business Insider that everyone on his flight has been told to disembark and wait. Lett said that, though the mood among passengers remains "chill," there is no telling whether his flight will be able to depart anytime soon. Planes are parked on the tarmac Planes wait on the tarmac at Chicago O'Hare International Airport in Chicago, on November 13, 2026. KAMIL KRZACZYNSKI / AFP via Getty Images Photos show planes parked back-to-back at Chicago O'Hare International Airport. National ground stops are historically rare for the FAA. In January 2023, the FAA halted flights because of an outage involving its pilot alert system. Before that, nationwide air traffic was halted following the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. Traffic outside the airports also began to pile up Traffic piles up outside a terminal at Dulles International in Virginia after the FAA issued a national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety" on Friday. Daniel Heuer/Reuters Passengers are stranded Air travelers wait inside the Frederick W. Smith International Airport in Memphis after the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13, 2026. Chris Day / The Commercial Appeal/Reuters Some passengers are settling in and preparing for a night spent at the airport. Air travelers could be seen camping out on the floor and napping. Luggage is slow to appear People line up to try and retrieve luggage during delays and cancellations at LaGuardia airport on November 13, 2026 in the Queens borough of New York City. Adam Gray/Getty Images Lines to collect luggage are also growing in some airports. It is unclear whether they are arriving passengers or travelers giving up on their flight for the day. Travelers are left sitting in the plane People wait whilst onboard a plane at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, Washington, DC Brendan SMIALOWSKI / AFP via Getty Images Not everyone has been ordered to disembark. Photos showed some passengers sitting in unmoving planes. The FAA has not issued any updates Emmanuel Romero, relaxes on the ground as his daughters Arianne Romero, left, Hannah Romero, right, and wife, Alejandra Para, wait in the terminal at St. Louis Lambert International Airport to hear if their flight to California will be cancelled on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. The family's flight is affected by the nationwide ground stop the FAA issued to all flights Friday afternoon. The family was in Missouri to see Hannah graduate from her Advanced Individual Training (AIT) with the Army at Fort Leonard Wood. (Photo by David Carson/St. Louis Post-Dispatch via Getty Images) David Carson/St. Louis Post-Dispatch via Getty Images As of 8 p.m., the FAA has not issued any new updates on when the ground stop will end. Some exhausted passengers with canceled flights are lying down on the floor to rest. Read the original article on Business Insider
